> 2. **(Intermediate)** Run a container with `--restart on-failure` and the command `sh -c 'sleep 2; exit 1'`. Watch its state changes with `docker events` and read `RestartCount` from `docker inspect`.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A container shows `Exited (137)`. How do you tell whether it was killed by the OOM killer or by an operator?" *Hint:* look at `.State.OOMKilled`, `docker events`, and the kernel log (`dmesg`).

<a id="32-interacting-with-containers"></a>
### 3.2 Interacting with Containers

This section covers how to get into a container, get data and output out of it, and read its full configuration.

#### Interactive and Detached Modes

**Why there are modes.** Containers serve two very different purposes: long-running services (a web server that should run in the background) and interactive sessions (a shell, a REPL, a one-off command whose output you want to see). Docker controls how your terminal is connected to the container's main process with three flags: `-i`, `-t`, and `-d`.

**What the flags do**

| Flag | Meaning | Without it |
|---|---|---|
| `-i`, `--interactive` | Keep the container's STDIN open and connected to yours | The process gets no input (immediate EOF) |
| `-t`, `--tty` | Allocate a pseudo-terminal: prompts, colors, line editing, Ctrl+C as a terminal signal | Plain pipes; programs behave as when output is redirected |
| `-d`, `--detach` | Run in the background and return immediately | Foreground: your terminal is attached to the output |

**Common combinations**

| Command | Use case |
|---|---|
| `docker run -it alpine sh` | Interactive shell |
| `docker run -d nginx` | Background service |
| `docker run -dit alpine sh` | Background container with a shell you can attach to later |
| `docker run --rm -i alpine sort < file.txt` | Feed data through STDIN (no `-t`, because input is a file) |
| `docker run --rm alpine ls /` | Foreground one-shot command, output only |

**Detaching without stopping.** In a container started with `-it`, the key sequence **Ctrl+P, Ctrl+Q** detaches your terminal and leaves the container running. Ctrl+C or `exit` instead ends the main process, and therefore the container.

**TTY side effects.** With `-t`, stdout and stderr are merged into a single terminal stream, and output may contain carriage returns (`\r\n`) and color codes. In scripts and CI pipelines, omit `-t`: without a real terminal, Docker fails with `the input device is not a TTY`.

```text
   foreground (-it)                         detached (-d)
   +------------+   stdin/stdout   +-----+  +------------+                 +-----+
   | your shell |<================>| PID1|  | your shell |  (returns ID)   | PID1| --> logs stored by
   +------------+   via the CLI    +-----+  +------------+                 +-----+     the logging driver
```

**Example**

```bash
# Interactive shell; the container is removed when you exit
docker run --rm -it ubuntu:24.04 bash
# root@3a1f0c2b9d7e:/# cat /etc/os-release | head -n 2
# root@3a1f0c2b9d7e:/# exit

# Without -t: no prompt, but input still flows (-i)
docker run --rm -i alpine:3.20 sh <<'EOF'
echo "running a script from a heredoc"
uname -a
EOF

# Pipe data through a container
printf 'banana\napple\ncherry\n' | docker run --rm -i alpine:3.20 sort
# apple
# banana
# cherry

# Detach from an interactive container without stopping it
docker run -it --name shell alpine:3.20 sh
# / # (press Ctrl+P then Ctrl+Q)
docker ps --filter name=shell --format '{{.Status}}'   # Up 12 seconds
docker attach shell                                      # back at the prompt; type exit to end it

# -t in a non-interactive context
echo hi | docker run --rm -it alpine:3.20 cat
# the input device is not a TTY
```

**Key takeaways**

- `-i` connects STDIN, `-t` allocates a terminal, `-d` runs in the background.
- Use `-it` for shells, `-d` for services, `-i` alone for piping data, and no `-t` in scripts.
- Ctrl+P, Ctrl+Q detaches from an `-it` container; Ctrl+C or `exit` usually stops it.
- A TTY merges stdout and stderr and adds terminal formatting to the output.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run `docker run --rm alpine sh`, `docker run --rm -i alpine sh`, and `docker run --rm -it alpine sh`. Describe the behavior of each and explain it with the table above.
> 2. **(Beginner)** Start a Python REPL in a container (`python:3.13-slim`), detach with Ctrl+P, Ctrl+Q, reattach, and confirm a variable you defined is still there.
> 3. **(Intermediate)** Run `docker run --rm -t alpine sh -c 'echo out; echo err >&2' 2>/dev/null` with and without `-t`. Explain why stderr is not filtered out in one of the two cases.

#### docker exec

**Why exec exists.** Once a service is running, you often need to look inside: check a configuration file, query a database with its own client, test connectivity, or inspect running processes. Stopping the container to do so would interrupt the service. `docker exec` starts an *additional* process inside the already-running container, sharing all its namespaces, cgroups, and filesystem.

**How it relates to the main process**

```text
  container "web"  (same namespaces, same cgroup, same filesystem)
  +-----------------------------------------------------------+
  |  PID 1   nginx: master process       <- main process      |
  |  PID 30  nginx: worker process                            |
  |  PID 41  sh                          <- docker exec -it   |
  |  PID 47  ps aux                      <- run from that sh  |
  +-----------------------------------------------------------+
  If PID 1 exits, the container stops and every exec'd process is killed with it.
```

**Rules to remember**

- The container must be **running** (not created, exited, or paused).
- The exec'd process is not PID 1 and does not affect the container's lifecycle when it exits.
- It inherits the container's environment and default user and working directory, which you can override with `-e`, `-u`, and `-w`.
- It is not remembered: after a container restart, exec'd processes are gone.
- The program must exist in the image. Minimal images (distroless, `scratch`) often have no shell; see [docker debug](#docker-debug) for alternatives.

**Example**

```bash
docker run -d --name web nginx:1.27-alpine

# Interactive shell inside the running container
docker exec -it web sh
# / # ps
# PID   USER     TIME  COMMAND
#     1 root      0:00 nginx: master process nginx -g daemon off;
#    30 nginx     0:00 nginx: worker process
#    41 root      0:00 sh
#    47 root      0:00 ps
# / # exit                      <- ends only the shell; nginx keeps running

# One-off, non-interactive commands
docker exec web nginx -t                      # validate the configuration
docker exec web cat /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
docker exec web nginx -s reload               # apply configuration changes

# Override user, working directory, and environment for this process only
docker exec -u nginx -w /tmp -e DEBUG=1 web sh -c 'id; pwd; echo $DEBUG'
# uid=101(nginx) gid=101(nginx) groups=101(nginx)
# /tmp
# 1

# Use the database client shipped in the image
docker run -d --name db -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret postgres:16
docker exec -it db psql -U postgres -c 'select version();'

# Run in the background inside the container (-d)
docker exec -d web sh -c 'sleep 300'

# The program must exist in the image
docker exec -it web bash
# OCI runtime exec failed: exec failed: unable to start container process:
# exec: "bash": executable file not found in $PATH   <- alpine has sh, not bash
```

**Key takeaways**

- `docker exec` runs an extra process in a running container, sharing its namespaces and filesystem.
- Exiting an exec'd process never stops the container; the main process controls the lifecycle.
- Use `-it` for shells, plain `exec` for one-off commands, and `-u`, `-w`, `-e` to adjust the context.
- Only programs present in the image can be executed; minimal images may have no shell at all.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run a `redis:7` container and use `docker exec` with `redis-cli` to set and read a key, without ever opening a shell.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Exec into a running nginx container, change the default page, then restart the container with `docker restart`. Is your change still there? What about after `docker rm` and a new `docker run`? Explain both results.
> 3. **Interview question:** "How would you debug a running container whose image contains no shell and no debugging tools?" *Hint:* consider sharing namespaces from another container (`--pid container:NAME`, `--network container:NAME`), `nsenter` on the host, and `docker debug`.

#### docker attach

**Why attach exists.** `docker exec` starts a *new* process. Sometimes you want to connect to the *main* process itself: to see its live output, or to type into an interactive program you started earlier with `-dit` (a shell, a REPL, a game server console). `docker attach` connects your terminal to the main process's STDIN, STDOUT, and STDERR.

**attach versus exec**

| | `docker attach` | `docker exec` |
|---|---|---|
| Target | The existing main process (PID 1) | A new process |
| Input | Goes to PID 1's STDIN | Goes to the new process |
| Ctrl+C | Sent to PID 1, usually stopping the container | Ends only the new process |
| Multiple users | Everyone attached shares the same session | Each exec is independent |
| Typical use | Consoles of interactive programs, watching output | Debugging, admin commands |

**Detaching safely.** If the container was started with `-it`, use **Ctrl+P, Ctrl+Q** to detach. You can change the sequence with `--detach-keys`. If it was started without `-t`, the detach sequence does not work and Ctrl+C will forward `SIGINT` to the process; use `--sig-proxy=false` so Ctrl+C only detaches your client. For simply watching output, `docker logs -f` is safer.

**Example**

```bash
# A container whose main process is an interactive shell
docker run -dit --name console alpine:3.20 sh
docker attach console
# / # echo "typed into PID 1"
# typed into PID 1
# (Ctrl+P, Ctrl+Q)  -> detached, container still running
docker ps --filter name=console --format '{{.Status}}'      # Up ...

# Attach to a service just to watch output; Ctrl+C detaches without stopping it
docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27-alpine
docker attach --sig-proxy=false web
# (in another terminal: curl localhost:8080)
# 172.17.0.1 - - [14/Oct/2026:10:15:02 +0000] "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200 615 ...
# ^C   <- only the client detaches

# Custom detach keys (Ctrl+X then x)
docker attach --detach-keys='ctrl-x,x' console

# Attach without sending input (read-only view)
docker attach --no-stdin console
```

**Key takeaways**

- `docker attach` connects your terminal to the container's main process; it starts nothing new.
- Ctrl+C while attached can stop the container; Ctrl+P, Ctrl+Q detaches if a TTY was allocated.
- Use `--sig-proxy=false` or `docker logs -f` when you only want to watch output.
- Prefer `docker exec` for debugging and administration.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Start `python:3.13-slim` with `-dit` and the command `python`. Attach, define a variable, detach, attach again, and print the variable.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Open two terminals and attach both to the same `-dit alpine sh` container. Type in one and observe the other. Explain the result.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A colleague attached to a production container to watch logs and pressed Ctrl+C, which took the service down. Why, and what should they have used?" *Hint:* think about where the signal goes and the difference between attaching and streaming logs.

#### Copying Files with docker cp

**Why copy instead of mount.** Volumes and bind mounts (chapter 6) are the right tool for ongoing data sharing, but they must be set up when the container is created. For ad-hoc transfers, such as grabbing a crash dump, a generated report, or a log file, or pushing in a quick configuration fix for testing, `docker cp` copies files between the host and any container, even a stopped one.

**Syntax**

```text
 docker cp [OPTIONS] CONTAINER:SRC_PATH  DEST_PATH          container -> host
 docker cp [OPTIONS] SRC_PATH            CONTAINER:DEST_PATH host -> container
 docker cp [OPTIONS] CONTAINER:SRC_PATH  -                  container -> tar stream on stdout
 docker cp [OPTIONS] -                   CONTAINER:DEST_PATH tar stream on stdin -> container
```

**Path semantics** (they mirror `cp -R`):

| Source | Destination | Result |
|---|---|---|
| File | Existing directory | File copied into the directory |
| File | Non-existent path | File saved under that name |
| `dir` | Non-existent path | Directory created with that name and contents |
| `dir` | Existing directory | `dir` copied *inside* it (`dest/dir/...`) |
| `dir/.` | Existing directory | Only the *contents* of `dir` copied into it |

**Details that surprise people**

- Files copied *into* a container are owned by root (UID 0) by default; `-a` (archive) preserves the original UID/GID.
- Copies only touch the container's filesystem view; files under `/proc`, `/sys`, `/dev`, and tmpfs mounts cannot be copied this way. For those, run `tar` through `docker exec` instead.
- Files placed into a running container do not trigger anything: the application must reread them (for example `nginx -s reload`).
- Changes are made in the writable layer and are lost when the container is removed.

**Example**

```bash
docker run -d --name web nginx:1.27-alpine

# Container -> host
docker cp web:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf ./nginx.conf

# Host -> container, then reload
echo 'server_tokens off;' > hardening.conf
docker cp hardening.conf web:/etc/nginx/conf.d/hardening.conf
docker exec web nginx -s reload

# Directory contents only (note the trailing /.)
mkdir -p site && echo '<h1>new</h1>' > site/index.html
docker cp site/. web:/usr/share/nginx/html/

# Works on stopped containers: retrieve output after a job has finished
docker run --name report alpine:3.20 sh -c 'date > /tmp/report.txt'
docker cp report:/tmp/report.txt .
docker rm report

# Stream as tar: archive a directory straight from the container
docker cp web:/var/cache/nginx - | gzip > nginx-cache.tar.gz

# Preserve ownership when copying in
docker cp -a ./site web:/srv/site
```

**Key takeaways**

- `docker cp` copies in either direction and works on running and stopped containers.
- A trailing `/.` copies a directory's contents rather than the directory itself.
- Copied-in files are owned by root unless you use `-a`.
- For permanent or continuous data exchange use volumes or bind mounts instead.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Copy `/etc/os-release` out of `ubuntu:24.04`, `debian:12`, and `alpine:3.20` containers without starting any of them (hint: `docker create`).
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Copy a directory into a container twice, once as `dir` and once as `dir/.`, into an existing destination directory. Use `docker exec ... ls -R` to show the difference.
> 3. **(Intermediate)** Copy a file owned by your user into a container with and without `-a`, and compare the ownership shown by `ls -ln` inside the container.

#### Viewing Logs

**Why logs go to stdout.** Inside a container there is usually no syslog, no log rotation daemon, and no one logged in to read files under `/var/log`. Docker's convention is that the main process writes logs to **stdout and stderr**. Docker captures both streams through a **logging driver**, stores them (by default as JSON files on the host), and serves them via `docker logs`. This keeps logging uniform across all containers and lets you redirect logs elsewhere without changing the application.

```text
  app (PID 1) --stdout--> +---------------+     json-file / local  --> docker logs
              --stderr--> | dockerd       | --> journald           --> docker logs
                          | logging driver|     syslog, fluentd,   --> external system
                          +---------------+     awslogs, gelf, ...     (docker logs via dual-logging cache)
```

Only the main process's output is captured. A process started with `docker exec`, or an app that writes to files inside the container, does not appear in `docker logs`. Official images work around file-based apps by symlinking log files to the standard streams (nginx links `/var/log/nginx/access.log` to `/dev/stdout`).

**Useful options**

| Option | Effect |
|---|---|
| `-f`, `--follow` | Stream new output continuously |
| `--tail N` | Show only the last N lines (`all` by default) |
| `--since`, `--until` | Time window: relative (`10m`, `2h`) or timestamp (`2026-10-14T09:00:00`) |
| `-t`, `--timestamps` | Prefix each line with Docker's receive timestamp |
| `--details` | Show extra attributes added by the logging driver (`--log-opt labels=...`) |

**Retention.** Logs are kept until the container is removed. The default `json-file` driver does **not** rotate logs, so a chatty container can fill the disk. Configure `max-size`/`max-file` per container or globally in [daemon.json](#daemonjson-configuration); logging drivers and rotation are covered in [12.1 Logging](#121-logging).

**Example**

```bash
docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27-alpine
curl -s localhost:8080 >/dev/null; curl -s localhost:8080/missing >/dev/null

docker logs web                     # everything since the container was created
docker logs --tail 2 -t web         # last two lines with timestamps
# 2026-10-14T10:20:11.402Z 172.17.0.1 - - [...] "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200 615 ...
# 2026-10-14T10:20:11.987Z 172.17.0.1 - - [...] "GET /missing HTTP/1.1" 404 153 ...

docker logs -f --since 5m web       # follow, starting 5 minutes back (Ctrl+C stops following only)

# stdout and stderr are kept separate: redirect both before piping
docker logs web 2>&1 | grep -c ' 404 '

# Per-container rotation: at most 3 files of 10 MB each
docker run -d --name chatty --log-opt max-size=10m --log-opt max-file=3 \
  alpine:3.20 sh -c 'while true; do date; sleep 0.1; done'

# Where the log file lives (json-file driver)
docker inspect -f '{{.LogPath}}' chatty
# /var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/<id>-json.log

# Logs of a crashed container remain readable until it is removed
docker run --name crash alpine:3.20 sh -c 'echo starting; echo "fatal: no config" >&2; exit 1'
docker logs crash
# starting
# fatal: no config
```

**Key takeaways**

- Containers should log to stdout/stderr; Docker captures only the main process's streams.
- `docker logs` supports following, tailing, time windows, and timestamps.
- stderr is returned on stderr, so use `2>&1` before piping to `grep`.
- The default driver does not rotate logs; always configure `max-size` and `max-file`.
- Logs survive stop but are deleted with the container.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run a container that prints a line every second, and use `docker logs` to show only lines from the last 10 seconds, then only the last 5 lines with timestamps.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Run a container that writes its log to `/app/app.log` instead of stdout and observe that `docker logs` is empty. Fix it without changing the application (hint: a symlink, or `tail -F` as a second process).
> 3. **Interview question:** "A host's disk is full and `/var/lib/docker/containers` is the largest directory. What happened and how do you prevent it?" *Hint:* consider the default logging driver's behavior and where rotation is configured.

#### Inspecting Containers

**Why inspect.** `docker ps` shows a one-line summary. When you need the real answer to "which IP does this container have?", "what command did it actually run?", "which volume is mounted where?", or "why did it exit?", `docker inspect` returns the container's complete low-level configuration and state as JSON.

**Structure of the output.** The most useful top-level sections:

| Section | Contains |
|---|---|
| `State` | Status, PID, exit code, `OOMKilled`, start/finish times, health status |
| `Config` | What runs: image, `Cmd`, `Entrypoint`, `Env`, `User`, `WorkingDir`, `Labels`, exposed ports (image defaults merged with your flags) |
| `HostConfig` | How it runs: port bindings, restart policy, resource limits, capabilities, log config |
| `NetworkSettings` | Networks, IP addresses, gateways, MAC addresses, published ports |
| `Mounts` | Volumes, bind mounts, and tmpfs mounts with source and destination |
| Top level | `Id`, `Name`, `Created`, `Image` (ID), `LogPath`, `RestartCount`, `Platform` |

**Formatting with Go templates.** The `-f`/`--format` flag extracts fields using Go template syntax, so you do not need extra tools for simple queries. For complex queries, pipe the JSON to `jq`.

| Template | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `{{.State.Status}}` | Access a field |
| `{{json .Mounts}}` | Print a sub-object as JSON |
| `{{range .Config.Env}}{{println .}}{{end}}` | Iterate over a list |
| `{{index .Config.Labels "com.example.team"}}` | Look up a map key with special characters |
| `{{range $k, $v := .NetworkSettings.Networks}}{{$k}}={{$v.IPAddress}} {{end}}` | Iterate over a map |
| `{{join .Config.Cmd " "}}` | Join a list into a string |

**Example**

```bash
docker network create appnet
docker run -d --name web --network appnet -p 8080:80 \
  -e MODE=prod --label com.example.team=platform \
  -v webdata:/data nginx:1.27-alpine

docker inspect web | less                     # the full JSON document (an array with one element)

# Targeted queries
docker inspect -f '{{.State.Status}} since {{.State.StartedAt}}' web
docker inspect -f '{{range $net, $cfg := .NetworkSettings.Networks}}{{$net}}: {{$cfg.IPAddress}}{{"\n"}}{{end}}' web
# appnet: 172.19.0.2
docker inspect -f '{{json .HostConfig.PortBindings}}' web
# {"80/tcp":[{"HostIp":"","HostPort":"8080"}]}
docker inspect -f '{{range .Mounts}}{{.Type}} {{.Name}} -> {{.Destination}}{{"\n"}}{{end}}' web
# volume webdata -> /data
docker inspect -f '{{index .Config.Labels "com.example.team"}}' web
# platform
docker inspect -f '{{range .Config.Env}}{{println .}}{{end}}' web
# Prints MODE=prod together with the variables inherited from the image
# (PATH=..., NGINX_VERSION=..., ...)

# Complex queries with jq
docker inspect web | jq '.[0].HostConfig | {RestartPolicy, Memory, NanoCpus}'

# Inspect several containers at once
docker inspect -f '{{.Name}} {{.State.Status}}' $(docker ps -aq)

# Disambiguate when an image and a container share a name
docker inspect --type container web
```

`docker inspect` also works on images, volumes, networks, and other objects; `docker container inspect` restricts it to containers.

**Key takeaways**

- `docker inspect` returns the complete configuration and state of a container as JSON.
- `Config` describes *what* runs, `HostConfig` *how* it runs, `State` *what happened*.
- Use `-f` with Go templates for quick answers and `jq` for complex filtering.
- Per-network IP addresses are under `.NetworkSettings.Networks`, not at the top level.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Write a `docker inspect -f` command that prints the image, restart policy, and exit code of a container on one line.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Write a one-liner that lists every container (running or not) with its name and all of its mount destinations.
> 3. **Interview question:** "An environment variable you set with `-e` does not seem to take effect in the application. How do you verify what the container actually received?" *Hint:* compare `.Config.Env` in `docker inspect` with what the running process sees in `/proc/1/environ`, and think about entrypoint scripts that may overwrite values.

<a id="33-container-configuration"></a>
### 3.3 Container Configuration

This section covers the options that shape how a single container runs: its environment, network exposure, identity, resilience, user, and startup command.

#### Environment Variables

**Why environment variables.** The same image should run unchanged in development, staging, and production; only its configuration differs (database URL, log level, feature flags). Baking those values into the image would require a separate build per environment. The widely adopted convention (from the Twelve-Factor App methodology) is to pass configuration through **environment variables** when the container starts.

**Where a container's environment comes from**

```text
  image ENV (Dockerfile)          PATH=..., NGINX_VERSION=1.27.x
          |   overridden by
          v
  --env-file FILE                 values read from the file, in order
          |   overridden by
          v
  -e KEY=value / -e KEY           command-line values (later flags win)
          |
          v
  Config.Env  -->  environment of the main process (and inherited by docker exec)
```

**Ways to set variables**

| Syntax | Effect |
|---|---|
| `-e KEY=value` | Set an explicit value |
| `-e KEY` | Copy `KEY` from the host shell's environment (omitted if unset on the host) |
| `--env-file FILE` | Read `KEY=value` lines from a file |

**`--env-file` format rules.** One `KEY=value` per line; lines starting with `#` are comments; a line with only `KEY` copies the host value. Quotes are **not** removed and no variable expansion happens: `NAME="web"` sets the value to `"web"` including the quotes. (Compose `.env` files follow different rules; see [Environment and env_file](#environment-and-env_file).)

**Limits of environment variables**

- They are fixed at creation time; changing one requires recreating the container.
- They are visible to anyone who can run `docker inspect` and to every process in the container (`/proc/*/environ`), and they often leak into logs and crash reports. Do not use them for highly sensitive secrets; see [10.4 Secrets Management](#104-secrets-management).

**Example**

```bash
# Explicit values
docker run --rm -e APP_ENV=staging -e LOG_LEVEL=debug alpine:3.20 sh -c 'echo $APP_ENV $LOG_LEVEL'
# staging debug

# Pass through a host variable without writing its value on the command line
export API_TOKEN=abc123
docker run --rm -e API_TOKEN alpine:3.20 printenv API_TOKEN
# abc123

# Env file
cat > app.env <<'EOF'
# database settings
DB_HOST=db.internal
DB_PORT=5432
QUOTED="kept literally"
API_TOKEN
EOF
docker run --rm --env-file app.env alpine:3.20 sh -c 'echo "$DB_HOST:$DB_PORT [$QUOTED] $API_TOKEN"'
# db.internal:5432 ["kept literally"] abc123

# -e overrides the env file and the image
docker run --rm --env-file app.env -e DB_PORT=6543 alpine:3.20 printenv DB_PORT
# 6543

# Typical real use: configuring an official image
docker run -d --name db \
  -e POSTGRES_USER=app \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=change-me \
  -e POSTGRES_DB=appdb \
  postgres:16

# Everything set on the container is visible to anyone with Docker access
docker inspect -f '{{range .Config.Env}}{{println .}}{{end}}' db | grep PASSWORD
# POSTGRES_PASSWORD=change-me
```

**Key takeaways**

- Environment variables let one image serve many environments.
- Precedence: image `ENV` < `--env-file` < `-e`.
- `--env-file` takes values literally: no quote stripping, no expansion.
- Environment variables are readable through `docker inspect`; prefer secrets mechanisms for credentials.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run `mysql:8` with the minimum environment variables required by its documentation and connect with `docker exec ... mysql`.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Create an env file containing a quoted value, a comment, and a pass-through variable. Predict the output of `printenv` in the container, then verify.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why are environment variables considered a weak place for secrets, and what would you use instead?" *Hint:* list everywhere an environment variable is visible (inspect output, child processes, `/proc`, crash dumps) and compare with file-based secrets.

#### Port Publishing

**Why publish ports.** Each container has its own network namespace with its own IP address on a private Docker network. Services listening inside it are not reachable from outside the host (and on Docker Desktop, not even from the host itself). **Publishing** a port creates a mapping from a port on the host to a port in the container, so external clients can reach the service.

```text
   client --> host 203.0.113.10:8080 --+
                                       |  NAT rule (iptables/nftables) or docker-proxy
                                       v
                          container 172.17.0.2:80  (nginx listening on 0.0.0.0:80)
```

**Syntax variants**

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `-p 8080:80` | Host port 8080 on all interfaces to container port 80 (TCP) |
| `-p 127.0.0.1:8080:80` | Only reachable from the host itself |
| `-p 80` | Container port 80 to a random free host port |
| `-p 5353:53/udp` | UDP instead of TCP |
| `-p 8000-8005:8000-8005` | A range of ports |
| `-P` | Publish every port declared with `EXPOSE` in the image, each to a random host port |

**`EXPOSE` is documentation.** `EXPOSE 80` in a Dockerfile only records metadata (used by `-P` and shown by `docker ps`); it publishes nothing. Conversely, containers on the same user-defined network can reach each other on any port without publishing (see [7. Docker Networking](#7-docker-networking)).

**Pitfalls**

| Problem | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| "Connection reset" although the port is published | The app listens on `127.0.0.1` *inside* the container | Make it listen on `0.0.0.0` |
| `port is already allocated` / `address already in use` | Another container or host process uses that host port | Choose another host port |
| Service reachable from the internet despite a host firewall (ufw/firewalld) | Docker inserts its own NAT and forwarding rules ahead of many firewall frontends' rules | Bind to `127.0.0.1` or configure the `DOCKER-USER` chain |

**Example**

```bash
docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27-alpine
curl -sI localhost:8080 | head -n 1           # HTTP/1.1 200 OK

# Local-only binding: not reachable from other machines
docker run -d --name admin -p 127.0.0.1:9000:80 nginx:1.27-alpine

# Random host port, then discover it
docker run -d --name rnd -p 80 nginx:1.27-alpine
docker port rnd
# 80/tcp -> 0.0.0.0:32768
# 80/tcp -> [::]:32768
curl -sI "localhost:$(docker port rnd 80/tcp | head -n 1 | cut -d: -f2)" | head -n 1

# Publish everything the image EXPOSEs
docker run -d --name all -P nginx:1.27-alpine
docker ps --filter name=all --format '{{.Ports}}'
# 0.0.0.0:32769->80/tcp, [::]:32769->80/tcp

# Port conflict
docker run -d --name web2 -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27-alpine
# docker: Error response from daemon: ... Bind for 0.0.0.0:8080 failed: port is already allocated

# The classic loopback mistake: a server bound to 127.0.0.1 inside the container
docker run -d --name loop -p 8000:8000 python:3.13-slim python -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1
curl localhost:8000                           # curl: (56) Recv failure: Connection reset by peer
                                              # (or "Empty reply from server", depending on the setup)
docker rm -f loop
docker run -d --name loop -p 8000:8000 python:3.13-slim python -m http.server 8000 --bind 0.0.0.0
curl -sI localhost:8000 | head -n 1           # HTTP/1.0 200 OK
```

**Key takeaways**

- `-p HOST:CONTAINER` maps a host port to a container port; the default binds to all host interfaces.
- Prefix with `127.0.0.1:` for services that must not be exposed to the network.
- `EXPOSE` documents ports but publishes nothing; `-P` publishes exposed ports to random host ports.
- The application must listen on `0.0.0.0` inside the container to be reachable.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run two nginx containers published on host ports 8081 and 8082, and show different content in each using `docker cp`.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Publish a port bound to `127.0.0.1` and another bound to all interfaces. From a second machine (or another container using the host's IP), show which one is reachable.
> 3. **Interview question:** "You enabled ufw and denied port 5432, but your containerized PostgreSQL published with `-p 5432:5432` is still reachable from the internet. Why?" *Hint:* think about the order in which Docker's iptables rules and ufw's rules are evaluated, and where published traffic is redirected.

#### Naming Containers

**Why names matter.** Every container gets a 64-character hexadecimal ID, which is unique but impossible to remember. Names give containers a stable, human-readable identity that you can use in commands, scripts, and, on user-defined networks, as DNS hostnames for container-to-container communication.

**How names work**

| Aspect | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Default | Random `adjective_surname` name (`quirky_hopper`, `elated_turing`) |
| Custom | `--name web`; allowed characters `[a-zA-Z0-9][a-zA-Z0-9_.-]*` |
| Uniqueness | Unique per Docker daemon, including **stopped** containers |
| Renaming | `docker rename OLD NEW`, also while running |
| ID prefixes | Any unique prefix of the ID works (`docker stop 9f2c`) |
| DNS | On user-defined networks, the name resolves to the container's IP |
| Hostname | Separate from the name; defaults to the short ID; set with `--hostname` |

**Name conflicts.** Because stopped containers keep their names, re-running `docker run --name web ...` fails until the old container is removed. Scripts usually remove the old container first, or use `--rm` so the name is freed automatically. Compose generates names automatically (`project-service-1`), which is one reason it is preferred for multi-container setups.

**Example**

```bash
docker run -d nginx:1.27-alpine
docker ps --format '{{.ID}} {{.Names}}'
# 6c1d8e0f2a3b  festive_lovelace       <- generated name

docker run -d --name web nginx:1.27-alpine
docker run -d --name web nginx:1.27-alpine
# docker: Error response from daemon: Conflict. The container name "/web" is already in use
# by container "9f2c5e1a...". You have to remove (or rename) that container to be able to reuse that name.

# Idempotent "replace" pattern used in scripts
docker rm -f web 2>/dev/null || true
docker run -d --name web nginx:1.27-alpine

docker rename web web-old

# Names as DNS names on a user-defined network
docker network create shop
docker run -d --name api --network shop nginx:1.27-alpine
docker run --rm --network shop alpine:3.20 wget -qO- http://api | head -n 4

# Name versus hostname
docker run --rm --name n1 alpine:3.20 hostname                  # short container ID
docker run --rm --name n1 --hostname builder alpine:3.20 hostname   # builder
```

**Key takeaways**

- Names are unique per daemon, including stopped containers; remove or rename the old one to reuse a name.
- Names double as DNS hostnames on user-defined networks, but not on the default bridge.
- Hostname and container name are independent settings.
- Any unique ID prefix can be used instead of a name.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Start three containers without names, rename them to `one`, `two`, `three`, and stop them by name.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Show that `ping api` works from another container on a user-defined network but fails when both containers are on the default bridge network.
> 3. **(Intermediate)** Write a shell function `redeploy NAME IMAGE` that replaces a running container with a fresh one under the same name, and explain what happens if `docker run` fails halfway.

#### Restart Policies

**Why restart policies.** Processes crash, hosts reboot, and the Docker daemon gets upgraded. Without a policy, a container that stops stays stopped until someone notices. A **restart policy** tells the daemon to bring the container back automatically, which gives single-host deployments basic self-healing without a separate supervisor.

**The four policies**

| Policy | Restart when the process exits? | After `docker stop` | When the daemon (or host) restarts |
|---|---|---|---|
| `no` (default) | Never | Stays stopped | Stays stopped |
| `on-failure[:N]` | Only on non-zero exit code, at most N times | Stays stopped | Not restarted |
| `always` | Always, whatever the exit code | Stays stopped *until the daemon restarts* | Started |
| `unless-stopped` | Always, whatever the exit code | Stays stopped, permanently | Started, unless it was stopped manually |

**Backoff.** To avoid hammering a crashing app, the delay before each restart doubles, starting at 100 ms and capped at one minute. The delay resets after the container has run for at least 10 seconds. A container in a crash loop shows `Restarting (1) X seconds ago` in `docker ps`, and `RestartCount` grows in `docker inspect`.

**What policies do not do**

- They do not react to failed health checks: a standalone container that is `unhealthy` but still running is **not** restarted (Swarm and Kubernetes do that).
- They cannot be combined with `--rm`.
- They restart the *same* container; they never recreate it from a newer image.

**Choosing a policy**

| Workload | Suggested policy |
|---|---|
| Long-running service on a single host | `unless-stopped` |
| Service that must always come back, even after manual stops | `always` |
| Batch job that should retry on failure, but not forever | `on-failure:5` |
| Development, tests, one-off commands | `no` (often with `--rm`) |

**Example**

```bash
# A service that should survive crashes and reboots
docker run -d --name web --restart unless-stopped nginx:1.27-alpine

# A job that fails: retried up to 3 times, then left exited
docker run -d --name flaky --restart on-failure:3 alpine:3.20 sh -c 'echo try; exit 1'
sleep 5
docker inspect -f 'status={{.State.Status}} restarts={{.RestartCount}}' flaky
# status=exited restarts=3
docker logs flaky
# try
# try
# try
# try          <- initial run + 3 restarts

# A crash loop as seen by docker ps
docker run -d --name loop --restart always alpine:3.20 sh -c 'exit 1'
docker ps --filter name=loop --format '{{.Status}}'
# Restarting (1) 2 seconds ago

# Change the policy of an existing container
docker update --restart no loop && docker stop loop

# Read the policy
docker inspect -f '{{.HostConfig.RestartPolicy.Name}}:{{.HostConfig.RestartPolicy.MaximumRetryCount}}' flaky
# on-failure:3
```

**Key takeaways**

- Policies: `no`, `on-failure[:N]`, `always`, `unless-stopped`.
- `unless-stopped` respects manual stops across daemon restarts; `always` does not.
- Restarts use exponential backoff (100 ms doubling, max 1 minute).
- Restart policies react to process exit, not to health checks.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run one container with `always` and one with `unless-stopped`, stop both manually, restart the Docker daemon, and explain which one comes back.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Run a container that exits with code 0 after 2 seconds, once with `on-failure` and once with `always`. Predict and verify the `RestartCount` of each after 30 seconds.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your container is running but its health check reports `unhealthy`. Why doesn't the restart policy restart it, and what are your options?" *Hint:* consider what event the restart policy listens for, and what orchestrators or a small watchdog using `docker events` could do.

#### Working Directory and User

**Why override them.** Images set a default working directory (`WORKDIR`) and user (`USER`), but you often need different values at run time: running a build tool in a mounted project folder, running a command as a specific user so files it creates on a bind mount belong to you, or running as non-root for security even though the image defaults to root.

**Working directory: `-w` / `--workdir`.** Sets the directory the main process starts in. Relative paths in the command are resolved from there. If the directory does not exist, Docker creates it.

**User: `-u` / `--user`.**

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `-u appuser` | Name looked up in the container's `/etc/passwd`; fails if it does not exist |
| `-u 1000` | Numeric UID; works even if no such user exists in the image |
| `-u 1000:1000` | UID and GID |
| `-u "$(id -u):$(id -g)"` | Your own host UID/GID, common with bind mounts |
| `--group-add GROUP` | Add supplementary groups |

**Why the UID matters.** Without user namespace remapping, UID 0 inside the container is UID 0 on the host kernel. Its power is reduced by capabilities, seccomp, and namespaces, but a container escape as root is far more dangerous than as an unprivileged user. Files written to bind mounts are owned by the container's UID as seen by the host. Running as a numeric non-root UID addresses both concerns; see [Running as Non-Root](#running-as-non-root).

```text
  host                                       container (-u 1000:1000)
  /home/alice/project  (owner 1000:1000)  <-->  /src   process runs as uid 1000
  files created here are owned by alice            no "root-owned files" left behind
```

**Example**

```bash
# Default user and directory of an image
docker run --rm node:22-alpine sh -c 'id; pwd'
# uid=0(root) gid=0(root) ...
# /

# Run as the image's existing non-root user, in a chosen directory
docker run --rm -u node -w /home/node node:22-alpine sh -c 'id; pwd'
# uid=1000(node) gid=1000(node) ...
# /home/node

# A name that does not exist in the image fails
docker run --rm -u alice alpine:3.20 id
# docker: Error response from daemon: unable to find user alice: no matching entries in passwd file

# A numeric UID without a passwd entry works
docker run --rm -u 4242:4242 alpine:3.20 sh -c 'id; echo HOME=$HOME'
# uid=4242 gid=4242 groups=4242
# HOME=/

# Run a tool on your project as yourself, so outputs are owned by you
docker run --rm -u "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD":/src -w /src alpine:3.20 touch built.txt
ls -l built.txt          # owned by your user, not by root

# Same command without -u: the file belongs to root on the host
docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/src -w /src alpine:3.20 touch root-owned.txt
ls -l root-owned.txt     # -rw-r--r-- 1 root root ...

# The working directory is created if missing
docker run --rm -w /does/not/exist alpine:3.20 pwd   # /does/not/exist
```

**Key takeaways**

- `-w` sets (and creates if needed) the starting directory; `-u` sets the user and group.
- User names must exist in the image; numeric UIDs always work.
- Root in a container is root on the host kernel unless user namespaces are used.
- Use `-u "$(id -u):$(id -g)"` with bind mounts to avoid root-owned files on the host.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Check the default user of `nginx`, `postgres`, `node`, and `python` images with `docker run --rm IMAGE id` (or `docker image inspect -f '{{.Config.User}}'`). Which ones default to root?
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Run `npm init -y` in a bind-mounted directory with and without `-u "$(id -u):$(id -g)"`, and compare the ownership of the generated `package.json`. Explain any errors you see when running as your UID (hint: `HOME`).
> 3. **Interview question:** "If processes in a container run as root, does that mean they have root on the host?" *Hint:* distinguish UID mapping from capabilities, seccomp, and namespaces, and consider what changes with user namespace remapping or rootless Docker.

#### Entrypoint and Command Overrides

**Why there are two settings.** An image has to define what runs when a container starts, but users should still be able to adjust it. Docker splits the startup command into two parts: `ENTRYPOINT`, the fixed executable, and `CMD`, the default arguments (or the default command when there is no entrypoint). This allows images that behave like a tool (`docker run mytool --help`) as well as images that run a default service but accept a different command.

**How the final command is built**

```text
   final process = ENTRYPOINT + CMD

   image:   ENTRYPOINT ["docker-entrypoint.sh"]      CMD ["postgres"]
   run:     docker run postgres:16                   --> docker-entrypoint.sh postgres
   run:     docker run postgres:16 postgres -c log_statement=all
                                                     --> docker-entrypoint.sh postgres -c log_statement=all
   run:     docker run --entrypoint bash postgres:16 -c 'id'
                                                     --> bash -c id   (image CMD is discarded)
```

**Override rules**

| You provide | ENTRYPOINT used | CMD used |
|---|---|---|
| Nothing | Image's | Image's |
| Arguments after the image name | Image's | Your arguments |
| `--entrypoint X` | `X` | **Empty** (image CMD is cleared) unless you add arguments |
| `--entrypoint X` + arguments | `X` | Your arguments |
| `--entrypoint ""` | None | Your arguments become the full command |

**Rules to remember**

- `--entrypoint` takes a single executable; its arguments go after the image name.
- Many official images use an entrypoint *script* that performs setup (create a database, fix permissions) and then runs `exec "$@"` with the CMD. Overriding the entrypoint skips that setup.
- How shell form versus exec form affects signal handling is covered in [Shell vs Exec Form](#shell-vs-exec-form).

**Example**

```bash
# What does an image run by default?
docker image inspect -f 'EP={{json .Config.Entrypoint}} CMD={{json .Config.Cmd}}' nginx:1.27-alpine
# EP=["/docker-entrypoint.sh"] CMD=["nginx","-g","daemon off;"]
docker image inspect -f 'EP={{json .Config.Entrypoint}} CMD={{json .Config.Cmd}}' alpine:3.20
# EP=null CMD=["/bin/sh"]

# Replace CMD: arguments after the image name
docker run --rm nginx:1.27-alpine nginx -v
# /docker-entrypoint.sh: ... (entrypoint setup messages)
# nginx version: nginx/1.27.x

# Replace ENTRYPOINT to get a shell, a common debugging trick
docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh nginx:1.27-alpine
# / #   <- no nginx started, no entrypoint script ran

# --entrypoint with arguments: the arguments follow the image
docker run --rm --entrypoint ls nginx:1.27-alpine -la /etc/nginx

# A tool-style image: ENTRYPOINT is the tool, CMD is the default argument
cat > Dockerfile <<'EOF'
FROM alpine:3.20
ENTRYPOINT ["ping", "-c", "3"]
CMD ["localhost"]
EOF
docker build -q -t pinger .
docker run --rm pinger                  # ping -c 3 localhost
docker run --rm pinger 1.1.1.1          # ping -c 3 1.1.1.1    (CMD replaced)
docker run --rm --entrypoint echo pinger hi   # echo hi        (both replaced)
```

**Key takeaways**

- The container runs `ENTRYPOINT + CMD`.
- Arguments after the image name replace `CMD`; `--entrypoint` replaces `ENTRYPOINT` and clears `CMD`.
- `docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh IMAGE` is the standard way to explore an image.
- Overriding an entrypoint script skips the initialization it would normally perform.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Inspect the entrypoint and command of `redis:7`, `python:3.13-slim`, and `postgres:16`, and predict what runs for `docker run IMAGE` and `docker run IMAGE bash`.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Run `postgres:16` with `--entrypoint postgres` (plus required arguments) and compare its startup with the default. Explain what the skipped entrypoint script normally does.
> 3. **Interview question:** "When would you put the executable in `ENTRYPOINT` instead of `CMD`, and what does that change for users of the image?" *Hint:* think about tool-style images, how arguments are appended, and how hard it is to override each one.

<a id="34-monitoring-and-housekeeping"></a>
### 3.4 Monitoring and Housekeeping

This section covers the built-in tools for seeing what is running and what it consumes, and for reclaiming the disk space Docker accumulates over time.

#### docker ps and Filtering

**Why filtering matters.** On a developer laptop or a busy server, dozens or hundreds of containers (many of them stopped) can exist at once. `docker ps` lists them, and its filtering and formatting options turn it into a query tool that scripts can rely on, for example "IDs of all exited containers from this image" or "every unhealthy container".

**Core options**

| Option | Effect |
|---|---|
| (none) | Running containers only |
| `-a`, `--all` | Include stopped, created, and dead containers |
| `-q`, `--quiet` | Print only IDs (ideal for piping into other commands) |
| `-l`, `--latest` / `-n N` | The most recently created container / the last N |
| `-s`, `--size` | Add writable-layer size (and virtual size including the image) |
| `--no-trunc` | Do not shorten IDs and commands |
| `-f`, `--filter KEY=VALUE` | Filter (repeatable) |
| `--format TEMPLATE` | Custom output with Go templates; prefix with `table` for aligned columns |

**Filters**

| Filter | Example | Matches |
|---|---|---|
| `status` | `status=exited` | `created`, `running`, `paused`, `restarting`, `exited`, `removing`, `dead` |
| `exited` | `exited=137` | Exit code |
| `name` | `name=web` | Part of the name (`name=^web$` for an exact match) |
| `ancestor` | `ancestor=nginx` | Containers created from an image or its descendants |
| `label` | `label=env=prod` | Label key, or key and value |
| `health` | `health=unhealthy` | `starting`, `healthy`, `unhealthy`, `none` |
| `network`, `volume` | `network=shop` | Attached network or mounted volume |
| `publish`, `expose` | `publish=8080` | Published or exposed port |
| `before`, `since` | `since=web` | Created before/after a given container |

Repeating the **same** filter key combines values with OR; **different** keys are combined with AND.

**Formatting placeholders.** `.ID`, `.Names`, `.Image`, `.Command`, `.CreatedAt`, `.RunningFor`, `.Status`, `.State`, `.Ports`, `.Size`, `.Labels`, `.Label "key"`, `.Mounts`, `.Networks`. A default format can be saved as `"psFormat"` in `~/.docker/config.json`.

**Example**

```bash
docker ps -a --filter status=exited --filter status=created   # exited OR created
docker ps --filter ancestor=nginx --filter publish=8080        # nginx AND publishing 8080
docker ps -a --filter exited=137                               # killed by SIGKILL (often OOM)
docker ps --filter health=unhealthy
docker ps --filter 'name=^web$'                                # exact name, not "web-old"

# Custom table
docker ps -a --format 'table {{.Names}}\t{{.Image}}\t{{.State}}\t{{.Status}}\t{{.Ports}}'
# NAMES   IMAGE               STATE     STATUS                     PORTS
# web     nginx:1.27-alpine   running   Up 2 hours                 0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp
# job     alpine:3.20         exited    Exited (1) 3 minutes ago

# Machine-readable output for scripts
docker ps -a --format '{{json .}}' | jq -r 'select(.State=="exited") | .Names'

# IDs feeding into other commands
docker ps -aq --filter status=exited | xargs -r docker rm
docker stop $(docker ps -q --filter label=env=dev)

# Size of each container's writable layer
docker ps -s --format 'table {{.Names}}\t{{.Size}}'
# NAMES   SIZE
# web     1.09kB (virtual 47.9MB)

# Persistent default format (merge into ~/.docker/config.json)
# { "psFormat": "table {{.Names}}\t{{.Image}}\t{{.Status}}\t{{.Ports}}" }
```

**Key takeaways**

- `docker ps` shows running containers; add `-a` for all.
- Same filter keys are OR-ed, different keys are AND-ed.
- `-q` plus filters is the standard building block for bulk operations.
- `--format` with `table` or `json` makes output readable for humans or scripts.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** List all containers created from `alpine` images that exited with a non-zero code, showing name, exit status, and age.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Label a few containers with `env=dev` and `env=test`, then stop all `dev` containers and remove all stopped `test` containers using only `docker ps` filters and pipes.
> 3. **(Intermediate)** Configure a `psFormat` in your Docker config file that shows name, image, state, and ports, and verify that `docker ps` uses it by default.

#### docker stats

**Why live statistics.** When a host slows down, the first question is "which container is using the CPU, memory, network, or disk?" `docker stats` shows live resource usage per container, read directly from each container's cgroup, without installing any monitoring stack.

**Columns**

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `CPU %` | Share of host CPU; 100% equals one full core, so 250% means two and a half cores |
| `MEM USAGE / LIMIT` | Memory in use (page cache that can be reclaimed is excluded) / the container's limit, or total host memory if none is set |
| `MEM %` | Usage relative to the limit |
| `NET I/O` | Bytes received / sent on the container's network interfaces |
| `BLOCK I/O` | Bytes read / written to block devices |
| `PIDS` | Number of processes and threads |

By default it refreshes continuously for running containers. `--no-stream` prints one snapshot (useful in scripts), `-a` includes stopped containers, and `--format` selects columns (`.Name`, `.CPUPerc`, `.MemUsage`, `.MemPerc`, `.NetIO`, `.BlockIO`, `.PIDs`).

**Limits of `docker stats`.** It shows only the present moment: no history, no alerts, no graphs. For trends and alerting, export the same cgroup metrics with tools such as cAdvisor and Prometheus (see [12.2 Monitoring](#122-monitoring)).

**Example**

```bash
docker run -d --name web --memory 128m nginx:1.27-alpine
docker run -d --name busy alpine:3.20 sh -c 'while :; do :; done'   # burns one CPU core

docker stats
# CONTAINER ID   NAME   CPU %     MEM USAGE / LIMIT     MEM %   NET I/O       BLOCK I/O    PIDS
# 7a1c...        busy   99.87%    412KiB / 15.5GiB      0.00%   1.1kB / 0B    0B / 0B      1
# 3f2b...        web    0.00%     3.2MiB / 128MiB       2.50%   1.3kB / 0B    0B / 4.1kB   9
#                                       ^ explicit limit vs. ^ host memory (no limit set)

# Single snapshot, chosen columns, sorted by memory usage
docker stats --no-stream --format '{{.MemPerc}}\t{{.Name}}\t{{.MemUsage}}' | sort -rn

# Watch specific containers only
docker stats web busy

docker rm -f busy
```

**Key takeaways**

- `docker stats` shows live CPU, memory, network, disk I/O, and process counts per container.
- CPU % is relative to one core; values above 100% are normal on multi-core hosts.
- The memory limit column shows host memory when no limit is set.
- Use `--no-stream` and `--format` in scripts; use a monitoring stack for history and alerting.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Start a container that writes a 500 MB file to its filesystem (`dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/f bs=1M count=500`) and watch the `BLOCK I/O` and `MEM USAGE` columns.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Run a CPU-bound container with `--cpus 0.5` and another without limits. Compare their `CPU %` and explain the numbers.
> 3. **Interview question:** "`docker stats` shows a container at 95% of its memory limit, but the application reports using much less. What could explain the difference?" *Hint:* think about what counts as container memory in cgroups (kernel memory, page cache, tmpfs) and what the application measures.

#### docker top

**Why top for containers.** `docker exec CONTAINER ps` only works if the image contains `ps`, and it shows PIDs and users as seen *inside* the container. `docker top` asks the host's `ps` to list the processes belonging to the container, so it works for any image (even distroless) and shows the **host's view**: real PIDs and real UIDs, which is what you need to correlate with host tools, `kill`, or kernel logs.

**Inside versus outside view**

```text
   docker exec web ps                 docker top web
   (container PID namespace)          (host PID namespace)
   PID  USER   COMMAND                UID   PID     PPID    CMD
   1    root   nginx: master          root  48211   48190   nginx: master process ...
   30   nginx  nginx: worker          101   48263   48211   nginx: worker process
                                            ^ real host PIDs; 101 is the nginx UID
                                              (host has no name for it)
```

**Syntax.** `docker top CONTAINER [ps OPTIONS]`. Any `ps` options can be passed, as long as the output keeps a `PID` column, which Docker uses to select the container's processes.

**Example**

```bash
docker run -d --name web nginx:1.27-alpine

docker top web
# UID    PID     PPID    C   STIME   TTY   TIME       CMD
# root   48211   48190   0   10:31   ?     00:00:00   nginx: master process nginx -g daemon off;
# 101    48263   48211   0   10:31   ?     00:00:00   nginx: worker process

# Custom ps columns (must include pid)
docker top web -o pid,ppid,user,rss,args
# PID     PPID    USER   RSS    COMMAND
# 48211   48190   root   7800   nginx: master process nginx -g daemon off;
# 48263   48211   101    3200   nginx: worker process

# Works even when the image has no shell and no ps (the pause image contains a single binary)
docker run -d --name tiny registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10
docker exec tiny ps
# OCI runtime exec failed: ... exec: "ps": executable file not found in $PATH
docker top tiny
# UID      PID     PPID    C   STIME   TTY   TIME       CMD
# 65535    49102   49080   0   10:33   ?     00:00:00   /pause

# The host PID can be used with host tools
sudo ls -l /proc/48211/ns | head -n 3      # namespaces of the container's PID 1
```

**Key takeaways**

- `docker top` lists a container's processes using the host's `ps`, so it works for every image.
- It shows host PIDs and host UIDs, unlike `ps` run inside the container.
- Extra `ps` options are allowed as long as a `PID` column remains.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run `postgres:16`, compare `docker top` with `docker exec ... ps aux` (install `procps` if needed), and map each container PID to its host PID.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Start a container with `-u 4242`, then find its process with `ps -u 4242` on the host. Explain why the user column shows a number instead of a name.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why can the same process have two different PIDs, and which one would you pass to `kill` on the host?" *Hint:* think about nested PID namespaces and which namespace your shell belongs to.

#### docker events

**Why an event stream.** Many questions are about *when* and *in what order* things happened: "Why did this container restart at 3 a.m.?", "Who removed that volume?", "Is a service crash-looping?". `docker events` streams everything the daemon does in real time and can also replay recent history, which makes it useful both for debugging and as a trigger for automation.

**What it reports**

| Object type | Example actions |
|---|---|
| `container` | `create`, `start`, `die`, `stop`, `kill`, `oom`, `restart`, `pause`, `destroy`, `exec_start`, `health_status` |
| `image` | `pull`, `tag`, `untag`, `delete`, `push` |
| `volume` | `create`, `mount`, `unmount`, `destroy` |
| `network` | `create`, `connect`, `disconnect`, `destroy` |
| `daemon` | `reload` |

**Options**

| Option | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--since`, `--until` | Replay past events (relative like `30m` or timestamps); with `--until`, the command exits instead of streaming |
| `-f`, `--filter` | `type=`, `event=`, `container=`, `image=`, `label=`, `network=`, `volume=` |
| `--format` | Go template over `.Type`, `.Action`, `.Actor.ID`, `.Actor.Attributes`, `.Time`; `{{json .}}` for full objects |

The daemon keeps only a limited buffer of recent events in memory (the last 1000), so it is not a long-term audit log; ship events to a logging system if you need history.

**Example**

```bash
# Terminal 1: watch container lifecycle events
docker events --filter type=container \
  --format '{{.Time}} {{.Action}} {{.Actor.Attributes.name}} {{.Actor.Attributes.exitCode}}'

# Terminal 2
docker run --rm --name demo alpine:3.20 sh -c 'exit 3'

# Terminal 1 output (Unix timestamps, then action, name, exit code)
# 1792058461 create demo
# 1792058461 attach demo
# 1792058461 start demo
# 1792058461 die demo 3
# 1792058461 destroy demo

# What happened in the last hour? (exits instead of streaming)
docker events --since 1h --until 0s --filter event=die --filter event=oom

# Detect a crash loop: many die/start pairs for the same container
docker events --since 10m --until 0s --filter container=web --filter event=die | wc -l

# Simple automation: react to every container death
docker events --filter event=die --format '{{json .}}' | while read -r ev; do
  name=$(jq -r '.Actor.Attributes.name' <<<"$ev")
  code=$(jq -r '.Actor.Attributes.exitCode' <<<"$ev")
  [ "$code" != "0" ] && echo "ALERT: $name exited with $code"
done
```

**Key takeaways**

- `docker events` streams daemon activity for containers, images, volumes, networks, and the daemon.
- `--since`/`--until` replays recent history; filters narrow the stream by type, action, or object.
- It is ideal for diagnosing restarts, OOM kills, and crash loops, and for lightweight automation.
- The in-memory history is short; export events if you need an audit trail.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run `docker events` while pulling an image, creating a volume, and creating a network. List every event type and action you observe.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Add a health check to a container (`--health-cmd 'exit 1' --health-interval 5s`) and capture the `health_status` events. Write a filter that shows only those.
> 3. **Interview question:** "How would you get notified within seconds whenever any container on a host is killed by the OOM killer, without installing a monitoring stack?" *Hint:* combine an event filter with a small long-running script, and think about how it should survive daemon restarts.

#### Pruning Unused Resources

**Why pruning is needed.** Docker almost never deletes anything on its own. Every build leaves intermediate images and cache, every `docker run` without `--rm` leaves a stopped container, every image update leaves the old version behind as a dangling image, and every removed container may leave an anonymous volume. On a development machine or CI runner this easily grows to tens of gigabytes. The `prune` commands remove these unused objects in bulk.

**What each prune command removes**

| Command | Removes by default | Wider scope option |
|---|---|---|
| `docker container prune` | All stopped containers | |
| `docker image prune` | Dangling images (untagged, unreferenced: `<none>:<none>`) | `-a`: every image not used by a container |
| `docker volume prune` | Unused **anonymous** volumes | `-a`: also unused **named** volumes |
| `docker network prune` | Custom networks not used by any container | |
| `docker builder prune` | Dangling build cache | `-a`: all build cache |
| `docker system prune` | Stopped containers, unused networks, dangling images, dangling build cache | `-a`: all unused images and build cache; `--volumes`: also unused anonymous volumes |

**Filters.** `--filter until=24h` keeps recent objects (not available for volumes), and `--filter label=...` / `label!=...` targets or protects objects by label. `-f` skips the confirmation prompt.

**Danger zone.** "Unused" means "not referenced by an existing container", not "unimportant". A database volume whose container you removed a minute ago is unused. Image pruning with `-a` will force the next deployment or offline start to pull everything again. Prefer targeted prunes with filters on servers, and protect important objects with labels.

**Example**

```bash
docker system df                         # see what is reclaimable first (next topic)

docker container prune -f
# Deleted Containers:
# 7a1c...
# Total reclaimed space: 12.4MB

docker image prune                       # dangling only, asks for confirmation
docker image prune -a --filter until=168h   # unused images older than 7 days

# Volumes: anonymous only by default
docker volume prune
docker volume prune -a --filter label!=keep=true   # unused named volumes too, except protected ones

docker builder prune --filter until=72h

# Everything at once (common on CI runners)
docker system prune -af --filter until=24h

# Protect a resource with a label, then exclude it
docker volume create --label keep=true pgdata
docker volume prune -af --filter label!=keep=true  # pgdata survives
```

**Key takeaways**

- Docker accumulates stopped containers, dangling images, unused volumes, networks, and build cache.
- Each object type has its own `prune`; `docker system prune` combines most of them.
- Volume pruning removes only anonymous volumes unless you add `-a`.
- "Unused" is not "safe to delete": use filters and labels on servers, and check `docker system df` first.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run `docker system df`, then `docker system prune`, then `docker system df` again. Record how much space was reclaimed per object type.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Create one anonymous volume, one named volume, and one named volume with `keep=true`, remove all containers, and design a single prune command that deletes only the first two.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Design a cleanup policy for a shared CI runner that keeps builds fast but never runs out of disk." *Hint:* balance build cache retention against disk usage using `until` filters, scheduled jobs, and BuildKit's own garbage collection settings.

#### Disk Usage with docker system df

**Why measure first.** Before deleting anything, you need to know where the space is going. Running `du` on `/var/lib/docker` gives confusing results because image layers are shared between images and overlay mounts are counted multiple times. `docker system df` reports Docker's own accounting, per object type, and estimates how much could be reclaimed.

**Reading the output**

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `TYPE` | Images, Containers (writable layers), Local Volumes, Build Cache |
| `TOTAL` | Number of objects |
| `ACTIVE` | Objects in use (images used by containers, volumes mounted by containers, running containers) |
| `SIZE` | Disk space used, counting shared image layers only once |
| `RECLAIMABLE` | Space that pruning could free (objects not in use) |

`-v` (verbose) breaks the totals down per image, container, volume, and cache entry. For images it shows `SHARED SIZE` (layers shared with other images) and `UNIQUE SIZE` (what removing that image alone would free), which is the number that matters when deciding what to delete.

**What it does not include.** Container log files (under `/var/lib/docker/containers/`) are not part of these numbers; check them separately with `du` or by configuring log rotation. On Docker Desktop, the data lives inside a VM disk image, and the space freed inside the VM may not immediately be returned to the host's filesystem.

**Example**

```bash
docker system df
# TYPE            TOTAL     ACTIVE    SIZE      RECLAIMABLE
# Images          14        3         3.12GB    2.41GB (77%)
# Containers      6         2         84.2MB    84.1MB (99%)
# Local Volumes   5         1         1.37GB    968MB (70%)
# Build Cache     52        0         1.9GB     1.9GB

docker system df -v
# Images space usage:
# REPOSITORY  TAG          IMAGE ID      CREATED      SIZE     SHARED SIZE  UNIQUE SIZE  CONTAINERS
# postgres    16           a1b2c3d4e5f6  2 weeks ago  453MB    74.8MB       378MB        1
# python      3.13-slim    0f9e8d7c6b5a  3 weeks ago  124MB    74.8MB       49.6MB       0
# ...
# Containers space usage:
# CONTAINER ID  IMAGE        COMMAND    LOCAL VOLUMES  SIZE     CREATED      STATUS      NAMES
# 9a8b...       alpine:3.20  "sh -c…"   0              84MB     1 hour ago   Exited (0)  bigwriter
# ...
# Local Volumes space usage:
# VOLUME NAME   LINKS   SIZE
# pgdata        1       398MB
# ...

# Per-type structured output for scripts
docker system df --format '{{.Type}}: {{.Size}} ({{.Reclaimable}} reclaimable)'

# Logs are not included: measure them separately
sudo du -sh /var/lib/docker/containers/*/*-json.log 2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail -n 3
```

**Key takeaways**

- `docker system df` shows space used per object type, counting shared layers once.
- `RECLAIMABLE` is what pruning unused objects would free; check it before pruning.
- `-v` shows per-object detail, including the unique size of each image.
- Container logs are not counted; monitor and rotate them separately.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run a container that writes a 100 MB file into its filesystem, stop it, and find it in `docker system df -v`. Then remove it and confirm the change.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Pull three images that share a base (for example `python:3.13-slim`, `python:3.12-slim`, and `debian:12-slim`). Use `docker system df -v` to explain why the sum of `SIZE` values exceeds the total reported for images.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A server's disk is filling up, but `docker system df` shows little reclaimable space. Where else would you look?" *Hint:* consider container logs, data written into containers' writable layers by running containers, volumes in use, and files outside Docker's accounting.

---

<a id="4-docker-images"></a>
## 4. Docker Images

Images are the unit of distribution in Docker: everything a container needs to run is packaged into an image, shipped through a registry, and unpacked on the target machine. This chapter looks at what an image actually is (layers, copy-on-write, tags, digests, base images), how to manage images on a host (tagging, removing, inspecting, moving them without a registry), and how registries store and serve them. Understanding images well is the foundation for writing good Dockerfiles in [chapter 5](#5-building-images-with-dockerfiles) and for securing your supply chain in [chapter 10](#10-docker-security).

<a id="41-image-fundamentals"></a>
### 4.1 Image Fundamentals

This section explains how an image is structured and identified, and how it gets onto your machine.

#### Image Layers

**Why layers exist.** Imagine shipping ten applications that all run on the same Debian base. If each image were one big monolithic archive, every host would download and store ten copies of Debian. Layers solve this: an image is split into a stack of independent filesystem archives, so the Debian part is stored and transferred only once and reused by every image built on it. Layers also make builds incremental, because a step that has not changed can reuse its previous layer.

**Analogy.** Think of an image as a lasagna. Each layer is added on top of the previous one and only contains what that step added (pasta, sauce, cheese). Two lasagnas with the same bottom three layers can literally share them, as long as nobody modifies a shared layer, which is guaranteed because layers are read-only.

**What a layer is.** A layer is a tar archive containing the *differences* a single build step made to the filesystem: files added, files modified, and whiteout markers for files deleted (see [Union File Systems](#union-file-systems)). In a Dockerfile, only instructions that change files (`RUN`, `COPY`, `ADD`) create layers; instructions such as `ENV`, `CMD`, `EXPOSE`, or `LABEL` only change the image config and produce a zero-byte history entry.

```text
 Dockerfile                          Resulting image
 ---------------------------         ------------------------------------------
 FROM python:3.13-slim        --->   layers 1..4: inherited from python:3.13-slim
 WORKDIR /app                 --->   layer 5: empty /app directory
 COPY requirements.txt .      --->   layer 6: requirements.txt            (1 KB)
 RUN pip install -r ...       --->   layer 7: site-packages               (45 MB)
 COPY . .                     --->   layer 8: application source          (300 KB)
 ENV PORT=8000                --->   config only (no layer)
 CMD ["python", "app.py"]     --->   config only (no layer)

 Stack seen by a container (bottom = oldest):

   +-----------------------------+
   | 8  app source               |  changes on every commit
   | 7  pip packages             |  changes when requirements change
   | 6  requirements.txt         |
   | 5  /app                     |
   | 1-4 python + debian slim    |  shared with every python:3.13-slim image
   +-----------------------------+
```

**Three identifiers per layer.** The same layer is referred to in three ways, which explains why different commands show different hashes:

| Identifier | Hash of | Where you see it |
|---|---|---|
| **Layer digest** | The *compressed* tar blob | Image manifest, registry, `docker pull` output (short form) |
| **DiffID** | The *uncompressed* tar | Image config (`rootfs.diff_ids`), `docker image inspect` (`.RootFS.Layers`) |
| **ChainID** | A layer *plus every layer beneath it* | Docker's local storage; identifies a stack, not a single diff |

The ChainID matters because a layer is only meaningful on top of its parents: the same diff applied on a different base gives a different filesystem.

**Practical consequences**

- Image size is the sum of all layers. Deleting a file in a later layer hides it but does not remove it from the earlier layer, so the image does not shrink.
- Ordering matters: put rarely-changing steps (dependencies) before frequently-changing ones (source code) so that rebuilds and pulls reuse more layers. This is developed in [Layer Ordering](#layer-ordering).
- There is a practical limit on stack depth (about 127 layers with overlay2), rarely reached by sensible Dockerfiles.

**Example**

```bash
docker pull python:3.13-slim

# DiffIDs: one entry per layer, base first
docker image inspect -f '{{range .RootFS.Layers}}{{println .}}{{end}}' python:3.13-slim
# sha256:2f2d7b1e...   <- debian base
# sha256:9a7c4e0b...
# sha256:e1f3a6d2...
# sha256:5c0d8b7f...   <- python itself

# Pull another image built on the same base and watch layers being reused
docker pull python:3.12-slim
# 2d429b9e73a6: Already exists        <- the debian layer, shared
# 1a3f5c7e9b20: Pull complete
# ...

# Per-step view: which instruction created which layer and how big it is
docker image history python:3.13-slim
```

**Key takeaways**

- An image is an ordered stack of read-only filesystem diffs plus a config.
- Only filesystem-changing instructions (`RUN`, `COPY`, `ADD`) create layers.
- Layers are content-addressed, so identical layers are stored and downloaded once.
- Deleted files still occupy space in the layer where they were added.
- Layer digest (compressed), DiffID (uncompressed), and ChainID (stack) are different hashes for related things.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Pull `nginx:alpine` and count its layers with `docker image inspect`. Compare that number with the rows in `docker image history` and explain why they differ.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Pull `node:22-slim` and `python:3.13-slim`. Using the DiffIDs from `docker image inspect`, find out whether they share a base layer, and confirm your answer with the "Already exists" lines in the pull output.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why does reordering two lines in a Dockerfile sometimes make CI builds and deployments several times faster?" *Hint:* think about which layers are invalidated on each commit and how many bytes the deployment target has to download.

#### Copy-on-Write

**Why copy-on-write.** Read-only layers are perfect for sharing, but a running container needs to write: log files, PID files, caches, temporary data. Copying the whole image for each container would be slow and wasteful. Copy-on-write (CoW) gives every container the *illusion* of a private, writable filesystem while physically sharing the image layers, and pays the copying cost only for files that actually change.

**Analogy.** A library lends the same reference book to everyone in the reading room, but nobody may write in it. If you want to annotate a page, you photocopy *that page* and write on the copy. Everyone else still reads the original, and only the pages you annotated cost extra paper.

**How it works for containers**

1. When a container is created, Docker adds a thin, empty **writable layer** (the container layer) on top of the image's read-only layers.
2. **Reads** go down the stack and return the first (topmost) version of the file found.
3. **First write** to an existing file triggers a **copy-up**: the whole file is copied from the image layer into the container layer, and the change is applied to the copy.
4. **New files** are written directly to the container layer.
5. **Deletes** create a whiteout in the container layer; the file stays in the image layer.

```text
     container A               container B               container C
   +--------------+          +--------------+          +--------------+
   | writable (A) |          | writable (B) |          | writable (C) |
   | nginx.conf*  |          | (empty)      |          | /tmp/upload  |
   +------+-------+          +------+-------+          +------+-------+
          |                         |                         |
          +-------------------------+-------------------------+
                                    |
                 +------------------v-------------------+
                 |  image nginx:alpine (read-only)      |  stored once on disk,
                 |  layers 1..N, incl. nginx.conf       |  and cached once in RAM
                 +--------------------------------------+
   * nginx.conf was copied up into A's layer when A modified it
```

**Consequences you will run into**

| Situation | Effect | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Starting many containers from one image | Near-instant start, almost no extra disk | Nothing; this is the benefit |
| Modifying a large file from the image (e.g. a 2 GB database file) | The first write copies the *entire* file, even for one changed byte | Keep such data in a volume |
| Write-heavy workloads in the container layer | Extra overhead of the union filesystem | Use volumes or bind mounts, which bypass CoW |
| Removing the container | The writable layer and all its data are deleted | Persist important data in volumes |
| Same image layers in many containers | The kernel page cache is shared, so memory is saved too | Nothing; another benefit |

**Two sizes per container.** `docker ps -s` reports `SIZE`, the data in the writable layer, and `virtual`, which also counts the shared read-only image layers. Only the first number is per-container cost.

**Example: watching a copy-up happen**

```bash
# Build an image containing one 200 MiB file (Dockerfile read from stdin, no build context)
docker build -t cow-demo - <<'EOF'
FROM alpine:3.20
RUN dd if=/dev/zero of=/big.bin bs=1M count=200
EOF

# Container 1 only reads the file: no copy-up
docker run --name reader cow-demo sh -c 'wc -c /big.bin'

# Container 2 appends a single byte: the whole file is copied up first
docker run --name writer cow-demo sh -c 'echo x >> /big.bin'

docker ps -a -s --filter name=reader --filter name=writer --format '{{.Names}}\t{{.Size}}'
# reader   0B (virtual 218MB)
# writer   210MB (virtual 428MB)      <- one byte written, 210 MB consumed

docker diff writer
# C /big.bin                          <- changed: lives in the writable layer now

docker rm reader writer
```

**Key takeaways**

- Every container gets its own thin writable layer on top of shared read-only image layers.
- A file is copied into the writable layer only when it is first modified (copy-up), and the whole file is copied.
- `docker ps -s` shows a container's own size and its virtual size including the image.
- Volumes bypass copy-on-write; use them for databases, uploads, and any write-heavy or persistent data.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Start three containers from `nginx:alpine`, modify a file in one of them with `docker exec`, and compare their sizes with `docker ps -s`. Explain each number.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Repeat the copy-up example, but time the first and second `echo x >> /big.bin` executed with `docker exec` in the same running container. Explain why the first one is slower.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A team runs PostgreSQL in a container without a volume, and write latency spikes after each restart. What could be going on?" *Hint:* consider where the data files live, what happens on their first modification, and what happens to them when the container is recreated.

#### Image Tags

**Why tags exist.** Image IDs and digests are 64-character hashes, impossible to remember or type. Humans need readable names such as `postgres:16` or `myapp:2.3.1`, and teams need a way to say "the current stable build". Tags are these human-friendly labels.
