**What a tag is.** A tag is a **mutable pointer** from a name to an image, much like a Git branch name pointing to a commit. The full reference has this shape:

```text
   [registry[:port]/][namespace/]repository[:tag][@digest]

   registry.example.com:5000/team/api:2.3.1
   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ^^^^ ^^^ ^^^^^
   registry (host:port)      ns   repo tag

   Defaults:  registry -> docker.io     namespace -> library (Docker Hub only)
              tag      -> latest
```

**Rules.** A tag can contain letters, digits, `_`, `.`, and `-`, cannot start with `.` or `-`, and is at most 128 characters long. Repository names must be lowercase.

**`latest` is not "newest".** `latest` is simply the tag used when you do not specify one. It is not updated automatically when a newer image is pushed under another tag, and in your own repositories it only points wherever the last `docker push ...:latest` left it. Relying on it makes deployments unpredictable.

**How publishers use tags.** One image usually carries several tags at once, from very specific to very general. A moving tag such as `16` is re-pointed each time a patch release is published:

```text
   postgres:16.4-bookworm   --+
   postgres:16.4             --+
   postgres:16-bookworm      --+-->  sha256:4f1c...   (one image)
   postgres:16               --+
   postgres:latest           --+

   ... a month later, 16.5 is released:
   postgres:16, postgres:latest  -->  sha256:9b2e...  (moved)
   postgres:16.4                 -->  sha256:4f1c...  (unchanged, usually)
```

**Common tagging conventions**

| Convention | Example | Mutable? | Good for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Semantic version | `2.3.1` | Should not be | Releases |
| Floating major/minor | `2`, `2.3` | Yes, by design | Picking up patches automatically |
| Git commit SHA | `git-3f9a1c2` | No | Traceability from image to code |
| Variant suffix | `2.3.1-alpine`, `-slim` | Same as the version part | Choosing the base flavor |
| Environment or channel | `staging`, `stable` | Yes | Promotion workflows (use with care) |
| `latest` | `latest` | Yes | Local experiments only |

Tagging strategies for CI are covered in [Image Tagging Strategies](#image-tagging-strategies).

**Example**

```bash
docker pull redis                       # same as docker.io/library/redis:latest
docker pull redis:7.4-alpine            # specific version and variant

# Several tags, one image ID
docker image ls redis
# REPOSITORY   TAG          IMAGE ID       CREATED       SIZE
# redis        7.4-alpine   8a5c3e7d2b1f   2 weeks ago   41.4MB
# redis        latest       1c9f0e4a7b62   2 weeks ago   117MB

# List remote tags without pulling (Docker Hub API)
curl -s "https://hub.docker.com/v2/repositories/library/redis/tags?page_size=10" \
  | jq -r '.results[].name'
```

**Key takeaways**

- A tag is a mutable, human-readable pointer to an image; it can be moved to another image at any time.
- Omitting the tag means `latest`, which is a convention, not a guarantee of recency.
- One image commonly has many tags (full version, minor, major, variant).
- Use specific, immutable-by-policy tags (version, commit SHA) for anything you deploy.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Write the fully expanded reference (registry, namespace, repository, tag) for `ubuntu`, `bitnami/nginx:1.27`, and `localhost:5000/app`.
> 2. **(Beginner)** Pull `alpine:3`, `alpine:3.20`, and `alpine:latest`. Use `docker image ls` to determine which of them currently point to the same image.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your production cluster suddenly runs a different version of a dependency even though nobody changed the deployment manifest. How can tags explain this?" *Hint:* think about floating tags, image pull policies, and nodes pulling at different times.

#### Image Digests

**Why digests exist.** A tag tells you a *name*; it does not guarantee *content*. If `myapp:1.0` is overwritten, two servers that pulled at different times can run different code under the same name. A digest is a cryptographic fingerprint of the content itself, so a reference by digest always means exactly the same bytes, and any tampering is detectable.

**What a digest is.** A digest is `algorithm:hex`, almost always `sha256:` followed by 64 hex characters, computed over a JSON document (manifest or index). Because the manifest lists the digests of the config and every layer, the digest of the manifest transitively pins the entire image, the way a Git commit hash pins the full source tree.

```text
   index digest  sha256:aaa...   <- what "docker pull nginx:1.27" prints as "Digest:"
        |
        +-- linux/amd64 manifest  sha256:bbb...
        |       +-- config  sha256:ccc...
        |       +-- layers  sha256:ddd..., sha256:eee...
        +-- linux/arm64 manifest  sha256:fff...
                +-- ...

   Change one byte in any layer -> its digest changes -> the manifest changes
   -> the manifest digest changes -> the index digest changes.
```

**IDs and digests compared**

| Value | What it hashes | Scope | Command |
|---|---|---|---|
| Repo digest | Manifest or index, as stored in the registry | Global, the same everywhere | `docker image inspect -f '{{.RepoDigests}}'` |
| Image ID | Config (classic store) or manifest/index (containerd store) | Local; may differ between engines | `docker image ls`, `.Id` |
| Platform manifest digest | One platform's manifest | Global | `docker buildx imagetools inspect` |

**Referencing by digest.** Add `@sha256:...` to the name. If a tag is also present (`nginx:1.27@sha256:...`), the digest wins and the tag is only documentation, a common and readable way to pin base images in Dockerfiles. Automated tools such as Renovate or Dependabot can update pinned digests through pull requests, so pinning does not mean never patching.

**Example**

```bash
docker pull nginx:1.27-alpine
# ...
# Digest: sha256:2140dad2...                      <- index digest (shortened here)
# Status: Downloaded newer image for nginx:1.27-alpine

# Digest of a local image (empty for images that were never pushed or pulled)
docker image inspect -f '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' nginx:1.27-alpine
# nginx@sha256:2140dad2...

# Remote digest without pulling: index digest and per-platform manifests
docker buildx imagetools inspect nginx:1.27-alpine
# Name:      docker.io/library/nginx:1.27-alpine
# MediaType: application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json
# Digest:    sha256:2140dad2...
# Manifests:
#   Name:      docker.io/library/nginx:1.27-alpine@sha256:7a1b...
#   Platform:  linux/amd64
#   ...

# Pull and run by digest: always the exact same content
REF=$(docker image inspect -f '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' nginx:1.27-alpine)
docker run --rm "$REF" nginx -v
```

```dockerfile
# Readable and reproducible: the tag documents intent, the digest is what is used
FROM node:22-alpine@sha256:<digest-from-imagetools-inspect>
```

**Key takeaways**

- A digest is a content hash; the same digest always means the same image.
- The manifest digest transitively covers the config and every layer.
- Multi-platform images have an index digest plus one manifest digest per platform.
- Pin by digest where reproducibility matters (base images, production deploys) and automate digest updates.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Pull `alpine:3.20`, note the digest, and then pull it again using only the digest. Confirm with `docker image ls --digests` that both references point to the same image.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Use `docker buildx imagetools inspect` to list the per-platform manifest digests of `alpine:3.20`. Explain why `docker image inspect` on an amd64 machine and on an arm64 machine can show the same repo digest but different layers.
> 3. **Interview question:** "If tags are mutable, what stops someone from pushing a malicious image under a digest you already trust?" *Hint:* think about what the digest is computed from and what a client verifies after downloading.

#### Base Images

**Why base images matter.** Almost no one builds an image from an empty filesystem. Your image starts `FROM` some other image that provides a C library, a shell, a package manager, or a language runtime. That choice decides a large part of your final image's size, attack surface, available tools, and how often you will need to patch it. It is one of the most consequential lines in a Dockerfile.

**Terminology.** Strictly, a *base image* is one built `FROM scratch` (an empty filesystem), and the image named in your `FROM` line is your *parent image*. In everyday use, "base image" means the parent image, and this guide follows that usage.

**Families of base images**

| Family | Examples | Approx. size | Shell / package manager | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Empty | `scratch` | 0 B | No / No | For static binaries (Go, Rust); you supply everything |
| Minimal distro | `alpine:3.20` | ~8 MB | `sh` / `apk` | Uses musl libc instead of glibc; some binaries and wheels behave differently |
| Slim distro | `debian:12-slim`, `ubuntu:24.04` | ~75-80 MB | `bash` / `apt` | glibc, broad compatibility, good default |
| Full distro | `debian:12`, `buildpack-deps` | 120 MB to 1 GB | Yes / Yes | Many build tools included; best for build stages |
| Language runtime | `python:3.13-slim`, `node:22-alpine`, `eclipse-temurin:21-jre` | 50-250 MB | Depends on variant | Runtime preinstalled and maintained upstream |
| Distroless / hardened | `gcr.io/distroless/static`, Chainguard images, Docker Hardened Images | 2-50 MB | Usually no / No | Minimal attack surface; debugging is harder |

Sizes are uncompressed, rough, and change between releases.

**Selection criteria**

- **Compatibility**: does your application need glibc, specific system libraries, or a shell at runtime?
- **Size and attack surface**: fewer packages mean fewer vulnerabilities to patch and faster pulls.
- **Maintenance**: is the image rebuilt regularly with security fixes? Official and verified images usually are (see [Official and Verified Images](#official-and-verified-images)).
- **Debuggability**: images without a shell cannot be entered with `docker exec sh`; plan for tools like `docker debug`.
- **Build versus run**: a large image with compilers for building and a tiny image for running is the multi-stage pattern in [5.4 Multi-Stage Builds](#54-multi-stage-builds).

Minimal choices are explored further in [Choosing Minimal Base Images](#choosing-minimal-base-images) and [Distroless and Scratch Images](#distroless-and-scratch-images).

**Example**

```bash
# Compare a few bases side by side
for img in alpine:3.20 debian:12-slim ubuntu:24.04 python:3.13-slim python:3.13; do
  docker pull -q "$img" >/dev/null
done
docker image ls --format 'table {{.Repository}}:{{.Tag}}\t{{.Size}}' | grep -E 'alpine|debian|ubuntu|python'

# Which C library and shell does each one have?
docker run --rm alpine:3.20     sh -c 'ldd --version 2>&1 | head -n1'   # musl libc
docker run --rm debian:12-slim  sh -c 'ldd --version | head -n1'        # ldd (Debian GLIBC 2.36-9...) 2.36

# Distroless has no shell at all
docker run --rm gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12 sh
# docker: Error response from daemon: ... exec: "sh": executable file not found in $PATH
```

```dockerfile
# Typical choices
FROM python:3.13-slim          # general Python service: glibc, small, maintained
# FROM alpine:3.20             # tiny utilities where musl is fine
# FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12   # statically linked Go binary in production
```

**Key takeaways**

- The parent image determines much of your image's size, vulnerabilities, and tooling.
- Alpine is tiny but uses musl; slim Debian/Ubuntu variants are a safe general default.
- Distroless and hardened images minimize attack surface at the cost of debuggability.
- Prefer maintained, regularly rebuilt images, and separate build-time and run-time bases with multi-stage builds.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run `cat /etc/os-release` in `alpine:3.20`, `debian:12-slim`, and `python:3.13-slim`. Which distribution is the Python image built on?
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Install the same package (for example `curl`) in an Alpine-based and a Debian-slim-based container. Compare the commands, the time taken, and the resulting writable layer size (`docker ps -s`).
> 3. **Interview question:** "A Python service is 1.2 GB as an image. How would you choose a better base, and what risks does switching to Alpine introduce?" *Hint:* consider the `-slim` variants, compiled dependencies (wheels built for glibc vs musl), and multi-stage builds.

#### Pulling and Listing Images

**Why it matters.** Before a container can run, its image must exist in the local image store. Pulling is how it gets there; listing is how you find out what is already there, how big it is, and which versions you have. Both commands have options that become important as soon as you deal with multiple architectures, many images, or scripts.

**What happens during a pull**

```text
 docker pull nginx:1.27-alpine
   1. resolve   docker.io/library/nginx:1.27-alpine -> GET manifest/index from registry
   2. select    index lists platforms -> choose the one matching the host (e.g. linux/amd64)
   3. compare   for each layer digest in the manifest: already in local store?
                   yes -> "Already exists"
                   no  -> download compressed blob ("Downloading"), verify digest
   4. unpack    decompress layers into the storage driver ("Extracting", "Pull complete")
   5. record    store config, set the tag, print "Digest:" and "Status:"
```

Layers are downloaded in parallel and verified against their digests, so a corrupted or tampered download is rejected.

**Useful pull options**

| Option | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--platform linux/arm64` | Pull a specific architecture instead of the host's |
| `-a`, `--all-tags` | Pull every tag of a repository (use with care) |
| `-q`, `--quiet` | Print only the final reference |
| `docker run --pull always` | Check the registry for a newer image before every run (`missing` is the default, `never` forbids pulling) |

**Listing images.** `docker image ls` (alias `docker images`) shows one row per tag. `SIZE` is the *uncompressed* size on disk, including shared layers, which is why it is larger than the download size shown on the registry. Images with no tag appear as `<none>:<none>`; these are **dangling** images, typically left behind when a tag is moved to a newer build.

| Filter / option | Example | Shows |
|---|---|---|
| Positional repository | `docker image ls nginx` | Only that repository |
| `reference` | `--filter reference='*/api:*'` | Names matching a pattern |
| `dangling` | `--filter dangling=true` | Untagged images |
| `before` / `since` | `--filter since=nginx:1.27` | Images created before/after another image |
| `label` | `--filter label=org.opencontainers.image.vendor=Acme` | Images with a label |
| `--digests` | | Adds a `DIGEST` column |
| `-q` | | Only image IDs (for scripting) |
| `--format` | `'{{.Repository}}:{{.Tag}} {{.Size}}'` | Custom output |

Recent CLI versions also offer `docker image ls --tree`, which groups the platform variants stored for each multi-platform image.

**Example**

```bash
docker pull nginx:1.27-alpine
# 1.27-alpine: Pulling from library/nginx
# 43c4264eed91: Already exists          <- alpine base layer already local
# 5b19511a843e: Pull complete
# ...
# Digest: sha256:2140dad2...
# Status: Downloaded newer image for nginx:1.27-alpine
# docker.io/library/nginx:1.27-alpine

docker pull nginx:1.27-alpine
# Status: Image is up to date for nginx:1.27-alpine   <- nothing downloaded

# Different architecture (runs under emulation, or for re-pushing / inspection)
docker pull --platform linux/arm64 alpine:3.20
docker image inspect -f '{{.Os}}/{{.Architecture}}' alpine:3.20

# Listing
docker image ls
docker image ls --digests nginx
docker image ls --filter dangling=true
docker image ls --format 'table {{.Repository}}\t{{.Tag}}\t{{.Size}}' | sort -k3 -h

# Script-friendly: IDs of all images from the "myapp" repository
docker image ls -q myapp
```

**Key takeaways**

- A pull resolves the reference, picks the matching platform, downloads only missing layers, and verifies every digest.
- `--platform` selects an architecture; `--pull always` on `docker run` refreshes moving tags.
- `docker image ls` shows uncompressed sizes; shared layers are counted in every image that uses them.
- `<none>:<none>` entries are dangling images; filter and prune them as needed.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Pull `postgres:16` and `postgres:16-alpine`. Compare the pull output (number of layers, "Already exists" lines) and the final sizes.
> 2. **(Beginner)** Produce a list of all local images sorted by size, showing only `repository:tag` and size, using `--format`.
> 3. **(Intermediate)** Build an image tagged `demo:1`, change the Dockerfile, and build it again with the same tag. Find the resulting dangling image with a filter and explain why it exists.

<a id="42-image-management"></a>
### 4.2 Image Management

This section covers the everyday operations on local images: naming, removing, and inspecting them, moving them between machines without a registry, and creating images from containers.

#### Tagging Images

**Why tag images yourself.** Tags are how you give an image a meaningful version, and also *where* it will be pushed: the registry and repository are part of the name. Before you can push `myapp` to `ghcr.io/acme/myapp:1.2.0`, the local image must carry that exact name. Tagging is also how you mark builds for promotion (`1.2.0` becomes `stable`) without rebuilding.

**What `docker tag` does.** `docker image tag SOURCE TARGET` (alias `docker tag`) adds a new name to an existing image. Nothing is copied: both names point to the same image ID, like a hard link or a second Git branch on the same commit. If `TARGET` already points to another image, it is moved, and the old image keeps its other tags or becomes dangling.

```text
 Before:   myapp:dev ---------------------> image 7c1d...

 docker tag myapp:dev myapp:1.2.0
 docker tag myapp:dev ghcr.io/acme/myapp:1.2.0

 After:    myapp:dev ------------------+
           myapp:1.2.0 ----------------+--> image 7c1d...   (stored once)
           ghcr.io/acme/myapp:1.2.0 ---+
                     ^
                     registry host in the name decides where "docker push" sends it
```

**Tagging at build time.** `docker build -t` accepts several tags at once, which avoids separate `docker tag` calls:

```bash
docker build -t myapp:1.2.0 -t myapp:1.2 -t ghcr.io/acme/myapp:1.2.0 .
```

**Example**

```bash
docker pull alpine:3.20

docker tag alpine:3.20 tools/base:1.0                    # local name
docker tag alpine:3.20 localhost:5000/tools/base:1.0     # name for a local registry
docker tag alpine:3.20 tools/base                        # no tag given -> tools/base:latest

docker image ls --filter reference='*/base' --filter reference='localhost:5000/*/*'
# REPOSITORY                  TAG      IMAGE ID       CREATED       SIZE
# tools/base                  1.0      91ef0af61f39   3 weeks ago   7.8MB
# tools/base                  latest   91ef0af61f39   3 weeks ago   7.8MB
# localhost:5000/tools/base   1.0      91ef0af61f39   3 weeks ago   7.8MB   <- same ID everywhere

# Tagging by image ID works too
docker tag 91ef0af61f39 tools/base:pinned

# Invalid names are rejected
docker tag alpine:3.20 Tools/Base:1.0
# Error parsing reference: "Tools/Base:1.0" is not a valid repository/tag: repository name must be lowercase
```

**Key takeaways**

- `docker tag` adds a name to an existing image; no data is copied.
- The name encodes the destination registry and repository for `docker push`.
- Re-tagging moves the name; the previously tagged image may become dangling.
- `docker build` can apply several tags in one go with repeated `-t`.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Tag `nginx:alpine` as `web:v1`, `web:v2`, and `web:latest`. Confirm with `docker image ls` that all three share one image ID.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Build two different images, tag the first as `app:current`, then re-tag the second as `app:current`. Show what happened to the first image and how you would find it again.
> 3. **Interview question:** "How would you promote an image from staging to production without rebuilding it, and why is not rebuilding important?" *Hint:* consider re-tagging (or copying by digest) between repositories and what a rebuild could change even from identical source code.

#### Removing Images

**Why removal needs care.** Images are shared by tags, by other images (as layers), and by containers. Docker therefore distinguishes between *removing a name* and *deleting image data*, and refuses deletions that would break something. Knowing these rules avoids both "why is the disk still full?" and "why can't I delete this?".

**How `docker image rm` decides**

```text
 docker image rm <reference>
        |
        +-- reference is a TAG and the image has other tags?
        |        -> "Untagged: ..."  only the name is removed, data stays
        |
        +-- it is the LAST tag (or an ID with one tag)?
        |        -> "Untagged: ..." then "Deleted: sha256:..."
        |           layers are freed unless another image still uses them
        |
        +-- a CONTAINER (running or stopped) uses the image?
        |        -> error "conflict: unable to remove repository reference ..."
        |           -f on a stopped container's image: untags, data kept until container is removed
        |           running container: refused even with -f
        |
        +-- an image ID with SEVERAL tags?
                 -> error "image is referenced in multiple repositories"; use -f or remove each tag
```

**Related commands**

| Command | Removes |
|---|---|
| `docker image rm IMAGE...` (alias `docker rmi`) | The given tags/images |
| `docker image prune` | Dangling (`<none>:<none>`) images |
| `docker image prune -a` | Every image not used by any container |
| `docker image prune -a --filter until=72h` | Unused images created more than 72 hours ago |
| `docker system prune` | Dangling images plus stopped containers, unused networks, build cache |

Bulk pruning is covered in [Pruning Unused Resources](#pruning-unused-resources).

**Example**

```bash
docker pull alpine:3.20
docker tag alpine:3.20 mybase:1

docker image rm mybase:1
# Untagged: mybase:1                              <- alpine:3.20 still holds the data

docker run --name holder alpine:3.20 true         # a stopped container now uses the image
docker image rm alpine:3.20
# Error response from daemon: conflict: unable to remove repository reference "alpine:3.20"
#   (must force) - container 4f2a... is using its referenced image 91ef0af61f39

docker rm holder
docker image rm alpine:3.20
# Untagged: alpine:3.20
# Untagged: alpine@sha256:beefdbd8...
# Deleted: sha256:91ef0af61f39...

# Remove every tag of one repository
docker image ls --format '{{.Repository}}:{{.Tag}}' myapp | xargs -r docker image rm

# Remove dangling images only
docker image prune -f
```

**Key takeaways**

- Removing a tag and deleting image data are different; data is deleted only when the last reference is gone.
- Images used by any container, even a stopped one, are protected; remove the container first.
- Shared layers survive as long as at least one image uses them.
- Use `docker image prune` for dangling images and `-a` with filters for wider cleanup.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Pull an image, give it two extra tags, and remove all three names one at a time. Note at which step the `Deleted:` line appears.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Pull `python:3.13-slim` and `python:3.12-slim`, remove one of them, and use `docker system df -v` before and after to show that shared layers were not freed.
> 3. **Interview question:** "`docker rmi -f` succeeded, but `docker system df` shows the space was not reclaimed. Why?" *Hint:* consider what `-f` does when a stopped container still references the image.

#### Inspecting Image History

**Why look at history.** When an image is unexpectedly large, behaves differently than expected, or comes from an unknown source, you need to know how it was built. `docker image history` lists the build steps that produced each layer, with their sizes, so you can see where the bytes come from and which commands were run.

**What it shows.** One row per history entry, newest first. Steps that only changed metadata (`ENV`, `CMD`, `EXPOSE`, ...) show `0B`. The `IMAGE` column shows `<missing>` for layers whose intermediate images do not exist locally, which is normal for every pulled image and for BuildKit builds; it does not mean anything is broken.

**Limits of history**

- It is **self-reported metadata** written by the builder. It can be incomplete or edited, so treat it as a hint, not proof. Use provenance attestations ([Build Provenance and Attestations](#build-provenance-and-attestations)) for verifiable build information.
- Multi-stage builds only show the steps of the final stage; build stages leave no trace.
- Commands are recorded **verbatim**, including build argument values used in `RUN`. Never pass secrets as build arguments; use secret mounts ([Build-Time Secrets](#build-time-secrets)).

**Example**

```bash
docker image history nginx:1.27-alpine
# IMAGE          CREATED       CREATED BY                                      SIZE      COMMENT
# 1ff4bb4faebc   2 weeks ago   CMD ["nginx" "-g" "daemon off;"]                0B        buildkit.dockerfile.v0
# <missing>      2 weeks ago   STOPSIGNAL SIGQUIT                              0B        buildkit.dockerfile.v0
# <missing>      2 weeks ago   EXPOSE map[80/tcp:{}]                           0B        buildkit.dockerfile.v0
# <missing>      2 weeks ago   ENTRYPOINT ["/docker-entrypoint.sh"]            0B        buildkit.dockerfile.v0
# <missing>      2 weeks ago   RUN /bin/sh -c set -x && addgroup -g 101 -S…   5.2MB     buildkit.dockerfile.v0
# ...
# <missing>      3 weeks ago   ADD alpine-minirootfs-3.20.3-x86_64.tar.gz /…   7.8MB     buildkit.dockerfile.v0

# Full commands, no truncation, human-readable sizes kept
docker image history --no-trunc --format '{{.Size}}\t{{.CreatedBy}}' nginx:1.27-alpine

# Find the biggest layers
docker image history --format '{{.Size}}\t{{.CreatedBy}}' python:3.13 | sort -h -r | head -n 5

# Demonstrate that build arguments leak into history
docker build -t leaky --build-arg TOKEN=s3cr3t - <<'EOF'
FROM alpine:3.20
ARG TOKEN
RUN echo "using token" > /dev/null
EOF
docker image history --no-trunc leaky | grep TOKEN
# ... RUN |1 TOKEN=s3cr3t /bin/sh -c echo "using token" > /dev/null ...   <- visible to anyone with the image
```

For an interactive, per-layer view of the files themselves, the third-party tool `dive` shows what each layer added, changed, or removed.

**Key takeaways**

- `docker image history` lists the build steps and the size each one added.
- `<missing>` in the `IMAGE` column is normal for pulled images and BuildKit builds.
- History is unverified metadata and omits earlier stages of multi-stage builds.
- Build argument values are recorded in history; never use them for secrets.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run `docker image history` on `redis:alpine` and identify the step that installs Redis and how much space it takes.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Write a Dockerfile with a `RUN` step that downloads a large file and a later `RUN` that deletes it. Use history to show that the image still carries the file's size, then fix the Dockerfile.
> 3. **Interview question:** "You are given an image from an unknown vendor. How would you find out what is in it and how it was built?" *Hint:* combine history, config inspection, filesystem exploration (`docker export`, `dive`), labels, SBOMs, and attestations, and consider which of these can be trusted.

#### Saving and Loading Images

**Why save and load.** Not every machine can reach a registry: air-gapped networks, factory floors, customer sites, or a CI job that hands an image to the next job as a file. `docker save` writes one or more images, *with all their layers, tags, and metadata*, into a tar archive; `docker load` restores them into another engine's image store exactly as they were.

**What is in the archive.** Recent Docker versions write an OCI image layout (see [OCI Image Specification](#oci-image-specification)) plus Docker's legacy `manifest.json`, so the archive can be read both by `docker load` and by OCI tools such as `skopeo`.

```text
 nginx.tar
 ├── oci-layout             OCI layout marker
 ├── index.json             entry point: tags -> manifests
 ├── manifest.json          Docker-format index for older tooling
 ├── repositories           legacy tag file
 └── blobs/sha256/
     ├── 2140dad2...        index / manifest
     ├── 1ff4bb4f...        config
     └── 43c4264e...        layer tars (one per layer)
```

**Example**

```bash
# Save one or several images (shared layers are written only once)
docker save -o images.tar nginx:1.27-alpine redis:7.4-alpine
ls -lh images.tar

# Compress on the fly; docker load detects gzip, bzip2, xz, and zstd automatically
docker save nginx:1.27-alpine | gzip > nginx.tar.gz

# Look inside
tar -tf images.tar | head

# Restore on another machine (tags and history are preserved)
docker load -i nginx.tar.gz
# Loaded image: nginx:1.27-alpine

# Copy straight to a remote host over SSH, no intermediate file
docker save myapp:1.2.0 | ssh deploy@edge-01 docker load

# Multi-platform images (containerd image store): choose what to export
docker save --platform linux/arm64 -o alpine-arm64.tar alpine:3.20
```

**Key takeaways**

- `docker save` exports images with all layers, tags, and config; `docker load` restores them unchanged.
- The archive is an OCI layout, readable by other OCI tools.
- Compress with `gzip` or `zstd`; `docker load` decompresses automatically.
- Use it for air-gapped transfers and CI artifacts; use a registry when one is available, because it transfers only missing layers.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Save `alpine:3.20` to a file, remove the image, load it back, and confirm the image ID did not change.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Save `python:3.13-slim` and `python:3.12-slim` in separate archives and then together in one archive. Compare the three file sizes and explain the result.
> 3. **Interview question:** "How would you deliver container updates to a fleet of machines with no internet access and limited bandwidth?" *Hint:* compare full `docker save` archives with a local registry or mirror inside the network, and think about which layers actually change between releases.

#### Exporting and Importing Containers

**Why export exists.** Sometimes you do not need an image with its history; you need *the filesystem* of a container, for example to examine it with ordinary tools, to extract build output, or to produce a single-layer root filesystem for another system. `docker export` writes a container's merged filesystem as a plain tar; `docker import` turns such a tar (from Docker or from anywhere else) into a new image with one layer.

**Export/import versus save/load**

| | `docker save` / `docker load` | `docker export` / `docker import` |
|---|---|---|
| Works on | Images | Containers (export), tarballs (import) |
| Layers | All preserved | Flattened into a single layer |
| History | Preserved | Lost |
| Config (`CMD`, `ENV`, `ENTRYPOINT`, ...) | Preserved | Lost; set again with `--change` on import |
| Includes container changes | No | Yes, the writable layer is merged in |
| Includes volume contents | No | No |
| Typical use | Moving images without a registry | Inspecting/extracting filesystems, creating base images from rootfs tarballs |

**Example**

```bash
docker run -d --name web nginx:1.27-alpine
docker exec web sh -c 'echo "<h1>exported</h1>" > /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html'

# Export the merged filesystem (image layers + container changes)
docker export -o web-rootfs.tar web
tar -tf web-rootfs.tar | grep index.html        # usr/share/nginx/html/index.html

# Extract only one directory from an image without running it
docker create --name tmp nginx:1.27-alpine
mkdir -p out
docker export tmp | tar -x -C out etc/nginx      # only etc/nginx is extracted
docker rm tmp

# Import as a new single-layer image: the config is gone ...
docker import web-rootfs.tar web:flat
docker run --rm web:flat
# docker: Error response from daemon: no command specified

# ... so restore what is needed with --change (Dockerfile syntax)
docker import \
  --change 'CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]' \
  --change 'EXPOSE 80' \
  web-rootfs.tar web:flat
docker image history web:flat                   # a single "Imported from -" layer

docker rm -f web
```

**Key takeaways**

- `docker export` dumps a container's merged filesystem; it is a filesystem, not an image.
- `docker import` creates a single-layer image with no history and no runtime config unless you add `--change`.
- Neither includes volume data.
- Use save/load to move images; use export/import to work with filesystems.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Export a `debian:12-slim` container and list the top-level directories in the archive. Compare the archive size with the image size.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Export a container that has a few modified files, import it, and compare `docker image history` and `docker image inspect -f '{{.Config.Cmd}}'` with the original image.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Someone suggests using `docker export` and `docker import` to shrink images by flattening layers. What do you gain and what do you lose?" *Hint:* consider layer sharing with other images, cached pulls, image config, history, and why multi-stage builds achieve the same goal better.

#### Committing Containers to Images

**Why commit exists.** `docker commit` takes a container's current state, including all changes in its writable layer, and saves it as a new image layer on top of the original image. It is useful for snapshots when debugging ("save this broken state so I can study it later"), for quick experiments, and for understanding that an image is nothing more than layers plus config. It is **not** a good way to produce images you ship.

**Why not for production.** A committed image is a black box: nobody can tell how it was produced, it cannot be rebuilt from source, it often contains leftovers (shell history, caches, temp files, sometimes credentials), and every update requires repeating manual steps. A Dockerfile records each step, is version-controlled and reviewable, and rebuilds the same way every time.

| | `docker commit` | Dockerfile + `docker build` |
|---|---|---|
| Reproducible | No | Yes |
| Reviewable / versioned | No | Yes, it is source code |
| Uses the build cache | No | Yes |
| Risk of leftovers | High | Low (with `.dockerignore` and multi-stage builds) |
| Good for | Debug snapshots, experiments, forensics | Everything you build and ship |

**How it works.** By default, the container is **paused** during commit for consistency (`--pause=false` disables this). `--change` applies Dockerfile instructions (`CMD`, `ENTRYPOINT`, `ENV`, `EXPOSE`, `LABEL`, `USER`, `VOLUME`, `WORKDIR`, `ONBUILD`) to the new image's config. Data in volumes is not included.

```text
   nginx:1.27-alpine layers (read-only)       myweb:snapshot
   +-------------------------------+          +-------------------------------+
   | ...                           |          | NEW layer = container's       |
   +-------------------------------+   commit |   writable layer contents     |
   container "web" writable layer  |  ------> +-------------------------------+
   (edited index.html)             |          | nginx:1.27-alpine layers      |
                                              | (reused, not copied)          |
                                              +-------------------------------+
```

**Example**

```bash
docker run -d --name web nginx:1.27-alpine
docker exec web sh -c 'echo "<h1>Hello from a commit</h1>" > /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html'

docker diff web                                   # what will be committed
# C /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
# C /var/cache/nginx ...                          <- leftovers get committed too

docker commit \
  -a "Jane Doe <jane@example.com>" \
  -m "Custom index page" \
  -c 'LABEL purpose=debug-snapshot' \
  web myweb:snapshot

docker image history myweb:snapshot | head -n 2
# IMAGE          CREATED          CREATED BY                          SIZE    COMMENT
# 6d0e2f1a9c3b   10 seconds ago   /docker-entrypoint.sh nginx -g 'da…   1.2kB   Custom index page

docker run -d --rm -p 8081:80 --name web2 myweb:snapshot
curl -s localhost:8081                             # <h1>Hello from a commit</h1>

docker rm -f web web2
```

The equivalent, reproducible version is a two-line Dockerfile:

```dockerfile
FROM nginx:1.27-alpine
COPY index.html /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html   # explicit, reviewable, rebuildable
```

**Key takeaways**

- `docker commit` turns a container's writable layer into a new image layer, keeping the parent layers.
- It pauses the container by default and does not include volume data.
- Use it for debugging snapshots and experiments, not for images you deploy.
- Anything committed can be reproduced, and should be, with a Dockerfile.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run `ubuntu:24.04` interactively, install `curl` with `apt`, exit, and commit the container. Check the size of the new layer with `docker image history`.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Write the Dockerfile that reproduces exercise 1, build it, and compare both images' sizes. Use `docker diff` on the original container to explain any difference.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A colleague's production image was created with `docker commit` two years ago and nobody knows how to rebuild it. How would you recover a maintainable build?" *Hint:* inspect history, config, and the filesystem diff against the parent image, then rebuild with a Dockerfile and compare the results.

<a id="43-image-registries"></a>
### 4.3 Image Registries

This section builds on the overview in [Registries](#registries) and covers the public and private registries you will work with, how pushing works, and how clients authenticate.

#### Docker Hub

**Why Docker Hub matters.** Docker Hub is the default registry: whenever an image name has no registry host, Docker looks it up on `docker.io`. Most base images, databases, and tools you use start there, so its namespaces, limits, and account features directly affect your builds and CI pipelines, even if you push your own images elsewhere.

**Structure.** Docker Hub hosts repositories under **namespaces**: `library/` for official images (hidden in short names), and one namespace per user or organization. Each repository is public or private and holds tags.

```text
   docker.io
   ├── library/            official images: "nginx" == "docker.io/library/nginx"
   │   ├── nginx
   │   ├── postgres
   │   └── ...
   ├── bitnami/            organization (verified publisher)
   │   └── redis
   └── jdoe/               personal namespace
       ├── hello           public repository
       └── internal-tool   private repository
```

**Main features**

| Feature | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Public and private repositories | Distribute images openly or only to your account/organization |
| Organizations and teams | Grant per-repository read/write/admin permissions to groups |
| Personal and organization access tokens | Scoped credentials for CLI and CI instead of your password |
| Webhooks | Notify other systems when a tag is pushed |
| Image analysis (Docker Scout) | Vulnerability and policy information per tag ([Docker Scout](#docker-scout)) |
| Search and image pages | Documentation, tag lists, pull counts, trust badges |

**Pull rate limits.** Docker Hub limits how many image pulls (manifest requests) a client may make in a time window. Anonymous pulls are limited per IP address and much more strictly than authenticated ones; paid plans raise or remove the limits. The exact numbers have changed several times, so check Docker's current documentation. Shared IPs (office NAT, CI runners) hit anonymous limits quickly, which shows up as `429 Too Many Requests` or `toomanyrequests` errors. Always authenticate in CI, and consider a pull-through cache ([Private Registries](#private-registries)).

**Example**

```bash
# Search from the CLI (limited compared to the web UI)
docker search --filter is-official=true --limit 3 postgres
# NAME       DESCRIPTION                                     STARS     OFFICIAL
# postgres   The PostgreSQL object-relational database sy…   14000     [OK]

# List tags through the Hub API
curl -s "https://hub.docker.com/v2/repositories/library/postgres/tags?page_size=5" \
  | jq -r '.results[] | "\(.name)\t\(.last_updated)"'

# Check your current rate limit (HEAD requests do not count as pulls)
TOKEN=$(curl -s "https://auth.docker.io/token?service=registry.docker.io&scope=repository:ratelimitpreview/test:pull" | jq -r .token)
curl -s --head -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  https://registry-1.docker.io/v2/ratelimitpreview/test/manifests/latest | grep -i ratelimit
# ratelimit-limit: <limit>;w=<window in seconds>
# ratelimit-remaining: <remaining>;w=<window in seconds>

# Log in to raise your limits (opens a browser/device-code flow, or use a token)
docker login
```

**Key takeaways**

- Docker Hub (`docker.io`) is the default registry; `library/` holds official images.
- Repositories live in user or organization namespaces and can be public or private.
- Pull rate limits are stricter for anonymous clients; authenticate, especially in CI.
- Use access tokens, not passwords, for CLI and automation.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Create a free Docker Hub account and a personal access token with read-only scope. Log in with it using `docker login -u <user> --password-stdin`.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Run the rate-limit check above anonymously and then with a token obtained using your credentials (`curl -u user:token "https://auth.docker.io/token?..."`). Compare the limits.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Several CI jobs started failing with `toomanyrequests` at the same time of day. How do you diagnose and fix it?" *Hint:* think about shared egress IPs, anonymous pulls, caching layers locally or in a mirror, and authentication in every job.

#### Official and Verified Images

**Why trust signals matter.** Anyone can publish an image on Docker Hub, and an image runs with whatever code its author put in it. Typosquatted names (`ngnix`, `postgress`), abandoned images full of known vulnerabilities, and images that mine cryptocurrency have all been found on public registries. Docker Hub's badges help you identify images that are curated or come from a verified source.

**The categories**

| Category | Namespace / badge | Who maintains it | What it guarantees |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Docker Official Images** | `library/` (short names like `nginx`) | Docker's team together with upstream maintainers | Reviewed Dockerfiles in a public repository, regular rebuilds for security fixes, best-practice conventions, multi-architecture support |
| **Verified Publisher** | Vendor namespace with a badge | The commercial vendor (e.g. a database or monitoring company) | The publisher's identity was verified by Docker |
| **Sponsored Open Source** | Project namespace with a badge | The open-source project | The project is part of Docker's open-source program |
| **Hardened images** | Separate catalog | Docker | Minimal, frequently patched images with SBOMs and provenance |
| Community | Any user or organization | Anyone | Nothing |

**How official images are made.** Each official image has public source (for example the `docker-library/postgres` repository on GitHub) and a definition file in the `docker-library/official-images` repository that maps tags to Git commits. Changes go through public review, and images are rebuilt when their base image or upstream software receives updates.

**A checklist for any image**

- Does it carry a badge, and does the namespace exactly match the project you expect?
- Is there a linked source repository and Dockerfile (`org.opencontainers.image.source` label)?
- When was it last updated? Old images accumulate vulnerabilities.
- What does a vulnerability scan show ([Vulnerability Scanning](#vulnerability-scanning))?
- Does it provide SBOM and provenance attestations, or signatures ([Image Signing and Verification](#image-signing-and-verification))?
- Pull counts and stars indicate popularity, not safety.

**Example**

```bash
# Only official images in search results
docker search --filter is-official=true redis

# Labels often point to the source and version
docker image inspect -f '{{json .Config.Labels}}' grafana/grafana:11.2.0 | jq .

# Attestations attached to an image (empty output if the image has none)
docker buildx imagetools inspect nginx:1.27-alpine --format '{{json .Provenance}}' | jq '.[] | .SLSA.buildType' 2>/dev/null
docker buildx imagetools inspect nginx:1.27-alpine --format '{{json .SBOM}}' | head -c 300; echo
```

**Key takeaways**

- Docker Official Images are curated, publicly reviewed, and rebuilt regularly; prefer them for base images.
- Verified Publisher and Sponsored Open Source badges confirm *who* publishes the image, not that it is free of vulnerabilities.
- Check the exact namespace to avoid typosquatting, and verify source, recency, scans, and attestations.
- Popularity is not a security signal.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Find the GitHub source of the `redis` official image from its Docker Hub page and locate the Dockerfile for the `alpine` variant.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Pick an official image and a popular community image providing the same software. Compare their update frequency, labels, size, and scan results (`docker scout quickview` if available).
> 3. **Interview question:** "What policy would you put in place to control which public images developers can use as base images in your company?" *Hint:* consider allowlists of trusted namespaces, internal mirrors of approved images, digest pinning, admission policies, and scanning in CI.

#### Pushing Images

**Why push.** Pushing uploads an image to a registry so that other machines, CI jobs, or orchestrators can pull it. It is the "publish" step that connects building on one machine with running anywhere else.

**How a push works.** `docker push` reads the registry and repository from the image name, then uploads only what the registry does not already have:

```text
 docker push ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2
   1. auth      get a token with push+pull scope for acme/api
   2. per layer HEAD /v2/acme/api/blobs/<digest>
                  exists                -> "Layer already exists"
                  exists in another repo -> cross-repository mount: "Mounted from acme/base"
                  missing               -> upload blob, registry verifies the digest -> "Pushed"
   3. config    upload the config blob the same way
   4. manifest  PUT /v2/acme/api/manifests/1.4.2   -> tag now points to the new manifest
   5. output    "1.4.2: digest: sha256:... size: ..."
```

Because layers are content-addressed, pushing a new version of an application usually uploads only the few top layers that changed.

**Requirements and common errors**

| Message | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `denied: requested access to the resource is denied` | Not logged in, or no write access to that namespace | `docker login`, check the namespace (your user or an organization you belong to) |
| `An image does not exist locally with the tag: ...` | The image was not tagged with the target name | `docker tag` first |
| `name unknown` / `repository does not exist` | Some registries (e.g. ECR) require creating the repository first | Create the repository |
| `tag invalid` / `immutable` | The registry enforces immutable tags | Push a new tag instead of overwriting |

**Pushing many tags and platforms.** `docker push --all-tags` (`-a`) pushes every local tag of a repository. Multi-platform images are normally built and pushed in one step with `docker buildx build --platform ... --push`, covered in [Multi-Architecture Images](#multi-architecture-images).

**Example**

```bash
docker login -u jdoe                                   # Docker Hub; token as password

docker build -t jdoe/hello:1.0 - <<'EOF'
FROM alpine:3.20
CMD ["echo", "hello from Docker Hub"]
EOF

docker push jdoe/hello:1.0
# The push refers to repository [docker.io/jdoe/hello]
# 63ca1fbb43ae: Mounted from library/alpine          <- base layer reused, no upload
# 1.0: digest: sha256:7d2f... size: 528

# Add more tags and push them all
docker tag jdoe/hello:1.0 jdoe/hello:1
docker tag jdoe/hello:1.0 jdoe/hello:latest
docker push --all-tags jdoe/hello
# ... Layer already exists ...                       <- only manifests are written

# Verify from anywhere: remove locally and pull again
docker image rm jdoe/hello:1.0 jdoe/hello:1 jdoe/hello:latest
docker run --rm jdoe/hello:1.0
```

**Key takeaways**

- The image name decides the destination; tag the image with the full target name before pushing.
- Only missing blobs are uploaded; existing and cross-repository layers are reused.
- The tag is moved only after all blobs and the manifest are successfully stored.
- Use `--all-tags` for several tags and `buildx --push` for multi-platform images.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Push an image to your Docker Hub namespace, delete it locally, and run it again from the registry.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Change only the `CMD` of the image and push it as `:1.1`. Which lines in the push output say `Pushed` and which say `Layer already exists`? Explain why.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Two CI pipelines push the same tag at the same moment. What ends up in the registry, and how would you prevent the ambiguity?" *Hint:* consider when the tag is written relative to the blobs, last-write-wins semantics, unique tags per build, and immutable tags.

#### Private Registries

**Why run your own registry.** Public registries are not always acceptable: proprietary code must stay inside the company, regulated environments require data residency, air-gapped networks cannot reach the internet, and large fleets benefit from a local cache that avoids rate limits and speeds up pulls. A private registry is any registry you control, whether a single container or a full platform.

**Options**

| Product | Type | Highlights |
|---|---|---|
| `registry` (CNCF Distribution) | Minimal open-source server | The reference implementation; a single container; no UI or user management |
| Harbor | Open-source platform (CNCF) | Projects, RBAC, vulnerability scanning, replication, signing, quotas |
| GitLab / Gitea / Forgejo Container Registry | Built into the Git platform | Permissions follow the code repository |
| Sonatype Nexus, JFrog Artifactory | Commercial / OSS artifact managers | Containers alongside Maven, npm, PyPI, and other formats |
| Zot | Open-source, OCI-native | Lightweight, OCI-only, built-in extensions |

**Pieces a production registry needs**

```text
   docker CLI / CI / Kubernetes nodes
                |
                |  HTTPS (TLS cert trusted by clients)
                v
   +----------------------------+        +-------------------------+
   | registry                   | -----> | storage backend         |
   |  - authentication (htpasswd|        |  filesystem, S3, Azure, |
   |    / token service / LDAP) |        |  GCS, ...               |
   |  - authorization           |        +-------------------------+
   |  - garbage collection      |
   +----------------------------+
```

- **TLS**: Docker refuses plain HTTP to any registry except `localhost`. Use a certificate trusted by the host, place a private CA in `/etc/docker/certs.d/<host>:<port>/ca.crt`, or (for labs only) list the host in `insecure-registries` in `daemon.json`.
- **Authentication**: the bare `registry` image supports htpasswd; larger setups use a token service, LDAP/OIDC, or a platform like Harbor.
- **Garbage collection**: deleting a tag or manifest does not free blob storage; a garbage-collection run does.
- **Pull-through cache**: a registry configured as a proxy for Docker Hub stores each image the first time it is pulled and serves later pulls locally.

**Example: a registry with TLS and basic authentication**

```bash
mkdir -p auth certs

# Self-signed certificate for registry.internal (lab use; use your CA in production)
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:4096 -nodes -sha256 -days 365 \
  -keyout certs/registry.key -out certs/registry.crt \
  -subj "/CN=registry.internal" -addext "subjectAltName=DNS:registry.internal"

# Bcrypt password file (the registry image no longer ships htpasswd)
docker run --rm --entrypoint htpasswd httpd:2 -Bbn alice 's3cret' > auth/htpasswd

docker run -d --name registry --restart unless-stopped -p 5000:5000 \
  -v "$PWD/auth:/auth:ro" -v "$PWD/certs:/certs:ro" \
  -v registry-data:/var/lib/registry \
  -e REGISTRY_AUTH=htpasswd \
  -e REGISTRY_AUTH_HTPASSWD_REALM="Internal Registry" \
  -e REGISTRY_AUTH_HTPASSWD_PATH=/auth/htpasswd \
  -e REGISTRY_HTTP_TLS_CERTIFICATE=/certs/registry.crt \
  -e REGISTRY_HTTP_TLS_KEY=/certs/registry.key \
  -e REGISTRY_STORAGE_DELETE_ENABLED=true \
  registry:2

# On every client: trust the certificate (directory name must match host:port)
sudo mkdir -p /etc/docker/certs.d/registry.internal:5000
sudo cp certs/registry.crt /etc/docker/certs.d/registry.internal:5000/ca.crt
# (and make "registry.internal" resolve, e.g. via DNS or /etc/hosts)

docker login registry.internal:5000 -u alice
docker tag alpine:3.20 registry.internal:5000/base/alpine:3.20
docker push registry.internal:5000/base/alpine:3.20

# Reclaim space after deleting manifests (run while nothing is pushing)
docker exec registry registry garbage-collect --delete-untagged /etc/docker/registry/config.yml
```

**Example: a Docker Hub pull-through cache**

```bash
docker run -d --name hub-mirror -p 5001:5000 \
  -e REGISTRY_PROXY_REMOTEURL=https://registry-1.docker.io \
  -e REGISTRY_PROXY_USERNAME=jdoe -e REGISTRY_PROXY_PASSWORD="$HUB_TOKEN" \
  registry:2
```

```json
{
  "registry-mirrors": ["https://mirror.internal:5001"]
}
```

With this in `/etc/docker/daemon.json` (and a daemon restart), pulls of Docker Hub images try the mirror first and fall back to Docker Hub. The mirror must be served over HTTPS (add the TLS variables from the previous example) unless it is listed in `insecure-registries`. Mirrors configured this way apply only to Docker Hub images.

**Key takeaways**

- A private registry keeps images in-house, supports air-gapped networks, and avoids public rate limits.
- `registry:2` is a minimal server; Harbor and artifact managers add RBAC, scanning, replication, and UI.
- Production registries need TLS, authentication, durable storage, and periodic garbage collection.
- A pull-through cache in front of Docker Hub speeds up pulls and reduces rate-limit problems.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run `registry:2` on `localhost:5000`, push two images, and list them through `curl http://localhost:5000/v2/_catalog`.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Set up the TLS and htpasswd registry above. Verify that pushing without logging in fails, that pushing after `docker login` succeeds, and that `curl -u alice:s3cret --cacert certs/registry.crt https://registry.internal:5000/v2/_catalog` lists the repository.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your self-hosted registry's disk keeps growing although old tags are deleted every week. Why, and what would you change?" *Hint:* think about the difference between deleting references and deleting blobs, garbage collection, untagged manifests, and retention policies.

#### Cloud Registries (ECR, GCR, ACR, GHCR)

**Why use a cloud registry.** If your workloads run on a cloud provider or your code lives on GitHub, the provider's registry is usually the simplest choice: no servers to operate, access controlled through the identity system you already use, fast pulls from the same region, and built-in features such as scanning, replication, and retention policies.

**Comparison**

| Registry | Image name format | Log in | Access control | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Amazon ECR** | `<account>.dkr.ecr.<region>.amazonaws.com/<repo>:<tag>` | `aws ecr get-login-password \| docker login --password-stdin` | AWS IAM | Login tokens last 12 hours; repositories are usually created before pushing; lifecycle policies, tag immutability, scanning |
| **Google Artifact Registry** (successor to GCR) | `<region>-docker.pkg.dev/<project>/<repo>/<image>:<tag>` | `gcloud auth configure-docker <region>-docker.pkg.dev` | Google Cloud IAM | Container Registry (`gcr.io`) has been shut down in favor of Artifact Registry; `gcr.io` names can be served by Artifact Registry |
| **Azure Container Registry** | `<name>.azurecr.io/<repo>:<tag>` | `az acr login --name <name>` | Microsoft Entra ID, tokens | Geo-replication and private endpoints (Premium tier), ACR Tasks for builds |
| **GitHub Container Registry** | `ghcr.io/<owner>/<image>:<tag>` | `docker login ghcr.io` with a token | GitHub users, organizations, repository permissions | `GITHUB_TOKEN` in Actions; images can be linked to a repository; free for public images |

**Common capabilities.** Most cloud registries offer: vulnerability scanning on push, tag immutability, lifecycle/retention rules that delete old images automatically, replication across regions, and integration with the provider's container services, which can then pull with machine identities instead of stored passwords.

**Example: logging in and pushing**

```bash
# --- Amazon ECR ---
ACCOUNT=123456789012; REGION=eu-central-1
REGISTRY=$ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.$REGION.amazonaws.com
aws ecr create-repository --repository-name api --image-tag-mutability IMMUTABLE
aws ecr get-login-password --region $REGION \
  | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin $REGISTRY     # the username is literally "AWS"
docker tag api:1.4.2 $REGISTRY/api:1.4.2
docker push $REGISTRY/api:1.4.2

# --- Google Artifact Registry ---
gcloud artifacts repositories create containers --repository-format=docker --location=europe-west1
gcloud auth configure-docker europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev          # adds a credential helper entry
docker tag api:1.4.2 europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev/my-project/containers/api:1.4.2
docker push europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev/my-project/containers/api:1.4.2

# --- Azure Container Registry ---
az acr login --name acmeregistry
docker tag api:1.4.2 acmeregistry.azurecr.io/api:1.4.2
docker push acmeregistry.azurecr.io/api:1.4.2

# --- GitHub Container Registry ---
echo "$GHCR_TOKEN" | docker login ghcr.io -u <github-user> --password-stdin   # token with write:packages
docker tag api:1.4.2 ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2
docker push ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2
```

```yaml
# GitHub Actions: push to GHCR with the built-in token (no stored secret)
permissions:
  contents: read
  packages: write
steps:
  - uses: docker/login-action@v3
    with:
      registry: ghcr.io
      username: ${{ github.actor }}
      password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
```

**Key takeaways**

- Cloud registries integrate with the provider's identity system, compute services, and regions.
- Each has its own image name format, which is part of every tag you push.
- Logins are usually short-lived tokens obtained through the provider's CLI or a credential helper.
- Use tag immutability and lifecycle rules to keep registries trustworthy and costs under control.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Push an image to GHCR from your machine using a personal access token, then make the package public and pull it without logging in.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** In a cloud registry of your choice, configure a lifecycle or cleanup rule that keeps only the 10 most recent tags matching `git-*`. Push 12 tags and verify the result.
> 3. **Interview question:** "How would you let a fleet of cloud VMs pull private images without storing any long-lived registry password on them?" *Hint:* think about instance or workload identities, short-lived tokens, and credential helpers.

#### Registry Authentication

**Why authentication is subtle.** Logging in seems trivial, but the details decide whether credentials end up in plain text on a shared CI runner, whether `sudo docker` finds them, and why a login that "worked" still yields `denied`. Knowing the protocol and where credentials are stored makes these problems easy to reason about.

**The token flow.** Most registries use bearer-token authentication. The client does not send your password to the registry on every request; it exchanges credentials for a short-lived token scoped to a specific repository and action:

```text
  client                                   registry                   auth service
    | GET /v2/library/alpine/manifests/3.20  |                              |
    |--------------------------------------->|                              |
    | 401  WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="https://auth.docker.io/token",   |
    |      service="registry.docker.io",scope="repository:library/alpine:pull"
    |<---------------------------------------|                              |
    | GET realm?service=...&scope=...  (with username/token, or anonymous)  |
    |---------------------------------------------------------------------->|
    | 200  {"token": "eyJ..."}   short-lived, limited to that scope         |
    |<----------------------------------------------------------------------|
    | GET manifest  Authorization: Bearer eyJ...                            |
    |--------------------------------------->|                              |
    | 200  manifest                          |                              |
```

**Where credentials are stored.** `docker login` writes to the client's `~/.docker/config.json` (or the directory in `$DOCKER_CONFIG`). Without further configuration, the credentials are stored there **base64-encoded, which is not encryption**. A credential store or helper keeps them in a secure backend instead:

| Setting in `config.json` | Effect | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| `auths` | Per-registry entries; contain `auth` (base64 `user:password`) if no store is used | Plain-file fallback |
| `credsStore` | Default store for all registries | `desktop`, `osxkeychain`, `wincred`, `secretservice`, `pass` |
| `credHelpers` | Helper per registry, overrides `credsStore` | `ecr-login`, `gcloud`, `acr-env` |

A helper named `x` is the executable `docker-credential-x` on the `PATH`. Cloud helpers can generate fresh tokens on demand, so no login step is needed at all.

```json
{
  "auths": {
    "https://index.docker.io/v1/": {},
    "ghcr.io": {}
  },
  "credsStore": "desktop",
  "credHelpers": {
    "123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com": "ecr-login",
    "europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev": "gcloud"
  }
}
```

**Good practices**

- Use access tokens with the smallest scope (read-only for pulling), not account passwords.
- Use `--password-stdin` so the secret does not appear in shell history or `ps` output.
- On shared CI runners, give each job its own `DOCKER_CONFIG` directory and run `docker logout` (or delete the directory) at the end.
- Credentials belong to the *client user*: `sudo docker login` writes to root's config, which your normal user does not read.
- Orchestrators need their own pull credentials (for example Kubernetes `imagePullSecrets` or node identities); your local login does not transfer.

**Example**

```bash
# Non-interactive login without exposing the token in history or ps
echo "$REGISTRY_TOKEN" | docker login ghcr.io -u ci-bot --password-stdin

# What was stored? (without a credential store, the secret is merely base64)
jq '.auths' ~/.docker/config.json
jq -r '.auths["ghcr.io"].auth' ~/.docker/config.json | base64 -d   # ci-bot:<token>  <- readable!

# Isolated credentials for one CI job
export DOCKER_CONFIG=$(mktemp -d)
echo "$REGISTRY_TOKEN" | docker login ghcr.io -u ci-bot --password-stdin
docker push ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2
docker logout ghcr.io && rm -rf "$DOCKER_CONFIG"

# Walk through the token flow by hand (anonymous pull scope)
curl -s -o /dev/null -D - https://registry-1.docker.io/v2/library/alpine/manifests/3.20 | grep -i www-authenticate
TOKEN=$(curl -s "https://auth.docker.io/token?service=registry.docker.io&scope=repository:library/alpine:pull" | jq -r .token)
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Accept: application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json" \
  https://registry-1.docker.io/v2/library/alpine/manifests/3.20 | jq '.manifests[].platform'
```

**Key takeaways**

- Registries use a challenge/token flow: credentials are exchanged for short-lived, scoped tokens.
- `docker login` stores credentials in the client's `config.json`; without a store they are only base64-encoded.
- Use credential stores or helpers, scoped access tokens, and `--password-stdin`.
- Credentials are per client user and per machine; CI jobs and orchestrators need their own.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Log in to a registry, inspect `~/.docker/config.json`, and determine whether your credentials are in a credential store or in the file. Log out and inspect it again.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Reproduce the token flow with `curl` for a private repository of your own, passing your username and token to the auth endpoint. Request a `pull,push` scope and observe what the auth service grants.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A developer reports that `docker pull` of a private image works on their laptop but fails with `denied` in CI and in Kubernetes. What would you check?" *Hint:* consider which user and `DOCKER_CONFIG` the CI job uses, token scopes and expiry, the exact registry hostname in the credentials, and how the cluster nodes obtain pull credentials.

---

<a id="5-building-images-with-dockerfiles"></a>
## 5. Building Images with Dockerfiles

A Dockerfile is the source code of an image: a plain-text recipe that the builder executes step by step to produce the layers and configuration described in [chapter 4](#4-docker-images). This chapter covers the instructions that shape the filesystem and the runtime behavior of an image, how `docker build` turns a directory into an image and how its cache decides what to rebuild, how multi-stage builds separate build tools from the shipped artifact, and the practices that keep images small, fast to build, and reproducible. Almost every container you run in development, CI, and production starts from a Dockerfile, so writing them well pays off everywhere else. BuildKit-specific features such as cache mounts, secrets, and multi-platform builds are covered later in [chapter 9](#9-advanced-builds-with-buildkit).

<a id="51-dockerfile-basics"></a>
### 5.1 Dockerfile Basics

This section introduces the Dockerfile format and the core instructions that select a base image and build up the image's filesystem.

#### Dockerfile Syntax

**Why a Dockerfile.** You could build an image by starting a container, installing things by hand, and running `docker commit` (see [Committing Containers to Images](#committing-containers-to-images)). The result is a black box: nobody knows exactly what was done, it cannot be reviewed or reproduced, and rebuilding it with a security patch means repeating the manual work. A Dockerfile turns the procedure into versioned, reviewable code that any machine can execute to obtain the same image.

**Analogy.** A Dockerfile is to an image what a recipe is to a cake. The recipe can be shared, reviewed, and improved; the cake is the output you serve. If you only kept cakes and never recipes, you could never bake the same one again with less sugar.

**The format.** A Dockerfile is a text file (named `Dockerfile` by default) containing one instruction per line:

```text
INSTRUCTION arguments
```

| Element | Rule |
|---|---|
| Instructions | Case-insensitive, but written in UPPERCASE by convention to distinguish them from arguments |
| Order | Executed top to bottom; the first instruction must be `FROM` (only parser directives, comments, and global `ARG`s may precede it) |
| Comments | A line starting with `#` is a comment; a `#` in the middle of a line is **not** a comment, it is passed as part of the argument |
| Line continuation | A trailing `\` joins the next line to the current one (the escape character can be changed with a parser directive) |
| Parser directives | Special comments `# directive=value` that must appear at the very top of the file, before any other line, comment, or blank line |
| Variable substitution | `$VAR` and `${VAR}` are expanded in `FROM`, `COPY`, `ADD`, `ENV`, `ARG`, `WORKDIR`, `USER`, `EXPOSE`, `LABEL`, `VOLUME`, `STOPSIGNAL`; in `RUN`, `CMD`, `ENTRYPOINT` expansion is done by the shell, if there is one |

**Parser directives** you will meet:

- `# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1` selects the Dockerfile frontend (the parser BuildKit uses), so you get the latest stable syntax features regardless of the Docker version installed. Covered in [Dockerfile Frontends and Syntax Directive](#dockerfile-frontends-and-syntax-directive).
- `` # escape=` `` changes the escape character to a backtick, useful on Windows where `\` is the path separator.
- `# check=skip=<rules>` or `# check=error=true` configures the build checks (linting) that BuildKit runs on the Dockerfile.

**Variable expansion modifiers.** Besides `$VAR` and `${VAR}`, two modifiers are supported for instructions the builder expands itself:

| Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `${VAR:-default}` | Use `default` if `VAR` is unset or empty |
| `${VAR:+alt}` | Use `alt` if `VAR` is set and non-empty, otherwise empty |

**Instruction overview.** Instructions fall into two groups, which mirror the two halves of an image (layers and config):

```text
  Filesystem instructions (create layers)     Metadata instructions (change config only)
  ---------------------------------------     ------------------------------------------
  RUN    execute a command                    CMD          default command
  COPY   copy files from the context          ENTRYPOINT   fixed executable
  ADD    copy files, URLs, archives           ENV          environment variables
                                              WORKDIR      working directory (*)
  Build-control instructions                  USER         default user
  ---------------------------------------     EXPOSE       documented ports
  FROM    start a stage from a base image     VOLUME       mount points
  ARG     build-time variable                 LABEL        metadata key/value pairs
  SHELL   default shell for shell form        HEALTHCHECK  health probe
  ONBUILD trigger for child images            STOPSIGNAL   stop signal

  (*) WORKDIR also creates the directory if it does not exist
```

**Example: an annotated Dockerfile**

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
# ^ parser directive: must be the very first line

# A normal comment. Blank lines are ignored.
FROM python:3.13-slim

# Metadata only, no layer
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.source="https://github.com/acme/hello"

WORKDIR /app

# Line continuation keeps long commands readable
RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

COPY app.py .

# The '#' below is NOT a Dockerfile comment: the whole line is handed to /bin/sh,
# which treats "# world" as a shell comment, so this prints "hello". In instructions
# without a shell (COPY, WORKDIR, CMD in exec form, ...) it would become an argument.
RUN echo hello # world

ENV PORT=8000
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
```

```bash
# Build the Dockerfile in the current directory and tag the result
docker build -t hello:dev .

# Lint the Dockerfile without building it (BuildKit build checks)
docker build --check .
```

**Key takeaways**

- A Dockerfile is the reproducible, reviewable source of an image; `docker commit` is not.
- One instruction per line, executed in order, starting with `FROM`.
- `#` starts a comment only at the beginning of a line; parser directives must be the very first lines.
- `RUN`, `COPY`, and `ADD` create layers; most other instructions only modify the image config.
- Use `# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1` to get current Dockerfile features independently of the installed Docker version.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Write a three-line Dockerfile based on `alpine:3.20` that prints a message at startup. Build it, run it, and use `docker image history` to see which lines produced layers.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Add `# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1` *after* a comment line and build again. Then move it to the first line. Explain what changed and why the position matters.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why do teams prefer Dockerfiles over `docker commit`, even for a one-off image?" *Hint:* think about review, auditability, rebuilding with patched base images, and caching.

#### FROM

**Why FROM.** Nobody wants to assemble a Linux userland, a language runtime, and its libraries from nothing for every application. `FROM` lets you stand on a maintained foundation (see [Base Images](#base-images)) and add only what is specific to your application. It also starts a new **build stage**, which is the building block of multi-stage builds.

**Syntax**

```dockerfile
FROM [--platform=<platform>] <image>[:<tag>|@<digest>] [AS <name>]
```

| Part | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `<image>` | Any image reference: `ubuntu`, `ghcr.io/acme/base`, a local image, or the special name `scratch` |
| `:<tag>` | Defaults to `latest` if omitted, which is almost never what you want |
| `@<digest>` | Pins the exact content; the tag, if present, becomes documentation only |
| `AS <name>` | Names the stage so later stages can reference it (`COPY --from=<name>`, `FROM <name>`) |
| `--platform` | Selects the platform variant of a multi-platform image, e.g. `linux/amd64`; mostly used with `$BUILDPLATFORM` for cross-compilation |

**What FROM does.** The builder resolves the reference, pulls the image if it is not available locally, and uses its layers and its config (environment, `CMD`, `ENTRYPOINT`, `WORKDIR`, `USER`, labels) as the starting point. Everything the base image defines is inherited until you override it.

```text
   FROM python:3.13-slim
          |
          v
   +-------------------------------------+
   | inherited layers  (debian + python) |
   | inherited config:                   |
   |   ENV PATH=/usr/local/bin:...       |
   |   ENV LANG=C.UTF-8                  |
   |   CMD ["python3"]                   |
   +-------------------------------------+
          |
          v   your instructions add layers on top and override config
```

**Special cases**

- `FROM scratch` starts from an empty filesystem with no shell, no libc, nothing. It is used for static binaries and is covered in [Distroless and Scratch Images](#distroless-and-scratch-images).
- A Dockerfile can contain several `FROM` lines. Each one starts a fresh stage; only the last stage (or the one selected with `--target`) becomes the output image.
- An `ARG` declared *before* the first `FROM` can be used in `FROM` lines, which lets you parameterize the base image.

**Choosing the reference.** Prefer a specific tag (`python:3.13-slim`), and for production pin a digest as well (see [Pinning Versions](#pinning-versions)). Avoid `latest`: the build will silently change when upstream publishes a new major version.

**Example**

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

# Global ARG: usable in FROM lines only (unless re-declared inside a stage)
ARG PYTHON_VERSION=3.13

# Tag for humans, digest for reproducibility
FROM python:${PYTHON_VERSION}-slim@sha256:<digest> AS base

# A second stage that starts from the first one
FROM base AS app
COPY app.py /app/app.py
CMD ["python", "/app/app.py"]
```

```bash
# Inspect what a base image will make you inherit
docker image inspect python:3.13-slim \
  --format 'Env: {{.Config.Env}}{{"\n"}}Cmd: {{.Config.Cmd}}{{"\n"}}User: "{{.Config.User}}"'

# Build against a different base version without editing the file
docker build --build-arg PYTHON_VERSION=3.12 -t app:py312 .
```

**Key takeaways**

- `FROM` selects the base image and starts a new build stage; it must come first.
- Layers *and* configuration (`ENV`, `CMD`, `USER`, ...) are inherited from the base image.
- Always use an explicit tag; pin a digest when you need reproducible builds.
- `AS <name>` names a stage for multi-stage builds; `FROM scratch` starts empty.
- `ARG` before `FROM` parameterizes the base image.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Build an image `FROM python:3.13-slim` with no other instructions and run it. Explain why you land in a Python REPL even though your Dockerfile has no `CMD`.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Parameterize the base image with a global `ARG`, then try to `RUN echo $PYTHON_VERSION` inside the stage. Explain the empty output and fix it.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A build that has not changed in months suddenly fails in CI with a dependency error. The Dockerfile starts with `FROM node`. What happened, and how do you prevent it?" *Hint:* think about what `latest` points to over time and what tags and digests guarantee.

#### RUN

**Why RUN.** A base image rarely has everything your application needs: system packages, a compiled dependency, a configured directory structure. `RUN` executes a command inside a temporary container during the build and saves the resulting filesystem changes as a new layer. It is how you "install things" into an image.

**How it works.**

```text
   previous layer stack
          |
          v
   +--------------------+   1. start a temporary container from the current state
   | temp container     |   2. execute the command (as the current USER, in WORKDIR)
   |  apt-get install   |   3. if the exit code is not 0, the build fails
   +--------------------+   4. snapshot the filesystem diff as a new layer
          |
          v
   new layer on top; the temp container is discarded
```

Only the **filesystem** survives. Processes started by `RUN` are killed when the step ends, and shell state (variables set with `export`, `cd`) does not carry over to the next `RUN`, because each one runs in a fresh shell.

**Two forms.**

```dockerfile
# Shell form: run through /bin/sh -c, so pipes, &&, and $VARS work
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl

# Exec form: run the binary directly, no shell processing
RUN ["/usr/local/bin/setup", "--mode", "prod"]
```

The differences are explored in [Shell vs Exec Form](#shell-vs-exec-form). For `RUN`, the shell form is used in the vast majority of cases.

**Writing robust RUN steps**

| Problem | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `apt-get install` uses a stale package index | `apt-get update` was cached in an earlier, separate `RUN` | Always `update` and `install` in the same `RUN` |
| Image is large after "cleaning up" | Cleanup in a later `RUN` only hides files from an earlier layer | Clean up in the **same** `RUN` that created the files |
| `curl ... \| tar x` "succeeds" though the download failed | `/bin/sh` returns the exit code of the last command in a pipe | `SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-o", "pipefail", "-c"]`, or `set -o pipefail` where supported |
| A command in a long chain fails silently | `;` continues after errors | Chain with `&&`, or start with `set -eux` |
| Build hangs waiting for input | Interactive prompts (tzdata, debconf) | `DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive` on that `RUN`, `-y` flags |

**Example**

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM debian:12-slim

# One logical step, one layer: update, install, clean up together
RUN set -eux; \
    apt-get update; \
    DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
        ca-certificates \
        curl; \
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*          # remove the package index in the same layer
```
