| External image | `COPY --from=nginx:alpine /etc/nginx/nginx.conf /etc/nginx/` | Pulls the image if needed; pin it like a base image |
| Named build context | `COPY --from=assets . /srv/static` | Context passed with `--build-context assets=...` |

**Useful flags**

- `--chown=uid:gid` and `--chmod=755` set ownership and permissions while copying, avoiding an extra layer.
- `--link` copies the files into an independent layer that does not depend on the layers beneath it. If the base image changes, the copied layer can be reused instead of being recreated, which speeds up rebuilds and "rebases".

**What runtime stages commonly need besides the binary**

```text
  From the builder (or an SDK image)          Why
  -----------------------------------------   ----------------------------------------
  /out/app                                    the application itself
  /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt          outbound HTTPS (TLS verification)
  /usr/share/zoneinfo (or embedded tz data)   time zone conversions
  /etc/passwd, /etc/group (minimal entries)   a named non-root user in scratch images
  static assets, templates, migrations        files the app reads at runtime
```

**Example**

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:22-slim AS frontend
WORKDIR /web
COPY web/package.json web/package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY web/ .
RUN npm run build
# Output in /web/dist

FROM golang:1.23 AS backend
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
# -tags timetzdata embeds the time zone database in the binary (no /usr/share/zoneinfo needed)
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -tags timetzdata -o /out/server ./cmd/server

FROM scratch
# Only the exact files needed, each with explicit ownership
COPY --from=backend  /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt /etc/ssl/certs/
COPY --from=backend  --chown=10001:10001 /out/server /server
COPY --from=frontend --chown=10001:10001 /web/dist /static
USER 10001:10001
ENTRYPOINT ["/server", "--static-dir=/static"]
```

```bash
docker build -t fullstack .

# Verify what reached the final image (scratch has no shell: export and list instead)
docker create --name probe fullstack
docker export probe | tar -t | head -20
docker rm probe
```

**Key takeaways**

- `COPY --from=<stage|image|context>` is the only bridge between stages.
- Copy exact paths, not whole working directories, so source, caches, and secrets stay behind.
- Name stages instead of using numeric indexes.
- Remember non-obvious runtime needs: CA certificates, time zone data, user entries, assets.
- `--chown`, `--chmod`, and `--link` make copies cleaner and rebuilds faster.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Copy `/etc/os-release` from `debian:12-slim` into an `alpine:3.20` image with `COPY --from`, then print both release files.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Remove the CA certificates line from the example and make the server perform an HTTPS request at startup. Observe the error, explain it, and restore the line.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A multi-stage image is unexpectedly large. How do you find out what was copied into it, and what typical mistakes cause this?" *Hint:* think about `docker image history`, layer inspection tools, and broad `COPY --from=build /app /app` lines.

#### Targeting Specific Stages

**Why target stages.** One Dockerfile can describe more than one useful image: a development image with debugging tools and hot reload, a test image that runs the test suite, and a slim production image. `--target` builds the Dockerfile only up to a named stage, so the same file serves every environment without duplication, and CI can run tests in exactly the same environment it builds for production.

**How it works.** `docker build --target <stage>` treats the named stage as the final one. BuildKit only builds the stages that this target depends on.

```text
                 +--> dev       (docker build --target dev)
                 |
  base --> deps -+--> test      (docker build --target test)   runs the test suite
                 |
                 +--> build --> prod   (default: last stage)
```

**Example**

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:22-slim AS base
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./

# All dependencies (including devDependencies)
FROM base AS deps
RUN npm ci

# Development: hot reload, source mounted at runtime
FROM deps AS dev
ENV NODE_ENV=development
CMD ["npm", "run", "dev"]

# Test: the build fails if any test fails
FROM deps AS test
COPY . .
RUN npm run lint && npm test

# Build the production bundle
FROM deps AS build
COPY . .
RUN npm run build && npm prune --omit=dev

# Production (last stage = default target)
FROM node:22-slim AS prod
ENV NODE_ENV=production
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build --chown=node:node /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build --chown=node:node /app/dist ./dist
USER node
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
```

```bash
docker build --target dev  -t web:dev .     # for docker compose / local work
docker build --target test -t web:test .    # CI: non-zero exit if tests fail
docker build -t web:1.0 .                   # prod: the last stage

# Export only test reports from a stage, without creating an image
# (requires a stage that copies reports to its root, e.g. FROM scratch AS reports)
docker build --target reports -o type=local,dest=./reports .
```

In Compose, the same idea is expressed with `build.target: dev` (see [build vs image](#build-vs-image)).

**Key takeaways**

- `--target <stage>` stops the build at a named stage and makes it the output.
- Only stages the target depends on are built (with BuildKit).
- A single Dockerfile can define dev, test, and prod images that share cached stages.
- A test stage that runs the suite in a `RUN` step makes the build itself fail on test failures.
- Without `--target`, the last stage is built, so put the production stage last.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Build the `dev` and `prod` targets of the example and compare their sizes and the presence of devDependencies.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Add a `FROM scratch AS reports` stage that copies a coverage report from the `test` stage, and export it to your machine with `-o type=local`.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your production stage is not the last one in the Dockerfile, and someone runs `docker build .` without `--target`. What happens, and how would you prevent mistakes?" *Hint:* think about the default target and conventions for stage ordering.

#### Language-Specific Patterns

**Why patterns differ by language.** Every ecosystem produces a different kind of artifact. Go and Rust can compile a single static binary; Java produces JARs that need a JVM; Node and Python ship interpreted source plus a dependency tree. The right multi-stage layout depends on *what* has to be carried from the builder to the runtime and *what* the runtime needs to execute it.

**Overview**

| Language | Builder base | Artifact to copy | Runtime base | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Go | `golang` | One static binary | `scratch`, `distroless/static` | `CGO_ENABLED=0`; add CA certificates if needed |
| Rust | `rust` | One binary | `distroless/cc`, `debian-slim`; `scratch` with musl target | Build dependencies first with a dummy `main.rs` or a cache mount |
| Java | `maven`, `gradle`, `eclipse-temurin:*-jdk` | JAR (or exploded layers) | `eclipse-temurin:*-jre`, `distroless/java` | Optional `jlink` for a custom minimal JRE |
| Node.js | `node` | `node_modules` (prod only) + built output | `node:*-slim`, `distroless/nodejs` | `npm ci`, then prune devDependencies |
| Python | `python` | Virtual environment + source | `python:*-slim` | Build native wheels in the builder; copy the venv |
| Static frontend | `node` | `dist/` folder | `nginx:alpine`, `caddy` | No Node.js in production at all |

**Go**

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM golang:1.23 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
# Static binary, stripped of debug info
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o /out/app ./cmd/app

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot
COPY --from=build /out/app /app
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]
```

**Java (Maven)**

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 AS build
WORKDIR /src
# Resolve dependencies first: cached until pom.xml changes
COPY pom.xml .
RUN mvn -B -q dependency:go-offline
COPY src ./src
RUN mvn -B -q package -DskipTests

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
RUN useradd --system --uid 10001 app
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /src/target/app.jar app.jar
USER 10001
# Respect the container's memory limit instead of the host's RAM
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75", "-jar", "app.jar"]
```

**Python**

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM python:3.13-slim AS build
RUN python -m venv /opt/venv
ENV PATH="/opt/venv/bin:$PATH"
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

FROM python:3.13-slim
# Same base and Python version as the builder, so the venv paths and ABI match
COPY --from=build /opt/venv /opt/venv
ENV PATH="/opt/venv/bin:$PATH" \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN useradd --system --uid 10001 app
USER 10001
CMD ["python", "-m", "gunicorn", "app:app", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"]
```

**Static frontend (React, Vue, Angular, ...)**

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:22-slim AS build
WORKDIR /web
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM nginx:alpine
COPY --from=build /web/dist /usr/share/nginx/html
# nginx.conf with SPA fallback (try_files $uri /index.html)
COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
```

**Cross-language rules of thumb**

- Copy dependency manifests and install dependencies before copying source code.
- Keep builder and runtime on compatible bases (same libc, same language version) unless the artifact is fully static.
- Install only runtime packages in the final stage; development headers stay in the builder.
- For faster dependency downloads across builds, use BuildKit cache mounts (see [Cache Mounts](#cache-mounts)).

**Key takeaways**

- The artifact type decides the pattern: static binary, JAR, venv, `node_modules` + bundle, or static files.
- Compiled languages can often run on `scratch` or distroless; interpreted ones need a slim runtime.
- Match libc and language versions between builder and runtime stages.
- Frontend builds should end in a web server image, not a Node.js image.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Containerize a small static website built with a JavaScript framework using the frontend pattern, and compare the final size with the `node:22-slim` image.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Build the Python pattern with a dependency that has native code (e.g. `psycopg2` or `lxml`). Then switch only the runtime stage to `python:3.13-alpine` and explain the failure.
> 3. **Interview question:** "How would you containerize a Spring Boot application so that rebuilds after a small code change are fast and the image is small?" *Hint:* think about caching Maven/Gradle dependencies, JDK versus JRE, layered JARs or `jlink`, and container-aware JVM memory flags.

<a id="55-dockerfile-best-practices"></a>
### 5.5 Dockerfile Best Practices

This section collects the practices that make images fast to build, small to ship, secure to run, and reproducible over time.

#### Layer Ordering

**Why ordering matters.** Because a cache miss invalidates every following step (see [Cache Invalidation](#cache-invalidation)), the position of each instruction decides how much work a typical rebuild does. The same instructions in a different order can mean a 5-second rebuild or a 5-minute one, and a 2 MB or 200 MB download for every deployment that has to pull the image.

**Analogy.** Think of packing a suitcase you repack every day. Things you never change (shoes, toiletries) go at the bottom; things you swap daily (today's shirt) go on top. If you put the daily shirt at the bottom, you have to unpack everything each morning.

**The principle: from stable to volatile**

```text
  Change frequency        Instruction examples
  ----------------        --------------------------------------------------------
  Almost never            FROM, system packages (apt/apk), users, WORKDIR
  Rarely                  language runtime config, tool downloads
  Sometimes               dependency manifests + install (package.json, go.mod,
                          requirements.txt, pom.xml)
  Every commit            COPY of source code, build of the application
  Metadata (cheap)        ENV, EXPOSE, USER, CMD (placement matters less, but
                          values that change per build, like a version label,
                          belong at the end)
```

**Bad vs good**

```dockerfile
# BAD: any source change re-runs npm ci and re-downloads all dependencies
FROM node:22-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm ci
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends tini \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

```dockerfile
# GOOD: stable steps first, dependencies cached until the manifests change
FROM node:22-slim
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends tini \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .
ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/bin/tini", "--"]
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

**Impact on deployments.** Ordering also affects pulls: when only the top layer changes, servers that already have the previous version download only that layer.

| Change | Bad ordering: rebuilt / pulled | Good ordering: rebuilt / pulled |
|---|---|---|
| Edit `server.js` | `COPY . .` + `npm ci` + apt step (~150 MB) | `COPY . .` only (~200 KB) |
| Add a dependency | Same as above | `npm ci` + `COPY . .` |
| Base image update | Everything | Everything |

**Key takeaways**

- Order instructions from least to most frequently changing.
- Copy dependency manifests and install dependencies before copying the source code.
- Good ordering speeds up both builds (cache hits) and deployments (fewer layers to pull).
- Place values that change on every build (version labels, build args) as late as possible.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Build both versions of the example, edit `server.js`, rebuild, and compare the time and the `CACHED` lines.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Push both versions to a local registry (`registry:2`), change one source line, push again, and compare how many bytes each push uploads.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Given a Dockerfile that copies the whole repository on its second line, how would you restructure it for a Python project using `requirements.txt`?" *Hint:* separate the manifest copy and install from the source copy, and think about what else changes rarely.

#### Minimizing Layers

**Why it matters, and why not too much.** Each `RUN`, `COPY`, and `ADD` creates a layer, and files written in one layer cannot be truly removed by a later one: a later delete only adds a whiteout on top while the bytes remain in the image. So the step that downloads, uses, and cleans up temporary files must be a single instruction. That is the real reason to merge commands. Reducing the layer count for its own sake brings little benefit, and merging unrelated steps hurts caching and readability.

**The deleted-file trap**

```dockerfile
# Three layers: the 300 MB archive is still inside layer 1
RUN curl -fsSLO https://example.com/sdk.tar.gz
RUN tar -xzf sdk.tar.gz -C /opt && /opt/sdk/install.sh
RUN rm sdk.tar.gz
```

```text
  layer 3: whiteout for sdk.tar.gz       0 B   (hides the file)
  layer 2: /opt/sdk + installed files    150 MB
  layer 1: sdk.tar.gz                    300 MB  <- still shipped and pulled
  ----------------------------------------------
  total                                  450 MB
```

```dockerfile
# One layer: the archive never reaches a committed layer
RUN set -eux; \
    curl -fsSLO https://example.com/sdk.tar.gz; \
    tar -xzf sdk.tar.gz -C /opt; \
    /opt/sdk/install.sh; \
    rm -rf sdk.tar.gz /opt/sdk/docs
```

**Guidelines**

| Do | Avoid |
|---|---|
| Merge a download/install/cleanup sequence into one `RUN` | Merging unrelated steps that change at different rates |
| Combine package installs into one `apt-get install` with a sorted list, one package per line | A separate `RUN apt-get install` per package |
| Use multi-stage builds to drop whole layers of build tooling | Fighting layer counts in a single stage with very long `RUN` lines |
| Use heredocs for readable multi-line scripts (see [Heredocs in Dockerfiles](#heredocs-in-dockerfiles)) | Unreadable 30-line chains of `&& \` |
| Remember that metadata instructions do not create layers | Squashing everything into one layer, which defeats layer sharing |

**Example: readable and minimal**

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM debian:12-slim

# One RUN, sorted package list, cleanup in the same layer
RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
      ca-certificates \
      curl \
      git \
      jq \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Heredoc form (Dockerfile syntax 1.4+): still one layer
RUN <<EOF
set -eux
curl -fsSLO https://example.com/sdk.tar.gz
tar -xzf sdk.tar.gz -C /opt
rm sdk.tar.gz
EOF
```

```bash
docker image history --format 'table {{.CreatedBy}}\t{{.Size}}' myimage
```

**Key takeaways**

- Deleting files in a later layer does not shrink the image; clean up in the same `RUN` that created them.
- Merge steps that belong together (download, install, clean); keep unrelated steps separate for caching.
- Sort multi-line package lists for readability and clean diffs.
- Multi-stage builds remove build-time layers more effectively than chaining commands.
- Fewer layers is a means, not a goal.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Reproduce the three-layer SDK example with any large file (e.g. `dd` 100 MB), then the single-layer version. Compare sizes with `docker image ls` and `docker image history`.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Take a Dockerfile with ten `RUN` lines and decide which ones to merge and which to keep separate. Justify each decision in terms of caching and size.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Is it always better to have fewer layers?" *Hint:* weigh removed-but-shipped files against cache granularity, parallel layer downloads, and sharing layers between images.

#### Choosing Minimal Base Images

**Why minimal.** Every package in the base image is something you ship, pull, scan, and patch, even if your application never uses it. A smaller base means faster pulls and startups, fewer CVEs in scanner reports, and fewer tools available to an attacker. But "minimal" has costs too: missing libraries, a different C library, or no shell for debugging. The goal is the smallest base that runs your application *reliably*. The families of base images are introduced in [Base Images](#base-images); this topic is about choosing between them.

**Variants of official images.** Most official language images come in several flavors:

| Tag suffix | Example | Based on | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| (none) / `-bookworm` | `python:3.13` | Full Debian with build tools | Builder stages |
| `-slim` / `-slim-bookworm` | `python:3.13-slim` | Debian slim, minimal packages | Default runtime choice |
| `-alpine` | `python:3.13-alpine` | Alpine Linux (musl) | Very small runtimes, when compatible |
| `-jre` vs `-jdk` | `eclipse-temurin:21-jre` | Runtime only vs full SDK | Java runtime vs build |

**Alpine and musl: what to watch for.** Alpine is small mainly because it uses musl libc and BusyBox instead of glibc and GNU tools. This is fine for many workloads, but:

- Prebuilt binaries and Python wheels built for glibc (`manylinux`) do not work; pip may have to compile packages from source, which makes builds slower and the builder stage bigger.
- DNS resolution, locale handling, and memory allocator performance differ from glibc and can show up as subtle behavior or performance changes.
- BusyBox tools accept fewer options than their GNU counterparts, so scripts may break.

**Decision guide**

```text
  Is the artifact a static binary (Go with CGO_ENABLED=0, Rust musl)?
     yes --> scratch or distroless/static
     no
      |
  Does it need only a language runtime + glibc?
     yes --> distroless (java, nodejs, cc, python) or <lang>:<ver>-slim
     no
      |
  Does it need extra system packages or a shell at runtime?
     yes --> debian-slim / ubuntu based image, or alpine if every dependency supports musl
```

**Example: comparing candidates**

```bash
for img in python:3.13 python:3.13-slim python:3.13-alpine; do
  docker pull -q "$img" >/dev/null
  printf '%-22s %s\n' "$img" "$(docker image inspect -f '{{.Size}}' "$img" | numfmt --to=iec)"
done
# python:3.13            ~1.0G
# python:3.13-slim       ~120M
# python:3.13-alpine     ~45M

# Package count, a rough proxy for attack surface
docker run --rm python:3.13-slim sh -c 'dpkg -l | grep -c ^ii'
docker run --rm python:3.13      sh -c 'dpkg -l | grep -c ^ii'
```

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
# Full image for building wheels, slim image for running them
FROM python:3.13 AS build
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip wheel --no-cache-dir --wheel-dir /wheels -r requirements.txt

FROM python:3.13-slim
COPY --from=build /wheels /wheels
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir /wheels/* && rm -rf /wheels
```

**Key takeaways**

- Choose the smallest base that runs your application reliably, not the smallest that exists.
- `-slim` variants are a safe default for runtimes; full images are best for builder stages.
- Alpine is small but uses musl and BusyBox; check binary, wheel, and script compatibility.
- Static binaries can use `scratch` or distroless; others need at least the runtime and libc.
- Fewer packages means fewer vulnerabilities to triage and patch.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Compare the sizes and package counts of `node:22`, `node:22-slim`, and `node:22-alpine`.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Install a Python package with native extensions (e.g. `pandas`) on `python:3.13-slim` and on `python:3.13-alpine`. Compare build times, final sizes, and whether prebuilt wheels were used.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your team switched to Alpine to shrink images, and now some requests are slower and one library crashes. What could be going on?" *Hint:* think about musl versus glibc, DNS resolver behavior, memory allocators, and binaries compiled for glibc.

#### Distroless and Scratch Images

**Why go further than slim.** Even a slim distro contains a shell, a package manager, and coreutils. Your application never calls them, but an attacker who gains code execution can use them to download tools and explore. **Distroless** images contain only the application's runtime dependencies (libc, CA certificates, time zone data, a passwd file, and the language runtime if needed), with no shell or package manager. **scratch** goes all the way: an empty filesystem in which you provide every file yourself.

**Analogy.** A slim image is a furnished studio apartment. Distroless is a hotel room: bed, light, and a lock, nothing to cook with. Scratch is an empty room into which you carry exactly the objects you need.

**Comparison**

| Aspect | `debian:12-slim` | Distroless (`gcr.io/distroless/*`) | `scratch` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shell / package manager | Yes / Yes | No / No | No / No |
| libc | glibc | glibc (`base`, `cc`), none in `static` | None (static binaries only) |
| CA certs, tzdata, `/etc/passwd` | Installable | Included | You copy them in |
| Non-root user | You create it | Built in (`:nonroot` tag, UID 65532) | You define it (numeric `USER`) |
| Typical size | ~75 MB | ~2 MB (`static`) to ~200 MB (`java`) | Size of your files |
| `docker exec sh` | Works | Fails (use the `:debug` tag or `docker debug`) | Fails |
| Shell-form `CMD`/`RUN` | Works | Fails: exec form only | Fails: exec form only |

**Distroless image families**

| Image | For |
|---|---|
| `gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12` | Static binaries (Go, Rust musl) |
| `gcr.io/distroless/base-debian12` | Dynamically linked binaries needing glibc |
| `gcr.io/distroless/cc-debian12` | Like `base`, plus `libgcc`/`libstdc++` (Rust, C++) |
| `gcr.io/distroless/java21-debian12` | JVM applications |
| `gcr.io/distroless/nodejs22-debian12` | Node.js applications |

Similar minimal, frequently rebuilt images are offered by other vendors, such as Chainguard Images and Docker Hardened Images.

**Example: scratch, done properly**

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM golang:1.23-alpine AS build
RUN apk add --no-cache ca-certificates \
 && echo 'app:x:10001:10001:app:/:/sbin/nologin' > /etc/passwd.min \
 && echo 'app:x:10001:' > /etc/group.min
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -tags timetzdata -ldflags="-s -w" -o /out/app ./cmd/app

FROM scratch
# TLS roots, minimal user database, the binary: nothing else
COPY --from=build /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt /etc/ssl/certs/
COPY --from=build /etc/passwd.min /etc/passwd
COPY --from=build /etc/group.min /etc/group
COPY --from=build /out/app /app
USER 10001:10001
# Exec form is mandatory: there is no /bin/sh
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]
```

**Debugging shell-less containers**

```bash
# Distroless debug variant includes a BusyBox shell
docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh gcr.io/distroless/base-debian12:debug

# Attach a toolbox to a running shell-less container (Docker Desktop feature)
docker debug mycontainer

# Generic approach: a tools container sharing the target's PID and network namespaces
docker run --rm -it --pid container:mycontainer --network container:mycontainer busybox sh
```

See [docker debug](#docker-debug) for more details.

**Key takeaways**

- Distroless images contain the runtime dependencies only: no shell, no package manager.
- `scratch` is empty; you must add CA certificates, time zone data, and user entries yourself if needed.
- Both require exec-form `CMD`/`ENTRYPOINT` and a `HEALTHCHECK` that does not depend on a shell.
- Use `:nonroot` distroless tags or a numeric `USER` in scratch images.
- Plan debugging in advance: `:debug` tags, `docker debug`, or namespace-sharing sidecar containers.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run `docker run --rm -it gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12 sh` and explain the error. Then try the `:debug` tag.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Build the scratch example without the CA certificates and make the app call an HTTPS endpoint. Then remove the `/etc/passwd` copy, change `USER` to `app`, and explain the second failure.
> 3. **Interview question:** "What are the trade-offs of distroless images, and how would you troubleshoot a production issue inside one?" *Hint:* weigh attack surface and CVE count against debuggability, and think about ephemeral debug containers and namespace sharing.

#### Pinning Versions

**Why pin.** A Dockerfile that says `FROM node` and `RUN apt-get install curl` describes a moving target: the same file produces a different image every week. That breaks reproducibility (a bug cannot be reproduced from last month's build), introduces surprise breakage (a new major version arrives silently), and weakens supply-chain security (a compromised or re-pushed tag is accepted automatically). Pinning makes inputs explicit, so changes become deliberate, reviewable updates.

**Analogy.** Pinning is like a lockfile for your operating system. Without it, "install the dependencies" means "install whatever is newest today".

**Levels of pinning**

| What | Loose | Better | Strict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Base image | `FROM node` (`latest`) | `FROM node:22.11-slim` | `FROM node:22.11-slim@sha256:<digest>` |
| OS packages | `apt-get install curl` | `curl=7.88.*` | Exact version, or a snapshot repository |
| Language dependencies | `pip install flask` | `flask==3.0.3` in `requirements.txt` | Lockfile with hashes (`pip-compile --generate-hashes`, `package-lock.json` + `npm ci`, `go.sum`) |
| Downloaded tools | `curl .../latest/tool` | Versioned URL | Versioned URL + checksum (`ADD --checksum`, `sha256sum -c`) |
| Dockerfile frontend | none | `# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1` | `# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.10` (or a digest) |

**The trade-off: reproducibility versus freshness.** A pinned digest never receives security fixes on its own. Pinning without an update process just freezes vulnerabilities in place. The solution is to pin *and* automate updates:

```text
   pin exact versions/digests  -->  bot opens PR when upstream changes  -->  CI builds & tests
         (reproducible)                (Renovate, Dependabot)                (safe to merge)
                ^                                                                    |
                +------------------------------ merge ---------------------------------+
```

**Example**

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

# Tag documents intent, digest guarantees content (Renovate/Dependabot can update both)
FROM python:3.13.1-slim-bookworm@sha256:<digest>

# Exact OS package versions (look them up with: apt-cache policy <pkg>)
RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
      libpq5=15.* \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Fully locked Python dependencies with hashes
COPY requirements.lock .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --require-hashes -r requirements.lock

# Pinned tool download with verification
ARG HADOLINT_VERSION=2.12.0
ARG HADOLINT_SHA256=<sha256>
RUN curl -fsSL -o /usr/local/bin/hadolint \
      "https://github.com/hadolint/hadolint/releases/download/v${HADOLINT_VERSION}/hadolint-Linux-x86_64" \
 && echo "${HADOLINT_SHA256}  /usr/local/bin/hadolint" | sha256sum -c - \
 && chmod +x /usr/local/bin/hadolint
```

```bash
# Find the digest currently behind a tag (the "Digest:" line of the index)
docker buildx imagetools inspect python:3.13.1-slim-bookworm | grep -m1 Digest

# or after pulling
docker image inspect python:3.13.1-slim-bookworm --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}'
```

**Key takeaways**

- Unpinned inputs make builds non-reproducible and can introduce silent breakage.
- Pin base images to a specific tag, and to a digest for strict reproducibility.
- Use lockfiles with hashes for language dependencies and checksums for downloaded tools.
- Pinning must be paired with automated update PRs, or you freeze vulnerabilities in place.
- Rebuild regularly even without code changes, so pinned bases still receive patches through updates.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Find the current digest of `alpine:3.20` and rewrite a `FROM` line to pin it. Verify that `docker build` uses that digest in its output.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Generate a hashed lockfile for a small Python project with `pip-compile --generate-hashes`, install it with `--require-hashes`, then modify one hash and observe the failure.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Pinning by digest improves reproducibility but seems to conflict with getting security updates. How do you reconcile the two?" *Hint:* think about automated dependency update tools, scheduled rebuilds, and vulnerability scanning in CI.

#### Reducing Image Size

**Why size matters.** Image size affects every place the image travels: CI upload time, registry storage costs, pull time when scaling out or recovering from a node failure, cold starts in serverless platforms, and the number of packages a scanner reports. Shrinking an image is usually a combination of the techniques from this chapter, applied in order of impact.

**Techniques, roughly by impact**

| Technique | Typical saving | Where it is covered |
|---|---|---|
| Multi-stage build: ship artifacts, not toolchains | 50-95% | [5.4 Multi-Stage Builds](#54-multi-stage-builds) |
| Smaller base image (slim, distroless, scratch) | 50-90% | [Choosing Minimal Base Images](#choosing-minimal-base-images) |
| Exclude unneeded files from the context | Varies; can be huge with `COPY . .` | [.dockerignore](#dockerignore) |
| Install only what is needed (`--no-install-recommends`, `--omit=dev`) | 10-50% | below |
| Clean caches in the same layer (`apt` lists, `pip`/`npm` caches) | 5-30% | [Minimizing Layers](#minimizing-layers) |
| Avoid duplicated data (`COPY` then `chown -R`) | Up to 2x per affected file | [COPY vs ADD](#copy-vs-add) |
| Strip binaries / remove debug symbols (`-ldflags="-s -w"`, `strip`) | 20-30% of the binary | below |

**Package manager flags that matter**

| Ecosystem | Smaller install |
|---|---|
| apt | `apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ... && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*` |
| apk | `apk add --no-cache ...` (no index stored in the layer) |
| pip | `pip install --no-cache-dir ...` |
| npm | `npm ci --omit=dev && npm cache clean --force` |
| Go | `go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w"` |

**Finding what takes space**

```bash
# Layer by layer: which instruction added how much
docker image history --format 'table {{.Size}}\t{{.CreatedBy}}' myapp:1.0

# Interactive layer explorer showing files per layer and wasted space
docker run --rm -it -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock wagoodman/dive myapp:1.0

# Largest directories inside the image (needs a shell in the image)
docker run --rm --entrypoint sh myapp:1.0 -c 'du -xh / 2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail -20'
```

**Worked example: from 1.1 GB to 60 MB**

```dockerfile
# BEFORE (~1.1 GB): full image, build tools shipped, caches kept, everything copied
FROM node:22
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm install
RUN npm run build
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
# AFTER (~60-150 MB depending on dependencies)
FROM node:22-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build \
 && npm prune --omit=dev \
 && npm cache clean --force

FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs22-debian12:nonroot
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
# The distroless nodejs entrypoint is "node", so CMD is just the script
CMD ["dist/server.js"]
```

Together with a `.dockerignore` that excludes `node_modules`, `.git`, and test data, this applies almost every technique in the table.

**Key takeaways**

- Size affects build, push, pull, storage, startup, and vulnerability exposure.
- Biggest wins first: multi-stage builds and a smaller base image.
- Then: `.dockerignore`, no recommended/dev packages, caches removed in the same layer, stripped binaries.
- Measure with `docker image history` and `dive` instead of guessing.
- Smaller is better only as long as the image remains correct and operable.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run `docker image history` on one of your images and identify the three largest layers and the instructions that created them.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Take the "before" Node.js Dockerfile (or one of your own) and reduce it step by step, recording the size after each change in a table. Which change had the largest effect?
> 3. **Interview question:** "An image has grown to 2 GB and deployments are slow. Walk me through how you would analyze and reduce it." *Hint:* start with measurement (history, dive), then look at the base image, multi-stage separation, context contents, package manager options, and duplicated files across layers.

---

<a id="6-data-persistence-and-storage"></a>
## 6. Data Persistence and Storage

Containers are designed to be disposable, but the data they produce (database files, uploads, caches, configuration) usually is not. This chapter explains where a container's files physically live, why anything written to the container filesystem is lost when the container is removed, and how volumes, bind mounts, and tmpfs mounts let you choose exactly where data is stored and how long it survives. It closes with the operational side of state: backing up, restoring, and migrating data, and running databases in containers without losing sleep (or rows).

<a id="61-storage-concepts"></a>
### 6.1 Storage Concepts

This section explains how a container's own filesystem is built and stored, which is the foundation for understanding why external storage is needed.

#### Ephemeral Container Filesystem

**Why "ephemeral" is a feature.** A container is meant to be a reproducible instance of an image: you should be able to delete it and start an identical one at any time, on any host. That is only possible if the container does not accumulate important, unique state of its own. Docker enforces this by tying the container's private filesystem changes to the container's lifetime: when the container is removed, its changes are removed too.

**Analogy.** A container is like a hotel room. Housekeeping resets it to the same standard state for every guest (the image). You can rearrange the furniture and leave things on the desk during your stay (stopping and starting the container keeps them), but when you check out (`docker rm`), everything you left behind is cleared. Valuables belong in the safe deposit box at the front desk, which is the role volumes play.

**What survives what**

| Event | Changes in the container filesystem | Data in a volume or bind mount |
|---|---|---|
| Process inside restarts (restart policy) | Kept | Kept |
| `docker stop` / `docker start` | Kept | Kept |
| `docker restart`, host reboot | Kept | Kept |
| `docker rm` | **Deleted** | Kept |
| Recreate with a new image version (`docker compose up` after a pull, rolling update) | **Deleted** (it is a new container) | Kept |
| `docker run` again from the same image | Not visible: a new container starts from the clean image | Visible, if mounted again |

The last two rows are the ones that surprise people: upgrading an application always means *replacing* the container, so any state kept inside it is lost on every deployment.

**The three ways out of the container filesystem**

```text
                         +-------------------------------+
                         |          container            |
                         |                               |
                         |  /            container layer  |  ephemeral: dies with
                         |  |            (copy-on-write)  |  the container
                         |  +-- /var/lib/db  ------------+-----> volume       (managed by Docker)
                         |  +-- /app/src     ------------+-----> bind mount   (any host path)
                         |  +-- /run/secret  ------------+-----> tmpfs        (host RAM only)
                         +-------------------------------+
```

| Mount type | Stored in | Survives `docker rm` | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Volume | Docker-managed area on the host (or a remote driver) | Yes | Databases, uploads, any application state |
| Bind mount | An existing host path you choose | Yes (it is just a host directory) | Source code in development, host config files |
| tmpfs | Host memory | No (gone on stop) | Scratch space, secrets, sensitive temporary files |

**Example: proving the lifecycle**

```bash
# Write a file into the container filesystem
docker run -d --name eph alpine:3.20 sleep 3600
docker exec eph sh -c 'echo "hello" > /note.txt'

# Stop/start keeps the writable layer
docker stop -t 1 eph && docker start eph
docker exec eph cat /note.txt                                         # prints "hello"

# Remove the container: the file is gone with it
docker rm -f eph
docker run --rm alpine:3.20 cat /note.txt
# cat: can't open '/note.txt': No such file or directory

# Same experiment with a volume: the data outlives both containers
docker run --rm -v notes:/data alpine:3.20 sh -c 'echo "hello" > /data/note.txt'
docker run --rm -v notes:/data alpine:3.20 cat /data/note.txt         # prints "hello"
docker volume rm notes
```

**Design consequence.** Treat the container filesystem as read-mostly scratch space. Many teams go further and run containers with `--read-only`, so any accidental write to the container filesystem fails loudly instead of silently disappearing later (see [Read-Only Root Filesystem](#read-only-root-filesystem)).

**Key takeaways**

- Changes to a container's filesystem survive stop, start, and restart, but are deleted with `docker rm`.
- Every upgrade or redeploy creates a new container, so in-container state is lost on each deployment.
- Persistent data must go to a volume or bind mount; temporary sensitive data can go to tmpfs.
- Treat the container filesystem as disposable; `--read-only` makes accidental writes visible.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Start an `nginx:alpine` container, edit `/usr/share/nginx/html/index.html` with `docker exec`, then stop and start it. Is the edit still there? Remove and recreate the container and check again.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Run `redis:7` with `--save 60 1` (snapshot every 60 seconds if at least one key changed), set a key, wait a minute, and recreate the container with and without a volume at `/data`. Explain the result in terms of the table above.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A service stored user uploads under `/app/uploads` and they vanished after Friday's deployment, although nobody deleted anything. What happened?" *Hint:* think about what a deployment does to the existing container and where those files were written.

#### Writable Container Layer

**Why it exists.** Applications expect to write files: PID files, logs, caches, temporary files. Image layers are read-only and shared, so each container needs a private place to put its writes. Docker gives every container one thin **writable layer** on top of the image layers (see [Copy-on-Write](#copy-on-write) for the mechanics). This section focuses on the practical side: where that layer lives, how to see what is in it, and why it should stay small.

**Where it lives.** With the classic `overlay2` storage driver, each container has a directory under `/var/lib/docker/overlay2/<id>/`, and its changes are in the `diff/` subdirectory. With the containerd image store, the equivalent is a containerd snapshot under the containerd root. In both cases it is plain files on the host's disk, inside Docker's data root, and it is deleted when the container is removed.

```text
 /var/lib/docker/
 +-- overlay2/<container-layer-id>/
 |   +-- diff/       <- files the container created or modified (the writable layer)
 |   +-- merged/     <- the combined view mounted as the container's /
 |   +-- work/       <- OverlayFS scratch directory
 +-- containers/<container-id>/
     +-- <id>-json.log   <- stdout/stderr logs: NOT part of the writable layer
     +-- config.v2.json, hostconfig.json, hostname, hosts, resolv.conf ...
```

**What is (and is not) in the writable layer**

| In the writable layer | Not in the writable layer |
|---|---|
| Files created or modified anywhere under `/` | Contents of volumes, bind mounts, and tmpfs mounts |
| Copied-up versions of modified image files | Container logs captured from stdout/stderr |
| Whiteouts for deleted image files | `/etc/hosts`, `/etc/resolv.conf`, `/etc/hostname` (bind-mounted by Docker) |
| Package caches, `/tmp`, log files the app writes itself | The image layers |

**Inspecting it**

```bash
docker run -d --name web nginx:alpine
docker exec web sh -c 'echo test > /tmp/x; rm /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf'

# What changed relative to the image (A = added, C = changed, D = deleted)
docker diff web
# C /tmp
# A /tmp/x
# C /etc/nginx/conf.d
# D /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
# ...

# Size of the writable layer vs. virtual size (writable + image)
docker ps -s --filter name=web --format '{{.Names}}\t{{.Size}}'
# web   1.1kB (virtual 52.4MB)

# Physical location (overlay2 storage driver)
docker inspect -f '{{.GraphDriver.Data.UpperDir}}' web
docker rm -f web
```

**Why it should stay small**

- **Data loss.** Anything there disappears on `docker rm`.
- **Performance.** Writes pass through the union filesystem, and the first modification of a large image file copies the whole file up.
- **Disk exhaustion.** By default the layer can grow until the host disk (Docker's data root) is full, affecting every container on the host. A per-container quota (`--storage-opt size=10G`) exists, but with `overlay2` it only works when the data root is on XFS mounted with the `pquota` option.
- **Opacity.** `docker commit` and `docker export` capture the writable layer, which tempts people to "save" containers instead of fixing the Dockerfile. Note that both ignore volume contents.

**Common accidental writers.** Applications logging to files instead of stdout, package managers run at container start, language caches (`~/.cache/pip`, `~/.npm`), and uploads saved to a working directory. Point these to stdout, a volume, or a tmpfs mount.

**Key takeaways**

- Each container has exactly one private writable layer on top of the shared, read-only image layers.
- It lives inside Docker's data root on the host disk and is deleted with the container.
- Volumes, bind mounts, tmpfs mounts, and stdout logs are not part of it.
- Use `docker diff` and `docker ps -s` to see what a container has written and how much.
- Keep it small: write-heavy or important data belongs elsewhere.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run `docker diff` on a freshly started `postgres:16` container (with `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` set) and on one started with a named volume at `/var/lib/postgresql/data`. Compare the outputs.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Run a container that writes 500 MB to `/tmp` with `dd`, check `docker ps -s` and `docker system df`, then repeat with `--tmpfs /tmp`. Explain where the bytes went each time.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Disk usage under `/var/lib/docker` keeps growing on a production host, but images and volumes have not changed. Where would you look?" *Hint:* consider writable layers of long-running containers, log files under `containers/`, and how to find which container is responsible.

#### Storage Drivers

**Why storage drivers exist.** The layered image model needs an implementation: something must stack read-only layers, add a writable layer, and handle copy-on-write. Linux offers several technologies that can do this (union filesystems, filesystem snapshots, block-level snapshots), each with different performance and requirements. A **storage driver** is the pluggable component of the Docker daemon that implements image and container layers on top of one of these technologies.

**Analogy.** The storage driver is the warehouse system behind a shop. Customers (containers) see the same shelves (a filesystem) no matter whether the warehouse uses forklifts or conveyor belts. The choice still matters for speed, capacity, and which buildings (backing filesystems) it can operate in.

**Scope: what a storage driver does not handle.** Storage drivers only manage image layers and container writable layers. Volumes and bind mounts bypass the storage driver completely and write directly to the host filesystem (or a volume driver's backend). This is the main reason volumes are faster for write-heavy workloads.

```text
   container process writes to ...
        |
        +-- /            -> storage driver (overlay2, ...) -> /var/lib/docker/overlay2/...
        |
        +-- /data (vol)  -> direct host filesystem I/O      -> /var/lib/docker/volumes/...
```

**Available drivers**

| Driver | Technology | Status and use |
|---|---|---|
| `overlay2` | OverlayFS (kernel union filesystem) | Default and recommended on all current Linux distributions |
| `fuse-overlayfs` | OverlayFS in user space (FUSE) | Rootless Docker on kernels older than 5.11; slower |
| `btrfs` | Btrfs subvolumes and snapshots | Only if the data root is on Btrfs |
| `zfs` | ZFS datasets and snapshots | Only if the data root is on ZFS; niche |
| `vfs` | Full copy of each layer, no copy-on-write | Testing or unsupported filesystems; very slow and disk-hungry |
| `aufs`, `devicemapper` | Legacy union / block-level snapshots | Removed or deprecated; migrate to `overlay2` |

**containerd image store and snapshotters.** Recent Docker Engine releases (and Docker Desktop) can delegate image and layer storage to containerd. In that mode the classic storage drivers are replaced by containerd **snapshotters** (`overlayfs`, `native`, `btrfs`, `zfs`, and lazy-pulling snapshotters such as `stargz`). The concepts in this chapter are identical; only the on-disk location and some inspect output differ. See [containerd Image Store](#containerd-image-store).

**Checking and configuring the driver**

```bash
docker info --format '{{.Driver}}'                   # e.g. overlay2 (or overlayfs with containerd)
docker info | grep -A5 'Storage Driver'
# Storage Driver: overlay2
#  Backing Filesystem: extfs
#  Supports d_type: true
#  Using metacopy: false
#  Native Overlay Diff: true
#  userxattr: false
```

```json
{
  "storage-driver": "overlay2"
}
```

The JSON above goes in `/etc/docker/daemon.json` and requires a daemon restart. Changing the driver does **not** convert existing data: images and containers stored by the old driver become invisible (they stay on disk until you delete them). Plan a driver change like a migration: push images to a registry and back up volumes first.

**Choosing a driver.** In practice: use `overlay2` unless you have a specific reason not to. Docker selects it automatically when the kernel and backing filesystem support it. Pick `btrfs` or `zfs` only if the host is already standardized on that filesystem and you want to use its native snapshots.

**Key takeaways**

- A storage driver implements image layers and the container writable layer; nothing else.
- Volumes and bind mounts bypass the storage driver, which is why they are faster for heavy writes.
- `overlay2` is the default and the right choice on almost every Linux host.
- With the containerd image store, snapshotters play the same role as storage drivers.
- Changing the storage driver hides existing images and containers; treat it as a migration.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run `docker info` and record the storage driver, backing filesystem, and whether `d_type` is supported. Find the corresponding directories under the data root.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** On a disposable VM, start the daemon with `"storage-driver": "vfs"`, pull an image with several layers, and compare the disk usage under the data root with `overlay2`. Explain the difference.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why does writing a database to a named volume usually perform better than writing to the container filesystem, even though both end up on the same disk?" *Hint:* follow the I/O path through the storage driver and think about copy-up.

#### overlay2

**Why overlay2 won.** Older drivers either were not in the mainline kernel (AUFS) or worked at block level with complex setup and poor density (devicemapper). OverlayFS is part of the mainline Linux kernel, works at the file level on ordinary ext4 or XFS filesystems, shares the page cache between containers that use the same image, and needs no configuration. `overlay2` is Docker's driver built on it, and it supports up to 128 lower layers natively.

**How Docker maps layers to OverlayFS.** Each image layer is a directory. When a container starts, Docker mounts an OverlayFS whose `lowerdir` is the list of image layer directories, whose `upperdir` is the container's own layer, and whose mount point (`merged`) becomes the container's root filesystem.

```text
 /var/lib/docker/overlay2/
 +-- l/                         short symlinks (e.g. l/ABCD1234 -> ../<layer-id>/diff)
 |                              used to keep the mount option string under one memory page
 +-- <layer-id-1>/              base image layer
 |   +-- diff/                  the layer's files
 |   +-- link                   its short name in l/
 +-- <layer-id-2>/              next image layer
 |   +-- diff/  link
 |   +-- lower                  "l/ABCD1234"  (layers below this one, top to bottom)
 +-- <container-id>/            container layer
     +-- diff/                  upperdir: the container's changes
     +-- work/                  workdir: OverlayFS internal scratch space
     +-- merged/                the mount point -> container's /
     +-- lower                  "l/EFGH5678:l/ABCD1234"

 mount -t overlay overlay \
   -o lowerdir=l/EFGH5678:l/ABCD1234,upperdir=<container-id>/diff,workdir=<container-id>/work \
   <container-id>/merged
```

**Example: following a container to its overlay mount**

```bash
docker run -d --name ov nginx:alpine
docker inspect -f '{{json .GraphDriver}}' ov | python3 -m json.tool
# {
#   "Data": {
#     "LowerDir": "/var/lib/docker/overlay2/<id>-init/diff:/var/lib/docker/overlay2/<layer>/diff:...",
#     "MergedDir": "/var/lib/docker/overlay2/<id>/merged",
#     "UpperDir": "/var/lib/docker/overlay2/<id>/diff",
#     "WorkDir": "/var/lib/docker/overlay2/<id>/work"
#   },
#   "Name": "overlay2"
# }

# The live kernel mount backing the container (run on the Docker host, as root)
mount | grep "$(docker inspect -f '{{.GraphDriver.Data.MergedDir}}' ov)"

# Create a file in the container and find it in the upper directory on the host
docker exec ov sh -c 'echo hi > /hello.txt'
sudo cat "$(docker inspect -f '{{.GraphDriver.Data.UpperDir}}' ov)/hello.txt"   # hi
docker rm -f ov
```

The `<id>-init` layer in `LowerDir` is a small layer Docker creates for each container with files it manages (`/etc/hosts`, `/etc/resolv.conf` placeholders), sitting between the image and the container layer.

**Requirements and behavior to know**

| Topic | Detail |
|---|---|
| Backing filesystem | ext4, or XFS formatted with `ftype=1` (`d_type` support); check "Supports d_type: true" in `docker info` |
| Page cache sharing | Containers from the same image share cached file pages, so memory use scales well |
| Copy-up cost | The first write to a large existing file copies the entire file; noticeable with big files |
| Inodes | Many small files across many layers can exhaust inodes on ext4 before space runs out |
| Directory renames | Renaming a directory that exists in a lower layer is handled by copy-up or redirect metadata; some old tools assumed a simpler model |
| Open file descriptors | A file opened read-only before being copied up keeps pointing to the lower version (older kernels); rarely matters in practice |
| Disk quotas | `--storage-opt size=` requires XFS with project quotas (`pquota`) |

**Key takeaways**

- `overlay2` stacks image layer directories (`lowerdir`) under a per-container `upperdir` and mounts the result as `/`.
- Each layer is a `diff/` directory under `/var/lib/docker/overlay2/`; short links in `l/` keep mount options short.
- It shares the page cache across containers and needs no setup on ext4 or XFS (`ftype=1`).
- Copy-up of large files and inode usage are the main performance and capacity concerns.
- `docker inspect` (`GraphDriver`) shows the exact directories used by a container.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Use `docker inspect` to find the `UpperDir` of a running container, create a file inside the container, and locate it on the host.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Pull an image with many layers (for example `python:3.13`), find its layer directories under `/var/lib/docker/overlay2`, and use the `lower` files to reconstruct the layer order. Compare it with `docker image history`.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why does Docker create the `l/` directory of short symlinks instead of passing the full layer paths to the mount call?" *Hint:* think about how mount options are passed to the kernel and what happens with dozens of long layer paths.

<a id="62-volumes"></a>
### 6.2 Volumes

This section covers volumes, the storage mechanism Docker manages for you and the recommended way to persist container data.

#### Named Volumes

**Why named volumes.** You need data that outlives containers, but you do not want to care where it lives on the host, which permissions the directory has, or how the path differs between Linux, macOS, and Windows. A **named volume** is a storage area created and tracked by Docker under a name you choose. Containers refer to it by name, Docker handles the rest, and the same command works on every platform.

**Analogy.** A named volume is like a labeled storage unit in a facility. You rent it under a name ("pgdata"), and whichever moving truck (container) shows up can be given the key. The facility (Docker) decides which building and shelf it is on; you never need to know.

**How it works**

- A named volume is stored by the default `local` driver in `/var/lib/docker/volumes/<name>/_data` on the Docker host (inside the VM on Docker Desktop).
- It is mounted into the container at a path you choose, hiding whatever the image had at that path.
- If the volume is **empty** and the image has content at the mount path, Docker **copies that content into the volume** on first mount (pre-population), including ownership and permissions.
- It exists independently of containers: it is not deleted by `docker rm`, only by `docker volume rm` or a prune.
- If you reference a name that does not exist yet, `docker run` creates it automatically.

```text
  docker run -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16

  container A  ----mount---->  +--------------------------------------+
  (postgres:16)                | volume "pgdata"                      |
                               | /var/lib/docker/volumes/pgdata/_data |
  container B  ----mount---->  |  (survives A, reused by B)           |
  (postgres:16, later)         +--------------------------------------+
```

**Example: data survives container replacement**

```bash
docker volume create pgdata

docker run -d --name db -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret \
  -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16
docker exec db sh -c 'until pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1 -U postgres; do sleep 1; done'   # TCP is up only after init
docker exec db psql -U postgres -c "CREATE TABLE t(x int); INSERT INTO t VALUES (42);"

# Replace the container (as an upgrade would) and reuse the volume
docker rm -f db
docker run -d --name db -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret \
  -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16
docker exec db sh -c 'until pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1 -U postgres; do sleep 1; done'
docker exec db psql -U postgres -c "SELECT * FROM t;"     # 42 is still there

docker rm -f db && docker volume rm pgdata
```

**Example: pre-population from the image**

```bash
# nginx:alpine ships default HTML in /usr/share/nginx/html
docker run --rm -v site:/usr/share/nginx/html nginx:alpine ls /usr/share/nginx/html
# 50x.html  index.html            <- copied into the empty volume on first mount

# Opt out of the copy with volume-nocopy (or ":nocopy" with -v)
docker run --rm --mount type=volume,src=empty,dst=/usr/share/nginx/html,volume-nocopy \
  nginx:alpine ls /usr/share/nginx/html   # (empty)
docker volume rm site empty
```

**Volume subpaths.** Since Docker Engine 26, `--mount type=volume,src=shared,dst=/data,volume-subpath=app1` mounts only a subdirectory of a volume, which lets several services use separate folders of one volume. The subdirectory must already exist.

**Key takeaways**

- Named volumes are Docker-managed storage referenced by name, portable across platforms.
- They live outside the container lifecycle and are reused when containers are replaced.
- An empty volume is pre-populated with the image's content at the mount path; `nocopy` disables this.
- `docker run -v name:/path` creates the volume if it does not exist, so a typo silently creates a new, empty volume.
- They are the default choice for any persistent application data.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Create a named volume, write a timestamp to it from one `alpine` container, and read it from a second container started later.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Mount a fresh volume at `/etc/nginx` in an `nginx:alpine` container, change a config file inside the volume, then start a new container with the same volume. Is the image's default config or your edited version used? What happens if you mount the same volume into an image that has *different* content at that path?
> 3. **Interview question:** "After a deployment, the database came up empty although the volume still exists on the host. What would you check?" *Hint:* compare the volume name and the mount path in the old and new configuration, and remember what `-v` does with an unknown name.

#### Anonymous Volumes

**Why anonymous volumes exist.** Sometimes a path must bypass the container layer (for performance or because the image author marked it with `VOLUME`), but nobody has decided on a name for it. Docker then creates an **anonymous volume**: a regular volume with a random 64-character hexadecimal name, attached to that one container.

**Where they come from**

| Source | Example |
|---|---|
| A `VOLUME` instruction in the image, with no mount supplied at runtime | `docker run postgres:16` creates one for `/var/lib/postgresql/data` |
| `-v` with only a container path | `docker run -v /data alpine` |
| `--mount` without a `source` | `docker run --mount type=volume,dst=/data alpine` |

**Lifecycle rules**

| Action | Anonymous volume |
|---|---|
| `docker rm <container>` | Kept (orphaned, hard to identify later) |
| `docker rm -v <container>` | Removed |
| `docker run --rm ...` | Removed when the container is removed |
| `docker volume prune` | Removed if unused (since Docker 23, prune only removes anonymous volumes unless you add `-a`) |
| `docker compose up` (recreating a service) | Compose re-attaches the previous container's anonymous volumes; `-V` / `--renew-anon-volumes` creates fresh ones |

**Example: an orphan is born**

```bash
docker run -d --name cache redis:7          # redis image declares VOLUME /data
docker inspect -f '{{range .Mounts}}{{.Type}} {{.Name}} -> {{.Destination}}{{end}}' cache
# volume 3f9c1e...(64 hex chars) -> /data

docker rm -f cache                           # container gone, volume left behind
docker volume ls -f dangling=true            # lists the orphaned 3f9c1e... volume
docker volume prune -f                       # removes unused anonymous volumes
```

**A legitimate use: shadowing a directory inside a bind mount.** In development you often bind-mount the project directory but want `node_modules` (built inside the container for Linux) to stay out of the host folder. An anonymous volume on the subdirectory takes precedence over the bind mount for that path:

```bash
# -v "$PWD":/app          project source from the host
# -v /app/node_modules    anonymous volume masks the host's node_modules
docker run --rm -it \
  -v "$PWD":/app \
  -v /app/node_modules \
  -w /app node:22 sh -c "npm ci && npm test"
```

**Key takeaways**

- Anonymous volumes are ordinary volumes with random names, created by `VOLUME` or by `-v /path`.
- They persist after `docker rm` unless you use `-v` or `--rm`, and pile up as unnamed orphans.
- `docker volume prune` removes unused anonymous volumes (named ones only with `-a`).
- Use named volumes for anything you care about; reserve anonymous volumes for scratch data and masking paths.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run `mysql:8` three times without a volume (set `MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD`), remove the containers without `-v`, and count the volumes left behind. Clean them up.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Find which of your images declare volumes with `docker image inspect -f '{{json .Config.Volumes}}' <image>`. For one of them, decide whether you would replace the anonymous volume with a named volume and why.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A CI runner's disk fills up every few days even though all containers are removed after each job. What could be the cause, and how would you fix it permanently?" *Hint:* consider which images the jobs run, how the containers are removed, and which prune variant is scheduled.

#### Creating and Managing Volumes

**Why manage volumes explicitly.** Relying on `docker run` to auto-create volumes is convenient but hides typos, gives no place for metadata, and makes cleanup guesswork. The `docker volume` command lets you create volumes deliberately with labels and driver options, inspect them, and remove them safely.

**Command overview**

| Command | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `docker volume create NAME` | Create a volume (optionally `--driver`, `--opt`, `--label`) |
| `docker volume ls` | List volumes; filter with `-f dangling=true`, `-f label=...`, `-f driver=...`, `-f name=...` |
| `docker volume inspect NAME` | Show driver, mount point, labels, options, scope, creation time |
| `docker volume rm NAME...` | Remove volumes (fails if a container, even a stopped one, uses it) |
| `docker volume prune` | Remove unused anonymous volumes; `-a` includes unused named volumes |
| `docker system df -v` | Show size and number of containers using each volume |

**Example: a managed lifecycle**

```bash
# Create with labels for ownership and lifecycle
docker volume create \
  --label app=shop \
  --label env=dev \
  shop-db

docker volume inspect shop-db
# [
#   {
#     "CreatedAt": "2026-10-14T09:12:03Z",
#     "Driver": "local",
#     "Labels": { "app": "shop", "env": "dev" },
#     "Mountpoint": "/var/lib/docker/volumes/shop-db/_data",
#     "Name": "shop-db",
#     "Options": null,
#     "Scope": "local"            # "local" = this host only; "global" = cluster-wide driver
#   }
# ]

# Find volumes by label, or volumes no container references
docker volume ls -f label=app=shop
docker volume ls -f dangling=true -q

# Which containers use a volume?
docker ps -a --filter volume=shop-db --format '{{.Names}}'

# Size per volume
docker system df -v | sed -n '/VOLUME NAME/,/^$/p'

# Removal fails while in use (even by a stopped container)
docker run -d --name tmp -v shop-db:/data alpine sleep 60
docker volume rm shop-db
# Error response from daemon: remove shop-db: volume is in use - [<container-id>]
docker rm -f tmp && docker volume rm shop-db

# Prune only unused volumes with a specific label
docker volume prune -a -f --filter label=env=dev
```

**Naming conventions.** Use predictable names such as `<project>-<service>-<purpose>` (Compose does this automatically as `<project>_<volume>`). Combine with labels to answer "who owns this?" months later.

**Safety rules.** `docker volume prune -a` and `docker compose down -v` delete data irreversibly. Make sure you are on the right host (`docker context show`; see [Docker Contexts](#docker-contexts)), and filter by label where possible.

**Key takeaways**

- Create important volumes explicitly with meaningful names and labels.
- `inspect` shows the driver, mount point, options, and scope; `system df -v` shows sizes.
- A volume in use by any container, running or stopped, cannot be removed.
- `prune` removes unused anonymous volumes by default; `-a` includes named ones, so filter carefully.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Create two volumes with different `env` labels, list them with a label filter, and remove only one of them using a filtered prune.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Write a shell one-liner that prints every volume together with the names of the containers using it (or "unused"). Use `docker volume ls -q` and `docker ps -a --filter volume=...`.
> 3. **Interview question:** "How would you design a safe periodic cleanup of volumes on a shared build server?" *Hint:* consider the difference between dangling anonymous and named volumes, labels to mark disposable data, and a dry-run step.

#### Volume Drivers

**Why volume drivers.** The default `local` driver stores data on the Docker host's disk. That is fine for a single machine, but it ties data to that host: if a container is rescheduled elsewhere, or the disk fails, the data is gone or unreachable. **Volume drivers** let a volume live somewhere else, such as an NFS server, an SMB share, cloud block storage, or a distributed storage system, while containers keep using the same `-v name:/path` syntax.

**Analogy.** The volume name is a phone number; the driver is the telephone network that routes the call. The container dials the same number whether the person answers from a desk phone (local disk) or a mobile on another continent (network storage).

**The local driver is more capable than it looks.** It accepts the same options as the Linux `mount` command, so it can mount network filesystems without any plugin:

| `--opt` | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `type` | Filesystem type passed to `mount` | `nfs`, `cifs`, `tmpfs`, `ext4`, `none` (bind) |
| `device` | What to mount | `:/exports/data`, `//fileserver/share`, `/dev/sdb1`, `tmpfs` |
| `o` | Comma-separated mount options | `addr=10.0.0.5,rw,nfsvers=4`, `size=100m` |

```bash
# NFS share as a volume (mounted lazily when a container first uses it)
docker volume create --driver local \
  --opt type=nfs \
  --opt o=addr=10.0.0.5,rw,nfsvers=4.1 \
  --opt device=:/exports/media \
  media

# SMB/CIFS share (credentials in options are visible in inspect output; prefer a credentials file)
docker volume create --driver local \
  --opt type=cifs \
  --opt device=//fileserver.local/reports \
  --opt o=addr=fileserver.local,username=svc,password=changeme,uid=1000,gid=1000,vers=3.0 \
  reports

# A dedicated block device formatted as ext4
docker volume create --driver local --opt type=ext4 --opt device=/dev/sdb1 fastdisk

docker run --rm -v media:/media alpine ls /media
```

**Plugin drivers.** Third-party drivers are installed as Docker plugins and implement a small HTTP API that the daemon calls:

```text
  docker run -v data:/data --volume-driver=<plugin> ...
          |
          v
   dockerd ---- /VolumeDriver.Create   ----> plugin  ----> storage backend
           ---- /VolumeDriver.Mount    ---->  (returns a host path that dockerd
           ---- /VolumeDriver.Unmount  ---->   bind-mounts into the container)
           ---- /VolumeDriver.Remove, .Path, .Get, .List, .Capabilities
```

```bash
# Generic plugin workflow (sshfs is the classic documentation example)
docker plugin install vieux/sshfs                         # grants requested privileges
docker volume create -d vieux/sshfs \
  -o sshcmd=user@host:/remote/path -o password=... remote
docker run --rm -v remote:/data alpine ls /data
```

Many historic plugins are unmaintained. For clustered environments, Kubernetes CSI drivers (and CSI-based cluster volumes in Swarm) are the modern equivalent. Writing plugins is covered in [Volume and Network Plugins](#volume-and-network-plugins).

**Things to evaluate before using remote storage**

| Concern | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Latency and fsync behavior | Databases on NFS can be slow or unsafe if locking and sync semantics are weak |
| Concurrent access | Most block-storage drivers allow only one host to mount a volume at a time |
| Availability | If the storage server is down, containers using it fail to start or hang |
| Credentials | Options passed with `--opt` are stored in the volume metadata and shown by `inspect` |

**Key takeaways**

- A volume driver decides where a volume's data actually lives; containers use the same syntax regardless.
- The `local` driver can already mount NFS, CIFS, tmpfs, and block devices through `--opt type/device/o`.
- Plugin drivers implement a simple Create/Mount/Unmount/Remove API; many are unmaintained, and CSI is the modern path in clusters.
- Remote storage adds latency and failure modes; test databases on it carefully.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Create a volume with the local driver and `--opt type=tmpfs --opt device=tmpfs --opt o=size=50m`. Write to it from one container, then read it from a second container started after the first has exited. Explain the result in terms of when the local driver mounts and unmounts the filesystem.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Run an NFS server in a container or VM, create an NFS-backed volume on another machine (or the same one), and mount it into two containers. Measure the write speed with `dd` compared to a local volume.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your team wants to run a PostgreSQL container on an NFS-backed volume so it can move between hosts. What concerns would you raise?" *Hint:* consider file locking, fsync guarantees, latency, split-brain if two hosts mount it, and alternatives like replication.

#### Sharing Volumes Between Containers

**Why share volumes.** Some designs split work across containers that need the same files: a web server serving assets built by another container, a sidecar shipping log files written by the application, or a one-off job that seeds data for a long-running service. Mounting the same volume into several containers is the simplest way to do this on a single host.

**Analogy.** A shared volume is a shared folder on a team drive: everybody sees the same files immediately. It also has the same problem: if two people edit the same spreadsheet at once without coordination, someone's work gets overwritten.

**Patterns**

```text
  Producer / consumer               Sidecar                         Init / seed
  -------------------               -------                         -----------
  [builder] --writes--> (assets)    [app] --writes--> (logs)        [seed job] --writes--> (data)
                           |                            |               (exits)              |
  [nginx]  <--reads(ro)----+        [shipper] <--reads--+           [service] <--reads/writes+
```

**Two ways to share**

| Method | Syntax | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Same volume name | `-v assets:/srv` in each container | Explicit, can mount at different paths and with different modes |
| `--volumes-from` | `--volumes-from other[:ro]` | Copies *all* mounts (volumes and bind mounts) of another container at the same paths; implicit and harder to read |

**Example: producer and read-only consumer**

```bash
docker volume create assets

# Producer writes a new file every 2 seconds
docker run -d --name producer -v assets:/out alpine:3.20 \
  sh -c 'while true; do date > /out/now.txt; sleep 2; done'

# Consumer serves the same files read-only
docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 -v assets:/usr/share/nginx/html:ro nginx:alpine
curl -s localhost:8080/now.txt        # changes every 2 seconds

# --volumes-from: inherit every mount of "producer" (here: /out), read-only
docker run --rm --volumes-from producer:ro alpine:3.20 cat /out/now.txt

docker rm -f producer web && docker volume rm assets
```

**Concurrency is your problem.** Docker does no locking or coordination. Sharing is safe when only one container writes, or when writers use separate files, or when the application itself is designed for shared storage (atomic renames, file locks). It is **not** safe to point two database server instances at the same data directory: at best one refuses to start because of a lock file, at worst the data is corrupted.

**Scope.** A `local` volume can only be shared by containers on the same host. Sharing across hosts requires a network-capable volume driver, and then the concurrency concerns become even more important.

**Key takeaways**

- The same volume can be mounted into many containers, at different paths and with different modes.
- `--volumes-from` copies all mounts of another container; explicit volume names are clearer.
- Docker does not coordinate concurrent writers; design for a single writer or application-level locking.
- Never let two database servers share one data directory.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run the producer/consumer example and confirm that the consumer cannot write to the volume (`docker exec web touch /usr/share/nginx/html/x`).
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Build a log-shipping sidecar: an `nginx` container writing access logs to a volume (configure `access_log /logs/access.log`) and a second container running `tail -F` on the same file. Then switch to `--volumes-from` and compare readability.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Two replicas of a service write uploads to a shared volume. Users occasionally get truncated files. What is likely happening and how would you fix it?" *Hint:* think about partial writes visible to readers, write-to-temp-then-rename, and whether object storage is a better fit.

#### Read-Only Volumes

**Why read-only.** The principle of least privilege applies to storage too. A container that only needs to *read* configuration, certificates, or static assets should not be able to modify them, whether because of a bug, a compromised process, or a mistaken script. Mounting a volume read-only turns accidental or malicious writes into immediate errors and protects shared data from consumers.

**Syntax**

| Flag | Read-only form |
|---|---|
| `-v` | `-v name:/path:ro` |
| `--mount` | `--mount type=volume,src=name,dst=/path,readonly` (or `ro`) |
| `--volumes-from` | `--volumes-from other:ro` |
| Compose | `- name:/path:ro` or `read_only: true` in the long syntax |

```bash
docker volume create config
docker run --rm -v config:/cfg alpine:3.20 sh -c 'echo "level=info" > /cfg/app.conf'

# Mount read-only: reading works, writing fails
docker run --rm --mount type=volume,src=config,dst=/etc/app,readonly alpine:3.20 sh -c '
  cat /etc/app/app.conf
  echo "level=debug" > /etc/app/app.conf'
# level=info
# sh: can't create /etc/app/app.conf: Read-only file system

docker volume rm config
```

**Read-only is per mount, not per volume.** The same volume can be mounted read-write in one container (the writer) and read-only in others (the readers). The restriction is enforced by the kernel through the mount flags in that container's mount namespace.

**Combining with a read-only root filesystem.** The strongest setup makes the whole container read-only and opens only the exact paths that need writing:

```bash
# --read-only        container filesystem cannot be written
# appdata            the one persistent writable path
# certs (readonly)   inputs are read-only
# --tmpfs /tmp       scratch space in memory
docker run -d --name hardened \
  --read-only \
  --mount type=volume,src=appdata,dst=/var/lib/app \
  --mount type=volume,src=certs,dst=/certs,readonly \
  --tmpfs /tmp:size=64m \
  myapp:1.0
```

See [Read-Only Root Filesystem](#read-only-root-filesystem) for more on hardening.

**Key takeaways**

- Mount volumes read-only (`:ro` / `readonly`) whenever a container only consumes the data.
- The mode applies to one mount: one writer and many read-only readers can share a volume.
- Writes fail with "Read-only file system", which surfaces mistakes early.
- Combine with `--read-only` and tmpfs mounts for a minimal writable surface.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Mount a volume read-only into an `alpine` container and try `touch`, `rm`, and `mkdir` on it. Note the error each time.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Run `nginx:alpine` with `--read-only`, observe why it fails to start, and add the minimal set of tmpfs mounts needed (hint: look at the error messages for cache and PID file paths).
> 3. **Interview question:** "Is mounting a volume read-only a sufficient security boundary to protect its data from a compromised container?" *Hint:* consider what a process with `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` or a privileged container can do with mounts, and what other containers can still write.

<a id="63-mounts"></a>
### 6.3 Mounts

This section covers the other two mount types, bind mounts and tmpfs mounts, the two syntaxes used to declare any mount, and the permission issues that come with sharing files between host and container.

#### Bind Mounts

**Why bind mounts.** Volumes hide their location on purpose, but sometimes the location is exactly the point: you want the container to see *your* source code as you edit it, read a configuration file that lives at a known host path, or write a report into a folder you can open on the host. A **bind mount** maps an existing host file or directory directly into the container.

**Analogy.** A volume is a storage unit managed by the facility; a bind mount is handing the container a key to a specific room in your own house. It is convenient and immediate, but the container now operates directly on your belongings.
