- Only `lo` (`127.0.0.1`) exists; there is no `eth0`, no routes, and no DNS server.
- Processes inside can still talk to each other over `localhost`.
- Volumes and bind mounts still work, so data can be exchanged through files.
- It is also a starting point for **custom networking**: external tooling can move interfaces into the namespace (this is how some orchestrators wired up containers before CNI support).

**Example**

```bash
docker run --rm --network none alpine ip addr
# 1: lo: <LOOPBACK,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 65536 ...
#     inet 127.0.0.1/8 scope host lo
# (no eth0)

docker run --rm --network none alpine wget -T 3 -qO- http://example.com
# wget: bad address 'example.com'

# Typical use: process untrusted input with no network access
mkdir -p in out && echo '# Title' > in/doc.md
docker run --rm --network none \
  -v "$PWD/in:/in:ro" \
  -v "$PWD/out:/out" \
  pandoc/core:3.5 /in/doc.md -o /out/doc.html   # converts the file; cannot phone home
ls out/
```

**Key takeaways**

- `--network none` gives a container loopback only: no external connectivity at all.
- It is a simple, strong control for batch jobs and processing untrusted data.
- Data exchange must happen through mounts, not the network.
- It can serve as an empty namespace for fully custom network setups.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Start a container with `--network none` and verify that it has no routes (`ip route`) and that DNS lookups fail.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Write a script that runs your project's unit tests inside a `--network none` container with the source code mounted read-only. Which tests fail, and what does that reveal about hidden network dependencies?
> 3. **Interview question:** "How would you design a service that converts user-uploaded files with a third-party tool you do not fully trust?" *Hint:* combine `--network none` with read-only mounts, resource limits, dropped capabilities, and a non-root user.

#### Overlay Network

**Why it is needed.** A bridge network ends at the host's edge. When containers on different machines must talk directly, as if they were on one switch, you need a network that **spans hosts**. The **overlay** driver builds a virtual layer 2 network on top of the existing host network (the *underlay*). Frames sent by a container are wrapped in UDP packets (**VXLAN** encapsulation), carried to the destination host, and unwrapped there.

**Analogy.** It is like sending a letter inside another envelope. The inner letter is addressed to `10.0.9.5` (a container IP that the physical network has never heard of). The outer envelope is addressed to `192.168.56.12` (the host that runs that container). The postal service only reads the outer envelope.

```text
    Host 1 (192.168.56.11)                          Host 2 (192.168.56.12)
   +---------------------------+                   +---------------------------+
   |  container A  10.0.9.4    |                   |  container B  10.0.9.5    |
   |        |                  |                   |        ^                  |
   |  overlay br0 + vxlan  ----+-- UDP 4789 -------+->  vxlan + br0            |
   |  [outer: 192.168.56.11 -> 192.168.56.12]       [inner: 10.0.9.4 -> 10.0.9.5]
   +---------------------------+                   +---------------------------+
             \______________ underlay network (LAN, VPC) ______________/
```

**Requirements.** Overlay networks need **Swarm mode**, which provides the control plane: membership, distribution of network state and encryption keys, and service discovery. These ports must be open between nodes:

| Port | Protocol | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| 2377 | TCP | Cluster management (to managers) |
| 7946 | TCP and UDP | Node communication and gossip about network state |
| 4789 | UDP | VXLAN data traffic |
| IP protocol 50 (ESP) | | Only for encrypted overlays |

**Example: two hosts, one network**

```bash
# --- node1 (becomes the manager) ---
docker swarm init --advertise-addr 192.168.56.11
# prints a "docker swarm join --token SWMTKN-1-... 192.168.56.11:2377" command

# --- node2 ---
docker swarm join --token SWMTKN-1-... 192.168.56.11:2377

# --- node1 ---
# --attachable lets plain "docker run" containers join (by default only Swarm services can)
docker network create -d overlay --attachable --subnet 10.0.9.0/24 multihost
docker run -d --name svc1 --network multihost nginx:1.27-alpine

# --- node2 --- (the network is created here on demand when a container needs it)
docker run --rm --network multihost alpine wget -qO- http://svc1 | head -n 4
# nginx welcome page served from node1, resolved by name across hosts

# --- Swarm services get a virtual IP (VIP) load-balanced across their tasks ---
docker service create --name api --replicas 3 --network multihost traefik/whoami
docker run --rm --network multihost alpine nslookup api         # one VIP
docker run --rm --network multihost alpine nslookup tasks.api   # one IP per task (3)
```

**Networks Swarm creates automatically**

| Network | Driver | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `ingress` | overlay | Carries traffic for ports published by services (see [Routing Mesh](#routing-mesh)) |
| `docker_gwbridge` | bridge | Connects containers on overlay networks to the outside world on each node |

**Encryption and MTU**

- Overlay traffic is unencrypted by default. `docker network create -d overlay --opt encrypted secure-net` encrypts data traffic between nodes with IPsec. It costs CPU and requires ESP to be allowed by firewalls and cloud security groups.
- VXLAN adds 50 bytes of headers, so the overlay MTU defaults to 1450 on a 1500-byte underlay. If the underlay itself is smaller (some clouds, VPNs), set `--opt com.docker.network.driver.mtu=<value>` accordingly, otherwise large packets are silently dropped.

**Key takeaways**

- Overlay networks connect containers across hosts by encapsulating layer 2 frames in VXLAN (UDP 4789).
- They require Swarm mode for the control plane; `--attachable` allows standalone containers to join.
- Swarm services get a VIP with built-in load balancing; `tasks.<service>` returns individual task IPs.
- Open the required ports between nodes, consider `--opt encrypted` on untrusted networks, and mind the MTU.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Using two VMs (or Play with Docker), create a Swarm and an attachable overlay network, then ping a container on node1 from a container on node2 by name.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Capture traffic on the underlay with `sudo tcpdump -ni eth0 udp port 4789` while the containers communicate. Identify the outer and inner IP headers. Repeat with an encrypted overlay and describe what changes.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Containers on an overlay network can ping each other, but HTTP requests with large responses hang. What is your first suspect?" *Hint:* compare the underlay MTU with the VXLAN overhead and check for blocked ICMP "fragmentation needed" messages.

#### Macvlan and IPvlan

**Why put containers on the physical LAN.** Some workloads expect to be first-class citizens of the physical network: legacy applications licensed to a MAC address, network appliances, monitoring tools that sniff traffic, or services that other devices must reach on a dedicated IP without port mapping. **Macvlan** and **IPvlan** attach containers directly to a host interface (the *parent*), bypassing the bridge and NAT. To the rest of the network, each container looks like a separate machine.

**How they differ**

| | Macvlan | IPvlan L2 | IPvlan L3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| MAC address per container | Own, unique MAC | Shares the parent's MAC | Shares the parent's MAC |
| Visible on the LAN as | Separate devices | Separate IPs behind one MAC | A routed subnet behind the host |
| Broadcast/multicast (ARP, mDNS) | Yes | Yes | No |
| Needs promiscuous mode / extra MACs allowed | Often | No | No |
| Router configuration | None | None | Static route for the container subnet via the host |
| Typical blocker | Switch port security, Wi-Fi, cloud anti-spoofing | | |

```text
   Macvlan (bridge mode)                         IPvlan L3
   LAN switch                                    router: 10.50.0.0/24 via 192.168.1.50
     |                                              |
   eth0 (host) MAC aa:..:01                       eth0 (host) 192.168.1.50  MAC aa:..:01
     |-- container 1  192.168.1.200  MAC 02:..:c8   |-- container 1  10.50.0.10 (same MAC)
     |-- container 2  192.168.1.201  MAC 02:..:c9   |-- container 2  10.50.0.11 (same MAC)
```

**Example: a macvlan network on the office LAN**

```bash
# LAN: 192.168.1.0/24, router 192.168.1.1. Reserve 192.168.1.192/27 for containers
# and exclude it from the DHCP server's range: Docker assigns these IPs itself, not DHCP.
#   --aux-address : keep 192.168.1.223 free for the host shim interface (below)
#   parent=eth0   : the physical NIC; use eth0.10 to place containers in 802.1Q VLAN 10
docker network create -d macvlan \
  --subnet 192.168.1.0/24 \
  --gateway 192.168.1.1 \
  --ip-range 192.168.1.192/27 \
  --aux-address 'host-shim=192.168.1.223' \
  -o parent=eth0 \
  lan

docker run -d --name kiosk --network lan --ip 192.168.1.200 nginx:1.27-alpine
# From another machine on the LAN:  curl http://192.168.1.200   -> works, no -p needed
# From the Docker host itself:      curl http://192.168.1.200   -> times out (see below)
```

**The host cannot reach its own macvlan containers.** By design, the kernel does not pass traffic between a parent interface and its macvlan children. The common workaround is a macvlan "shim" interface on the host:

```bash
sudo ip link add lan-shim link eth0 type macvlan mode bridge
sudo ip addr add 192.168.1.223/32 dev lan-shim
sudo ip link set lan-shim up
sudo ip route add 192.168.1.192/27 dev lan-shim   # reach containers through the shim
curl -sI http://192.168.1.200 | head -n 1          # HTTP/1.1 200 OK
```

**Example: an IPvlan L3 network**

```bash
# Containers live in 10.50.0.0/24, routed by the host; no ARP on the LAN for these IPs
docker network create -d ipvlan \
  --subnet 10.50.0.0/24 \
  -o parent=eth0 \
  -o ipvlan_mode=l3 \
  routed-net
docker run -d --name svc --network routed-net --ip 10.50.0.10 nginx:1.27-alpine
# On the LAN router: add a static route 10.50.0.0/24 via 192.168.1.50 (the Docker host)
```

**Pitfalls**

- **Wi-Fi.** Most wireless drivers and access points drop frames from MAC addresses that did not associate, so macvlan rarely works over Wi-Fi. Use IPvlan instead.
- **Cloud VPCs.** AWS, Azure, and GCP drop traffic from unknown MAC and IP addresses. Use the provider's own mechanisms (secondary IPs, CNI plugins) instead.
- **Switch limits.** Port security may cap the number of MACs per port and shut the port down.
- **No published ports and no Docker NAT.** Firewalling must be done on the network, not with `-p` bindings.

**Key takeaways**

- Macvlan gives each container its own MAC and IP on the physical network; IPvlan shares the parent's MAC.
- Use IPvlan L2 where extra MACs are forbidden, and IPvlan L3 for a routed design without broadcast traffic.
- Docker assigns the IPs: reserve a range outside the LAN's DHCP pool.
- The host cannot talk to its macvlan containers without a shim interface; Wi-Fi and cloud networks usually block macvlan.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** On a Linux VM with a bridged network adapter, create a macvlan network and run nginx on a LAN IP. Reach it from another device on the LAN, then try (and fail) from the host.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Add the shim interface to restore host-to-container connectivity. Then recreate the network as IPvlan L2 and compare the MAC addresses seen in the router's or another machine's ARP table (`ip neigh`).
> 3. **Interview question:** "A security appliance vendor ships its product as a container that must capture traffic on a mirrored switch port and have its own management IP. How would you network it?" *Hint:* consider separate parent interfaces for capture and management, macvlan versus host mode, and the capabilities packet capture requires.

<a id="73-container-communication"></a>
### 7.3 Container Communication

This section focuses on how containers find and reach each other: service discovery, naming, multi-network topologies, isolation, and diagnosing what goes wrong.

#### Embedded DNS and Service Discovery

**Why names instead of IPs.** Container IP addresses are assigned dynamically and change whenever a container is recreated. Hard-coding `172.18.0.3` into a configuration breaks on the next deployment. **Service discovery** means finding a service by a stable name instead. On user-defined networks, Docker provides it with an **embedded DNS server** that every container reaches at `127.0.0.11`.

**How it works**

1. Docker writes `nameserver 127.0.0.11` into the container's `/etc/resolv.conf`.
2. Inside the container's namespace, Docker adds NAT rules that redirect `127.0.0.11:53` to a socket that `dockerd` listens on in that namespace.
3. `dockerd` answers queries for **container names, network aliases, and short container IDs** of containers that share a network with the requester.
4. Any other name is forwarded to the **upstream resolvers**: the host's resolvers (Docker reads the real list from `systemd-resolved` when the host uses the `127.0.0.53` stub), or the servers given with `--dns`.

```text
   container "api" (network appnet)
     getaddrinfo("db") --> /etc/resolv.conf: nameserver 127.0.0.11
                               |
                               v (NAT inside the container namespace)
                         dockerd embedded DNS
                          |                     \
            "db" is on appnet?                   "example.com"?
                yes -> 172.18.0.3                forward to upstream (host resolvers / --dns)
```

Names are **network-scoped**: a container resolves only the names of containers it shares at least one network with.

**Example**

```bash
docker network create appnet
docker run -d --name db --network appnet -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret postgres:16

docker run --rm --network appnet alpine cat /etc/resolv.conf
# nameserver 127.0.0.11
# options ndots:0

docker run --rm --network appnet alpine nslookup db
# Server:    127.0.0.11
# Address:   127.0.0.11:53
# Name:      db
# Address:   172.18.0.2

# External names are forwarded upstream
docker run --rm --network appnet alpine nslookup docker.com | tail -n 2

# The redirection rules inside the container's namespace
PID=$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' db)
sudo nsenter -t "$PID" -n iptables -t nat -S DOCKER_OUTPUT
# -A DOCKER_OUTPUT -d 127.0.0.11/32 -p tcp -m tcp --dport 53 -j DNAT --to-destination 127.0.0.11:39811
# -A DOCKER_OUTPUT -d 127.0.0.11/32 -p udp -m udp --dport 53 -j DNAT --to-destination 127.0.0.11:45123

docker rm -f db && docker network rm appnet
```

**DNS-related `docker run` options**

| Option | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--dns 10.0.0.53` | Upstream server for external names (on user-defined networks, `127.0.0.11` stays the container's resolver) |
| `--dns-search corp.example` | Search domain appended to short names |
| `--dns-option ndots:2` | Resolver options written to `resolv.conf` |
| `--add-host api.local:10.0.0.7` | Static entry in the container's `/etc/hosts` |
| `--add-host host.docker.internal:host-gateway` | Name for the Docker host (built in on Docker Desktop; needs this flag on Linux) |
| `--hostname` | The container's own hostname, which by itself is **not** resolvable by other containers |

**Pitfall: clients that cache DNS forever.** Some software resolves a name once at startup. If the target container is recreated with a new IP, connections fail until the client restarts. nginx is the classic example: `proxy_pass http://api:8000;` resolves `api` only when the configuration loads. Force runtime resolution by using a variable together with a `resolver` directive:

```nginx
server {
    listen 80;
    resolver 127.0.0.11 valid=10s;          # Docker's embedded DNS, re-resolve every 10 s
    location / {
        set $upstream http://api:8000;      # a variable forces resolution at request time
        proxy_pass $upstream;
    }
}
```

The JVM (`networkaddress.cache.ttl`) and connection pools have similar settings.

**Key takeaways**

- On user-defined networks, every container uses Docker's embedded DNS server at `127.0.0.11`.
- It resolves container names, aliases, and short IDs of containers on shared networks, and forwards everything else upstream.
- Name resolution is network-scoped and unavailable on the default bridge.
- Use `--dns`, `--dns-search`, and `--add-host` for custom resolution, and make sure clients re-resolve names when containers are recreated.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** On a user-defined network, resolve another container by its name, by its short ID, and by its `--hostname`. Which ones work?
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Put nginx in front of an API container using `proxy_pass http://api:8000;`. Recreate the API container so it gets a new IP and observe the 502 errors. Then fix the configuration with `resolver` and a variable, and repeat the test.
> 3. **Interview question:** "How can a containerized application on Linux reach a database that runs directly on the Docker host, without hard-coding the host's IP?" *Hint:* look at the special `host-gateway` value for `--add-host`, and consider which host interface the database must listen on.

#### Network Aliases

**Why extra names.** A container name is unique per host and tied to one container. Often you want a name that describes a *role* rather than a specific container: `search` instead of `elasticsearch-blue-2`, or the same name for several interchangeable replicas. A **network alias** is an additional DNS name for a container, valid only on a specific network. Several containers can share an alias, in which case the embedded DNS returns all of their addresses (simple **DNS round-robin**).

**Analogy.** A container name is a person's legal name; an alias is a job title. "Ask the on-call engineer" keeps working when the person on call changes, and several people can share the title.

**Setting aliases**

```bash
# At start time (applies to the network given with --network)
docker run -d --name search-1 --network appnet --network-alias search traefik/whoami

# When connecting an existing container to a network (one alias per network)
docker network connect --alias cache appnet redis-primary

# Aliases do not work on the default bridge:
docker run --rm --network-alias foo alpine true
# docker: Error response from daemon: network-scoped alias is supported only for containers in user defined networks.
```

**Example: round-robin across two replicas and a blue/green switch**

```bash
docker network create searchnet
docker run -d --name search-1 --network searchnet --network-alias search traefik/whoami
docker run -d --name search-2 --network searchnet --network-alias search traefik/whoami

docker run --rm --network searchnet alpine nslookup search
# Name:   search
# Address: 172.20.0.2
# Name:   search
# Address: 172.20.0.3

# Requests are spread across replicas (whoami prints the serving container's hostname)
for i in 1 2 3 4; do
  docker run --rm --network searchnet alpine wget -qO- http://search | grep Hostname
done

# Which DNS names does a container answer to on this network?
docker inspect -f '{{json .NetworkSettings.Networks.searchnet.DNSNames}}' search-1
# ["search-1","search","9c1e2f3a4b5d"]

# Blue/green: start "green" with the alias, then remove "blue" from the network
docker run -d --name search-green --network searchnet --network-alias search traefik/whoami
docker network disconnect searchnet search-1
docker network disconnect searchnet search-2

docker rm -f search-1 search-2 search-green && docker network rm searchnet
```

**Aliases in Compose.** Every Compose service name is automatically an alias on the project networks, which is why `db:5432` works between services. Additional names go under `networks.<name>.aliases`:

```yaml
services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16
    networks:
      backend:
        aliases:
          - db              # reachable as "postgres" and "db" on backend
          - db.internal
networks:
  backend:
```

**Limits of DNS round-robin.** It is not a load balancer: there are no health checks, clients often cache or always pick the first address, and long-lived connections stick to one replica. Use a real proxy (nginx, HAProxy, Traefik) or Swarm's VIP mode when balancing matters.

**Key takeaways**

- A network alias is an extra DNS name for a container, scoped to one network.
- Several containers can share an alias; DNS then returns all their IPs (round-robin).
- Set aliases with `--network-alias` or `docker network connect --alias`; they require user-defined networks.
- Compose service names are aliases; DNS round-robin is not health-aware load balancing.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Give a Redis container the aliases `cache` and `sessions` on one network and verify that both names resolve to the same IP.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Connect one container to two networks with a *different* alias on each. Show that clients on each network can resolve only the alias of their own network.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Three API replicas share the alias `api`, yet one of them receives almost all the traffic. Explain possible reasons." *Hint:* think about client-side DNS caching, connection pooling and keep-alive, and resolver libraries that sort or prefer addresses.

#### Connecting Containers to Multiple Networks

**Why multiple networks.** Real architectures have tiers. A reverse proxy must reach the application, the application must reach the database, but the proxy (exposed to the internet) should never reach the database directly. With Docker, you express this by creating one network per tier and connecting only the containers that bridge two tiers to both. Each network a container joins gives it another interface (`eth0`, `eth1`, ...) with its own IP.

```text
            internet
               |  -p 443:443
        +------v------+
        |    proxy    |                      network "frontend"
   =====+=============+======+=============================
                             |
                      +------v------+
                      |     api     |  (eth0 on frontend, eth1 on backend)
                      +------+------+
   ==========================+======+======================  network "backend" (--internal)
                                    |
                             +------v------+
                             |     db      |  unreachable from proxy
                             +-------------+
```

**Commands**

| Command | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `docker run --network frontend --network backend ...` | Join several networks at creation (Engine 25+) |
| `docker network connect backend api` | Attach a running container to another network |
| `docker network connect --ip 10.10.0.20 --alias svc backend api` | Same, with a static IP and alias on that network |
| `docker network disconnect frontend api` | Detach from a network without stopping the container |
| `docker run --network name=frontend,gw-priority=1 ...` | Choose which network provides the default route (Engine 28+) |

**Example**

```bash
docker network create frontend
docker network create --internal backend

docker run -d --name db --network backend -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret postgres:16
docker run -d --name api --network backend alpine sleep 1d
docker network connect frontend api                       # api now bridges both tiers
docker run -d --name proxy --network frontend -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27-alpine

# One IP per network
docker inspect -f '{{range $n, $c := .NetworkSettings.Networks}}{{$n}} {{$c.IPAddress}}{{"\n"}}{{end}}' api
# backend 172.21.0.3
# frontend 172.22.0.2

docker exec api nslookup db | tail -n 1          # resolves: shares "backend" with db
docker exec api nslookup proxy | tail -n 1       # resolves: shares "frontend" with proxy
docker exec proxy nslookup db                    # fails: proxy is not on backend

# Outbound traffic uses the default route of ONE network; here the non-internal one
docker exec api ip route
# default via 172.22.0.1 dev eth1          (interface names and order may vary)

docker rm -f db api proxy && docker network rm frontend backend
```

**Pitfalls**

- **Interface order.** Do not assume `eth0` belongs to a particular network; look up interfaces by IP or subnet.
- **Default gateway.** Only one network provides the default route. If it is an `--internal` network, the container has no internet access; use `gw-priority` on newer Engines to choose explicitly.
- **Listening addresses.** An application that binds to one specific IP is reachable only on that network; bind to `0.0.0.0` to serve all of them.
- **Name collisions.** If a name or alias exists on two networks with different containers, the answer depends on which network the query is resolved for; keep names unique.

**Key takeaways**

- Connect a container to several networks to build tiered topologies; it gets one interface and IP per network.
- Use `docker network connect`/`disconnect` to change membership at runtime, or repeat `--network` at creation.
- Containers resolve only the names of containers on networks they share.
- Only one network supplies the default route; control it explicitly when it matters.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Build the proxy/api/db topology above and prove with `ping` or `nc -zv` which containers can reach which.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Without restarting anything, move `api` from network `blue` to network `green` using `docker network connect` and `disconnect`, while a client loop keeps resolving and calling it. Record how long resolution fails, if at all.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why is connecting the reverse proxy directly to the database network a security problem, even though the proxy does not need the database?" *Hint:* consider what an attacker gains after exploiting the internet-facing component, and lateral movement.

#### Network Isolation

**Why isolation matters.** A single compromised container should not be a door into everything else on the host. Docker's networks provide boundaries, and you can tighten them further. Isolation is about **reducing what can talk to what**: between applications, between tiers, between containers and the internet, and between the network and published ports.

**The isolation toolbox**

| Mechanism | What it blocks | How |
|---|---|---|
| Separate user-defined networks | Traffic between unrelated applications | Docker drops forwarding between different bridge networks |
| `--internal` network | Any traffic to or from outside the network; no default route, published ports unusable | `docker network create --internal backend` |
| Disable ICC on a network | Container-to-container traffic within the same network (published ports still work) | `-o com.docker.network.bridge.enable_icc=false` |
| `"icc": false` in `daemon.json` | Container-to-container traffic on the default bridge | Daemon option |
| Bind published ports to localhost | Access to a published port from other machines | `-p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432` |
| `DOCKER-USER` rules | Arbitrary traffic patterns, e.g. by source network | iptables rules (see [iptables and Docker](#iptables-and-docker)) |
| `--network none` | All network traffic | No interfaces besides loopback |

**Analogy.** Networks are separate floors of a building with no stairs between them. `--internal` is a floor with no exit to the street. Disabling ICC is putting each office on a floor behind a locked door. `DOCKER-USER` is the security desk checking visitors' badges.

**Example: verifying each boundary**

```bash
docker network create app-a
docker network create app-b
docker network create --internal secure
docker network create -o com.docker.network.bridge.enable_icc=false noicc

# 1. Separate networks cannot reach each other
docker run -d --name a1 --network app-a nginx:1.27-alpine
# "index" is required because Go templates do not accept "-" in field names
A1_IP=$(docker inspect -f '{{(index .NetworkSettings.Networks "app-a").IPAddress}}' a1)
docker run --rm --network app-b alpine wget -T 3 -qO- "http://$A1_IP" \
  || echo "blocked: different network"

# 2. An internal network has no route to the outside
docker run --rm --network secure alpine wget -T 3 -qO- http://example.com \
  || echo "blocked: internal network"

# 3. ICC disabled: neighbors on the same network cannot talk directly
docker run -d --name n1 --network noicc nginx:1.27-alpine
docker run --rm --network noicc alpine wget -T 3 -qO- http://n1 \
  || echo "blocked: inter-container communication disabled"

docker rm -f a1 n1 && docker network rm app-a app-b secure noicc
```

**What network isolation does not do**

- It does not **encrypt** traffic. Containers on the same network, and anyone with root on the host, can observe it; use TLS (or encrypted overlays across hosts).
- It does not **authenticate**. Anything on the network can connect to an open port; services still need credentials.
- It does not protect against a container with `--network host`, `NET_ADMIN`, or access to the Docker socket, which can bypass or change the rules.

Recent Engines (28+) also harden the edges: by default, other machines on the LAN can no longer reach unpublished container ports by routing directly to container IPs, and ports published on `127.0.0.1` are no longer reachable from neighboring hosts.

**Key takeaways**

- Give each application, and each tier, its own network; Docker blocks traffic between networks.
- Use `--internal` for networks that must never reach or be reached from outside, such as databases.
- Disable ICC where containers on a network should only be reached through published ports.
- Bind sensitive published ports to `127.0.0.1` and add `DOCKER-USER` rules for finer control; isolation complements, but does not replace, TLS and authentication.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run the three verification tests above, then repeat test 2 after `docker network connect app-a <container>` on the internal-network container. Explain why it can now reach the internet.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Design and implement the networks for a stack of `proxy`, `web`, `worker`, `redis`, and `postgres`, where only `proxy` is public, `worker` has no internet access, and `redis` and `postgres` are reachable only by the services that use them. Document your network-to-container matrix.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Is a container on an `--internal` network fully safe from data exfiltration?" *Hint:* consider other containers on the same network that do have internet access, DNS, shared volumes, and what the host itself can see.

#### Troubleshooting Connectivity

**Why a method matters.** "It can't connect" has a dozen possible causes, from a typo in a hostname to an MTU mismatch on a VPN. Random changes waste hours. Work through the network **layer by layer, from the inside out**: is the service listening, can the client resolve the name, can it reach the IP, is the port published, and is a firewall interfering? Each step either finds the problem or rules out a whole class of causes.

```text
   1. Is the target running and LISTENING on 0.0.0.0:<container port>?   -> ss -lntp in its namespace
                 |
   2. Do client and target share a network?                             -> docker inspect / network inspect
                 |
   3. Does the name resolve from the client?                            -> nslookup / getent hosts
                 |
   4. Does a TCP connection to IP:port succeed?                         -> nc -zv / curl -v
                 |
   5. From outside: is the port published and bound to the right IP?    -> docker port / ss on host
                 |
   6. Firewall, NAT, forwarding, MTU?                                   -> iptables, sysctl, tcpdump
```

**Toolbox**

| Tool | Use |
|---|---|
| `nicolaka/netshoot` | Image with `curl`, `dig`, `nc`, `ss`, `tcpdump`, `iperf3`, `mtr`, and more |
| `docker run --network container:<name> nicolaka/netshoot` | Debug **inside** a target's namespace without adding tools to its image |
| `nsenter -t <pid> -n <cmd>` | Run host binaries in a container's network namespace |
| `docker network inspect <net>` | Which containers are attached, with which IPs |
| `docker port <container>` | Actual host port bindings |
| `tcpdump -i docker0` / `-i vethXXXX` | See whether packets arrive and replies leave |
| `docker debug <container>` | Debug shell for minimal images (Docker Desktop feature, see [docker debug](#docker-debug)) |

**Example: a systematic session**

```bash
# Scenario: "api" cannot connect to "db:5432"

# 1. Is PostgreSQL listening, and on which address? Attach a toolbox to db's namespace
docker run --rm --network container:db nicolaka/netshoot ss -lntp
# LISTEN 0 244 0.0.0.0:5432 0.0.0.0:*        <- good; "127.0.0.1:5432" would be the bug

# 2. Do they share a network?
docker inspect -f '{{range $n, $_ := .NetworkSettings.Networks}}{{$n}} {{end}}' api db
# appnet
# backend                                     <- different networks: the bug in this scenario

# 3. Name resolution from the client's point of view
docker run --rm --network container:api nicolaka/netshoot dig +short db
# (empty) -> name not visible from api's networks

# Fix and re-test the TCP connection
docker network connect backend api
docker run --rm --network container:api nicolaka/netshoot nc -zv db 5432
# Connection to db (172.21.0.2) 5432 port [tcp/postgresql] succeeded!

# 5-6. Outside access problems: bindings, then packets on the bridge
docker port web
sudo tcpdump -ni docker0 tcp port 80 -c 10
```

**Common symptoms**

| Symptom | Likely cause | Check or fix |
|---|---|---|
| `bad address 'db'` / `Name or service not known` | Not on a shared user-defined network, default bridge, typo, target not running | `docker network inspect`; use a user-defined network |
| `Connection refused` | Nothing listening on that port: app bound to `127.0.0.1`, wrong port (host port used instead of container port), app still starting | `ss -lntp` in the target namespace; use the container port between containers |
| Timeout | Isolation between networks, `--internal`, `DOCKER-USER` rules, ICC disabled, app hung | `iptables -L DOCKER-USER -nv`; check network options |
| Works from the host, not from other machines | Port bound to `127.0.0.1`, cloud security group, upstream firewall | `docker port`; `ss -lntp` on the host |
| Container cannot reach the internet | `ip_forward` disabled, Docker rules flushed, internal network, upstream DNS unreachable, corporate proxy required | `sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward`; restart `dockerd`; test `ping 1.1.1.1` versus `ping example.com` |
| Small requests work, large transfers or TLS handshakes hang | MTU mismatch (VPN, overlay, cloud) | `ping -M do -s 1472 <target>`; lower the network MTU |
| Some internal hosts unreachable after Docker starts | Docker subnet overlaps a LAN or VPN route | `ip route`; change `bip` and `default-address-pools` |
| `localhost:5432` fails from another container | `localhost` is the container itself | Use the service or container name |

For daemon-level diagnostics and deeper packet analysis, see [Inspecting Network Issues](#inspecting-network-issues).

**Key takeaways**

- Diagnose from the inside out: listening socket, shared network, DNS, TCP reachability, publishing, firewall and MTU.
- Attach `nicolaka/netshoot` with `--network container:<name>` to debug any container without modifying its image.
- `Connection refused` means "reached the host, nothing listening"; a timeout points to filtering, isolation, or routing.
- Between containers, use names and **container** ports; published host ports and `localhost` are for the outside and the container itself.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Start a Python HTTP server bound to `127.0.0.1` inside a container on a user-defined network, try to reach it from another container, and use `netshoot` to diagnose and fix it.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Ask a colleague (or write a script) to break a working two-container setup in one of three ways: different networks, a `DOCKER-USER` drop rule, or a lowered MTU on one network. Diagnose each case using only the step-by-step method, and note which step revealed the cause.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A containerized service intermittently fails to reach an external API with timeouts, while other containers on the same host are fine. How would you investigate?" *Hint:* compare the networks and DNS settings of the affected containers, capture traffic on the container's veth, and consider conntrack table exhaustion, source port exhaustion (SNAT), and DNS caching.

---

<a id="8-docker-compose"></a>
## 8. Docker Compose

Real applications are rarely one container: a typical stack has a web server, an API, a database, a cache, and a background worker, each with its own image, ports, volumes, networks, and environment. Docker Compose lets you describe that whole stack in one declarative YAML file and manage it as a unit with a handful of commands. This chapter covers the file format, how each `docker run` option maps to Compose, the features that make one file serve many environments, and the workflows (development, testing, multi-service deployments) where Compose is the everyday tool.

<a id="81-compose-fundamentals"></a>
### 8.1 Compose Fundamentals

This section explains what Compose is, how it is installed and run, how a Compose file is organized, and the commands that manage an application's lifecycle.

#### What Is Docker Compose

**The problem.** Starting a three-tier application by hand means typing a long sequence of commands, in the right order, with exactly the right options:

```bash
docker network create shop
docker volume create shop-db
docker run -d --name db  --network shop -v shop-db:/var/lib/postgresql/data \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret postgres:17
docker run -d --name api --network shop -e DATABASE_URL=postgres://postgres:secret@db/postgres \
  shop/api:1.4
docker run -d --name web --network shop -p 8080:80 shop/web:1.4
```

The commands are easy to get wrong, hard to share, and leave no record of what the "correct" setup is. Tearing the stack down requires another sequence in reverse. Changing one option means remembering which container to recreate.

**The solution.** **Docker Compose** is a tool for defining and running multi-container applications. You describe the desired state (services, networks, volumes, configuration) in a YAML file, usually `compose.yaml`, and Compose talks to the Docker Engine API to make reality match that description.

**Analogy.** A `docker run` command is like giving a builder verbal instructions one wall at a time. A Compose file is the architectural blueprint: anyone can read it, it lives in version control, and the builder can construct the whole house (or rebuild one room) from it.

The same stack as above, expressed declaratively:

```yaml
# compose.yaml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
    volumes:
      - db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data   # named volume declared below

  api:
    image: shop/api:1.4
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:secret@db/postgres   # "db" resolves via Compose DNS
    depends_on:
      - db

  web:
    image: shop/web:1.4
    ports:
      - "8080:80"
    depends_on:
      - api

volumes:
  db-data:
```

```bash
docker compose up -d      # create network, volume, and all three containers
docker compose down       # stop and remove containers and the network (volume is kept)
```

**Key ideas**

| Concept | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Project** | One application instance managed by Compose. Named after the directory by default; all its resources share the project name as a prefix and carry a `com.docker.compose.project` label. |
| **Service** | A named definition of how to run one component (image, ports, environment...). Compose creates one or more containers from it. |
| **Desired state** | The Compose file says *what* should exist; Compose computes the create/recreate/remove actions. |
| **Idempotency** | Running `docker compose up` again changes nothing if the file did not change. If one service's configuration changed, only that service's containers are recreated. |

**What Compose is (and is not)**

```text
   compose.yaml  --->  docker compose (CLI plugin)  --->  Docker Engine API  --->  containers,
   (desired state)     computes the diff, orders          (same API as            networks,
                       operations by dependencies          docker run)             volumes
```

- Compose is a **client**. It has no daemon of its own; it creates ordinary containers, networks, and volumes that you can also see with `docker ps`, `docker network ls`, and `docker volume ls`.
- Compose targets **one Docker host** (or whatever host the current context points to). It does not schedule containers across machines, reschedule after a node failure, or perform rolling updates. That is the job of orchestrators such as Swarm and Kubernetes (Chapter 14).
- The file format is the open **Compose Specification**, also implemented by `podman compose`, `nerdctl compose`, and Swarm stacks (with differences).

**Typical uses**

| Use case | Why Compose fits |
|---|---|
| Local development | One command starts the app plus its databases and queues |
| Automated tests / CI | Reproducible, disposable environments per test run |
| Demos and onboarding | `git clone && docker compose up` is the whole setup guide |
| Single-host production | Small apps, internal tools, home servers, edge devices |

**Key takeaways**

- Compose turns a sequence of imperative `docker` commands into one declarative, version-controlled YAML file.
- A **project** groups **services**, networks, and volumes; resource names are prefixed with the project name.
- Compose is a client of the Engine API, not a separate runtime; everything it creates is a normal Docker object.
- It manages a single host; multi-node scheduling and self-healing belong to orchestrators.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Translate three `docker run` commands you have used before (with ports, a volume, and environment variables) into one `compose.yaml`, start it with `docker compose up -d`, and confirm with `docker ps` that the containers are ordinary Docker containers with project labels.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Run `docker compose up -d` twice in a row, then change one service's environment variable and run it again. Observe which containers are recreated and explain why the others are left untouched.
> 3. **Interview question:** "When would you choose Compose over Kubernetes for running an application in production, and when would that choice become a problem?" *Hint:* think about the number of hosts, failure handling, rolling updates, and operational complexity.

#### Compose V2 Plugin

**A short history.** The original Compose (now called **Compose V1**) was a separate Python program invoked as `docker-compose` (with a hyphen). It had its own release cycle, its own dependencies, and occasionally lagged behind Engine features. **Compose V2** is a rewrite in Go, shipped as a **Docker CLI plugin** and invoked as `docker compose` (with a space). V1 reached end of life in mid-2023 and no longer receives updates; all current Docker installations use V2.

**How CLI plugins work.** When you type `docker compose`, the Docker CLI looks for an executable named `docker-compose` in its plugin directories and runs it, passing along the global configuration (current context, TLS settings, config file). This is why Compose automatically follows `docker context use`.

```text
   docker compose up
      |
      v
   docker CLI ---- finds plugin ----> ~/.docker/cli-plugins/docker-compose          (per user)
                                      /usr/local/lib/docker/cli-plugins/            (system)
                                      /usr/libexec/docker/cli-plugins/              (packages)
                                          |
                                          v
                                      Compose talks to the daemon of the current context
```

**V1 vs V2 differences that still matter**

| Aspect | Compose V1 | Compose V2 |
|---|---|---|
| Command | `docker-compose` | `docker compose` |
| Language / distribution | Python, standalone binary or pip | Go, CLI plugin |
| Container names | `project_web_1` (underscores) | `project-web-1` (hyphens, valid DNS names) |
| `version:` key in the file | Required to select a file format | Obsolete; ignored with a warning |
| File format | Versions 2.x and 3.x | The unified Compose Specification |
| BuildKit | Optional | Always used (builds go through Buildx) |
| Status | End of life (2023) | Actively maintained |

The container-name change matters for scripts that parse `docker ps` output or hard-code names such as `myapp_db_1`; prefer `docker compose ps` or label filters instead.

**Installing and checking**

```bash
# Docker Desktop: included. Linux with Docker's repository:
sudo apt-get install docker-compose-plugin      # or: sudo dnf install docker-compose-plugin

docker compose version
# Docker Compose version v2.40.0

# Manual install for a single user (pick the right release and architecture)
mkdir -p ~/.docker/cli-plugins
curl -SL https://github.com/docker/compose/releases/download/v2.40.0/docker-compose-linux-x86_64 \
  -o ~/.docker/cli-plugins/docker-compose
chmod +x ~/.docker/cli-plugins/docker-compose

# Old scripts still call "docker-compose"? Prefer updating them; as a stopgap, a small wrapper works:
# printf '#!/bin/sh\nexec docker compose "$@"\n' | sudo tee /usr/local/bin/docker-compose && sudo chmod +x $_
```

**Key takeaways**

- Use `docker compose` (V2, Go, CLI plugin); `docker-compose` (V1, Python) is end of life.
- As a CLI plugin, Compose respects Docker contexts and CLI configuration automatically.
- V2 names containers `project-service-N` with hyphens; avoid hard-coding container names in scripts.
- The top-level `version:` key is obsolete and should be removed from files.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run `docker compose version` and `docker info --format '{{json .ClientInfo.Plugins}}'` (or `docker info` and read the plugin list) to find where the Compose plugin is installed on your machine.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Take an old `docker-compose.yml` with `version: "3.8"`, run it with `docker compose config`, note the warning, remove the key, and check that the rendered configuration is identical.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A CI pipeline broke after an upgrade because a script ran `docker exec myapp_db_1 ...`. What changed and how would you make the script robust?" *Hint:* compare V1 and V2 naming, then look at `docker compose exec` and label-based filters.

#### compose.yaml Structure

**Why a fixed structure.** A Compose file describes several kinds of resources: the containers to run, the networks connecting them, the volumes storing their data, and the configuration and secrets they consume. Grouping each kind under its own top-level key keeps the file readable and lets services refer to shared resources by name.

**File discovery.** Compose looks in the current directory (and then parent directories) for the first of these names:

| Priority | File name | Note |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `compose.yaml` | Canonical name |
| 2 | `compose.yml` | |
| 3 | `docker-compose.yaml` | Legacy name, still supported |
| 4 | `docker-compose.yml` | Legacy name, still supported |

If a `compose.override.yaml` (or `docker-compose.override.yml`) exists next to it, it is merged automatically (see [Multiple Compose Files and Overrides](#multiple-compose-files-and-overrides)). Use `-f <file>` to choose files explicitly.

**Top-level elements**

```yaml
name: shop                    # project name (optional; default: directory name)

include:                      # pull in other Compose files (8.3)
  - ./monitoring/compose.yaml

services:                     # REQUIRED in practice: the containers to run
  api:
    image: shop/api:1.4

networks:                     # custom networks (a "default" network is created if omitted)
  backend:

volumes:                      # named volumes
  db-data:

configs:                      # non-sensitive configuration files mounted into services
  nginx-conf:
    file: ./nginx.conf

secrets:                      # sensitive data mounted under /run/secrets
  db-password:
    file: ./secrets/db-password.txt

x-common: &common             # extension field: ignored by Compose, used for YAML reuse
  restart: unless-stopped
```

| Element | Purpose | Covered in |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | Project name | Below |
| `services` | Container definitions | [Services](#services) |
| `networks` | Networks services attach to | [Networks in Compose](#networks-in-compose) |
| `volumes` | Named volumes | [Volumes in Compose](#volumes-in-compose) |
| `configs`, `secrets` | Files injected into containers | [Secrets and Configs in Compose](#secrets-and-configs-in-compose) |
| `include` | Compose files to import | [Extends and Include](#extends-and-include) |
| `x-*` | Reusable fragments | Below |
| `version` | Obsolete | Remove it |

**The project name.** It determines resource names (`shop-api-1`, `shop_default`, `shop_db-data`) and therefore which containers belong to which project. Precedence, highest first: `-p` flag, `COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME` environment variable, top-level `name:`, the project directory's name. Two checkouts of the same repository in directories with the same name will collide unless one sets a different project name.

**Reuse with YAML anchors and extension fields.** YAML **anchors** (`&name`) label a node, **aliases** (`*name`) reuse it, and the **merge key** (`<<:`) copies a mapping's keys into another mapping. Compose ignores any top-level key starting with `x-`, which makes it a safe place to store anchored fragments.

```yaml
x-logging: &default-logging           # anchor a fragment
  driver: json-file
  options:
    max-size: "10m"
    max-file: "3"

x-app: &app-defaults
  restart: unless-stopped
  logging: *default-logging           # alias: reuse the whole fragment
  environment:
    TZ: Europe/Rome

services:
  api:
    <<: *app-defaults                 # merge all keys of x-app into this service
    image: shop/api:1.4
  worker:
    <<: *app-defaults
    image: shop/api:1.4
    command: ["python", "-m", "worker"]
    environment:                      # CAUTION: replaces the whole merged "environment" map
      TZ: Europe/Rome
      QUEUE: default
```

The merge key is shallow: a key defined locally replaces the merged one entirely (it is not deep-merged). Run `docker compose config` to see the fully resolved file.

**YAML pitfalls**

| Pitfall | Example | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Sexagesimal (base-60) numbers in YAML 1.1 parsers | `- 22:22` may parse as an integer | Always quote ports: `"22:22"` |
| Booleans in YAML 1.1 tools | `restart: no` may be read as `false` | `restart: "no"` |
| Tabs | Indentation with tabs | Spaces only |
| `$` in values | `password: pa$word` is interpolated | Escape as `$$` (see [Variable Interpolation](#variable-interpolation)) |

**Key takeaways**

- Compose discovers `compose.yaml` automatically and merges `compose.override.yaml` if present.
- Top-level keys: `name`, `services`, `networks`, `volumes`, `configs`, `secrets`, `include`, and `x-*` extensions; `version` is obsolete.
- The project name prefixes every resource; set it with `-p`, `COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME`, or `name:`.
- Use `x-` fields with anchors and aliases for reuse, remembering that `<<:` merges are shallow.
- `docker compose config` prints the final, resolved model and catches most syntax mistakes.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Write a `compose.yaml` with two services, one named volume, and one custom network. Run `docker compose config` and identify where Compose added defaults you did not write.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Refactor three services that share `restart`, `logging`, and `labels` settings into an `x-` fragment with anchors. Verify with `docker compose config` that the output matches the original file.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Two developers clone the same repository into `~/work/app` and `~/old/app` on the same machine and run `docker compose up`. What happens, and how do you prevent it?" *Hint:* consider how the default project name is derived and what resources it prefixes.

#### Services

**What a service is.** A **service** is a named template for running one component of the application. It specifies the image (or how to build it) and everything you would otherwise pass to `docker run`. Compose creates one container per **replica** of the service (one by default) and names it `<project>-<service>-<index>`. Other services reach it by its service name.

**Analogy.** A service is a job description ("API server: uses this image, listens on 8000, needs these settings"); containers are the employees hired to fill it. You can hire more of them (scale) or replace them (recreate) without rewriting the description.

**Mapping `docker run` to a service**

| `docker run` option | Service key |
|---|---|
| `IMAGE` | `image:` |
| `--name` | `container_name:` (avoid; prevents scaling) |
| `COMMAND`, `--entrypoint` | `command:`, `entrypoint:` |
| `-p` | `ports:` |
| `-e`, `--env-file` | `environment:`, `env_file:` |
| `-v`, `--mount` | `volumes:` |
| `--network`, `--network-alias` | `networks:` |
| `--restart` | `restart:` |
| `-u`, `-w`, `-h` | `user:`, `working_dir:`, `hostname:` |
| `--init` | `init: true` |
| `--read-only`, `--tmpfs` | `read_only: true`, `tmpfs:` |
| `--cap-drop`, `--cap-add` | `cap_drop:`, `cap_add:` |
| `--memory`, `--cpus` | `deploy.resources.limits.memory`, `deploy.resources.limits.cpus` (or `mem_limit`, `cpus`) |
| `--health-cmd` ... | `healthcheck:` |
| `--stop-timeout`, `--stop-signal` | `stop_grace_period:`, `stop_signal:` |
| `-l` | `labels:` |
| `--log-driver`, `--log-opt` | `logging:` |

**Example: a well-defined service**

```yaml
services:
  api:
    image: ghcr.io/acme/shop-api:1.4.2       # pin a version, never rely on "latest"
    command: ["gunicorn", "app:create_app()", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"]   # exec form: no shell
    restart: unless-stopped                   # come back after crashes and daemon restarts
    init: true                                # tiny init as PID 1: reaps zombies, forwards signals
    user: "10001:10001"                       # run as an unprivileged user
    read_only: true                           # immutable root filesystem...
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp                                  # ...with a writable scratch area
    cap_drop: [ALL]
    stop_grace_period: 20s                    # time between SIGTERM and SIGKILL on stop
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "1.5"
          memory: 512M
    labels:
      com.acme.team: payments
```

**`command` and `entrypoint` forms.** Both accept a string (run through a shell parser, not a shell; no pipes or variables expanded at runtime) or a list (exec form, recommended). `command` replaces the image's `CMD`; `entrypoint` replaces the image's `ENTRYPOINT` and also clears its default `CMD`.

```yaml
command: npm run dev                          # string: split into ["npm", "run", "dev"]
command: ["sh", "-c", "echo $$HOSTNAME && exec node server.js"]   # need a shell? ask for one; $$ escapes Compose interpolation
```

**Restart policies**

| Value | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `"no"` (default) | Never restart. Quote it so no YAML tool reads it as a boolean. |
| `always` | Always restart; a manually stopped container stays stopped until the daemon restarts, then starts again |
| `on-failure[:N]` | Restart only on non-zero exit, optionally at most N times |
| `unless-stopped` | Like `always`, but not if you stopped it explicitly; a common choice for long-running services |

**Why avoid `container_name`.** A fixed name must be unique on the whole host, so the service cannot be scaled and two projects (say, two branches) cannot run side by side. Other services should use the service name for DNS anyway.

**Key takeaways**

- A service is a template; Compose creates containers named `<project>-<service>-<index>` from it.
- Nearly every `docker run` flag has an equivalent service key.
- Prefer exec-form lists for `command`/`entrypoint`, pinned image tags, `restart: unless-stopped`, and `init: true` for long-running processes.
- Avoid `container_name`; address services by service name.
- Quote values that YAML could misinterpret, such as `restart: "no"` and port mappings.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Convert this command into a service and run it: `docker run -d --name cache --restart unless-stopped -p 6379:6379 --memory 256m redis:7-alpine redis-server --appendonly yes`.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Harden a service with `read_only`, `tmpfs`, `cap_drop: [ALL]`, and a non-root `user`. Run it, find what breaks (if anything), and fix it with the minimum extra permissions.
> 3. **Interview question:** "What is the difference between overriding `command` and `entrypoint` in a Compose service, and when would overriding the entrypoint break an official image?" *Hint:* think about wrapper scripts like `docker-entrypoint.sh` that initialize state before running `CMD`.

#### Compose CLI Commands

**The lifecycle at a glance.** Compose commands operate on a project (the current directory's by default) and optionally on specific services. Most mirror a familiar `docker` command, but act on all matching containers at once.

```text
                 docker compose up -d
   compose.yaml ----------------------> [ created + running ]
                                          |      ^
                     docker compose stop  |      |  docker compose start
                                          v      |
                                        [ stopped ]
                                          |
                     docker compose down  v      (also removes networks; -v removes volumes)
                                        [ removed ]
```

**Global options** (placed before the subcommand)

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `-f, --file` | Compose file(s) to use; repeatable |
| `-p, --project-name` | Project name |
| `--project-directory` | Base directory for relative paths and `.env` |
| `--profile` | Enable a profile; repeatable |
| `--env-file` | Alternative file(s) for interpolation variables |

**Core commands**

| Command | What it does | Useful flags |
|---|---|---|
| `up` | Create/recreate and start services (builds or pulls images if needed) | `-d`, `--build`, `--wait`, `--force-recreate`, `--no-deps`, `--remove-orphans`, `--scale svc=N`, `--watch` |
| `down` | Stop and remove containers and networks | `-v` (also volumes), `--rmi local\|all`, `--remove-orphans` |
| `ps` | List the project's containers | `-a`, `--services`, `--format json` |
| `logs` | Show aggregated, color-prefixed logs | `-f`, `--tail N`, `--since 10m`, `-t` |
| `exec` | Run a command in a **running** container | `-u`, `-w`, `-e`, `--index N`, `-T` (no TTY) |
| `run` | Start a **new one-off** container for a service | `--rm`, `--service-ports`, `--no-deps`, `-e`, `--entrypoint` |
| `build` | Build images for services with `build:` | `--no-cache`, `--pull`, `--build-arg` |
| `pull` / `push` | Pull or push service images | `--ignore-pull-failures` |
| `config` | Validate and print the resolved model | `--services`, `--volumes`, `--profiles`, `--format json`, `-q` |
| `start` / `stop` / `restart` | Lifecycle of existing containers | `-t` (timeout) |
| `kill`, `pause`, `unpause`, `rm` | Same as the `docker` equivalents, per service | |
| `top`, `port`, `images`, `events`, `cp` | Inspection and file copy | |
| `ls` | List all Compose projects on the host | `-a` |
| `watch` | Sync/rebuild on file changes (8.3) | `--no-up` |
| `scale` | Change replica counts | |
| `wait` | Block until services' containers exit | |

**`exec` vs `run`.** This distinction trips up many newcomers:

| | `docker compose exec api sh` | `docker compose run --rm api sh` |
|---|---|---|
| Container | The existing running container | A brand-new container from the service definition |
| Requires service running | Yes | No (starts dependencies unless `--no-deps`) |
| Published `ports:` | n/a | Not published unless `--service-ports` |
| Typical use | Inspect live state, run a quick admin command | Migrations, tests, one-off scripts, a REPL |

**A typical session**

```bash
docker compose up -d --build --wait     # build changed images, start everything, wait until healthy
docker compose ps
# NAME          IMAGE          COMMAND                  SERVICE   STATUS                   PORTS
# shop-api-1    shop-api       "gunicorn app:create…"   api       Up 12 seconds (healthy)  8000/tcp
# shop-db-1     postgres:17    "docker-entrypoint.s…"   db        Up 18 seconds (healthy)  5432/tcp
# shop-web-1    nginx:1.27     "/docker-entrypoint.…"   web       Up 11 seconds            0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp

docker compose logs -f --tail 50 api    # follow one service's logs
docker compose exec db psql -U postgres # shell into the running database
docker compose run --rm api flask db upgrade   # one-off migration in a fresh container

docker compose up -d --no-deps api      # recreate only "api" after changing its config
docker compose config --services        # list service names (handy in scripts)
docker compose ls                       # every Compose project on this host

docker compose down --remove-orphans    # remove containers + networks; keep volumes
# docker compose down -v                # ALSO deletes named volumes: data loss!
```

**How `up` decides what to recreate.** Compose stores a hash of each service's resolved configuration in the container label `com.docker.compose.config-hash`. On `up`, it compares hashes: unchanged services are left running, changed ones are recreated, and services removed from the file become **orphans** (warned about, removed with `--remove-orphans`). A changed image tag counts as a change; a new image pushed under the *same* tag does not, so run `docker compose pull` first (or `up --pull always`).

**Key takeaways**

- `up -d` converges the project to the file; `down` removes containers and networks; `down -v` also deletes volumes.
- `exec` enters a running container; `run` creates a new one-off container (without published ports by default).
- `up --wait` blocks until services are running and healthy, which is ideal for scripts and CI.
- Only services whose configuration hash changed are recreated; pull first to pick up new images under the same tag.
- `config` is the first debugging tool: it shows exactly what Compose will do.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Start a two-service project, then use `ps`, `logs -f`, `exec`, `stop`, `start`, and `down` in turn, noting what each does to the containers and the network.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Use `docker compose run --rm` to execute a database migration, then compare `docker ps -a` before and after with and without `--rm`. Repeat with `--service-ports` and check which ports are published.
> 3. **Interview question:** "You pushed a fixed image under the same tag and ran `docker compose up -d` on the server, but the bug is still there. Why?" *Hint:* consider what Compose compares to decide whether a container must be recreated, and when it pulls images.

<a id="82-configuring-services"></a>
### 8.2 Configuring Services

This section covers the service keys you will write most often: where the image comes from, how traffic reaches the service, how it is configured, where it stores data, which networks it joins, and how startup is coordinated with health checks.

#### build vs image

**Two ways to get an image.** A service needs an image. Either it already exists in a registry (an official database, a release of your own app) and Compose should **pull** it, or it must be **built** from source in the repository. `image:` and `build:` express these two cases, and combining them expresses a third: "build it, and give the result this name".

**The three combinations**

| Keys present | What Compose does | Resulting image name | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `image` only | Pulls the image if it is not present locally | The given name | Third-party services, deployments of released versions |
| `build` only | Builds from the context | `<project>-<service>` (for example `shop-api`) | Local-only development images |
| `image` + `build` | Uses a local image with that name if present; otherwise tries to pull it and builds if the pull fails. `docker compose build` always builds and tags it with that name | The given name | Build locally, then `docker compose push` to a registry |

```yaml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:17.2                     # pull only

  api:
    build: ./api                             # short form: just the context directory

  web:
    image: ghcr.io/acme/shop-web:${TAG:-dev} # name/tag for the built image
    build:
      context: ./web                         # files sent to the builder
      dockerfile: docker/Dockerfile          # relative to the context
      target: runtime                        # stop at this multi-stage target
      args:                                  # Dockerfile ARG values
        NODE_VERSION: "22"
      cache_from:
        - type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/acme/shop-web:buildcache
      platforms: [linux/amd64, linux/arm64]  # multi-platform (needs a capable builder)
      secrets:
        - npm_token                          # build secret, see 8.4
      additional_contexts:
        shared: ../shared                    # usable as COPY --from=shared ...
    pull_policy: build                       # always build on "up", never pull
```

**Build keys at a glance**

| Key | Equivalent `docker build` option |
|---|---|
| `context` | Positional context (path or Git URL) |
| `dockerfile` / `dockerfile_inline` | `-f` / Dockerfile content embedded in YAML |
| `args` | `--build-arg` |
| `target` | `--target` |
| `cache_from` / `cache_to` | `--cache-from` / `--cache-to` |
| `ssh`, `secrets` | `--ssh`, `--secret` |
| `platforms` | `--platform` |
| `tags`, `labels` | `-t` (extra tags), `--label` |
| `no_cache`, `pull` | `--no-cache`, `--pull` |

**When does Compose rebuild?** `docker compose up` does **not** rebuild an image that already exists just because source files changed; it only builds missing images. Use `docker compose up --build` (or `docker compose build` first) after code changes, or let [Compose Watch](#compose-watch-for-development) do it.

**`pull_policy` values**

| Value | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `missing` (default) | Pull only if the image is not available locally |
| `always` | Pull on every `up` |
| `never` | Never pull; fail if absent |
| `build` | Always build (requires `build:`) |
| `daily`, `weekly`, `every_<duration>` | Pull again if the local copy is older than that |

**Pattern: one file, two sources.** In development, build from source; in production, pull a released tag. The base file holds `image:` and an override adds `build:` (see [Multiple Compose Files and Overrides](#multiple-compose-files-and-overrides)):

```yaml
# compose.yaml (used everywhere)
services:
  api:
    image: ghcr.io/acme/shop-api:${TAG:-latest}

# compose.override.yaml (loaded automatically on dev machines, absent on servers)
services:
  api:
    build:
      context: ./api
      target: dev
```

**Key takeaways**

- `image` alone pulls; `build` alone builds and names the image `<project>-<service>`; both together build and tag with the `image` name.
- `build` accepts most `docker build` options: `context`, `dockerfile`, `args`, `target`, caches, secrets, SSH, platforms.
- `up` does not rebuild existing images; use `up --build`, `pull_policy: build`, or Compose Watch.
- Splitting `image` (base file) and `build` (dev override) lets one project build in development and pull in production.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Create a service with only `build: .`, run `docker compose up -d`, and find the resulting image name with `docker compose images`. Then add `image: myapp:dev` and repeat.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Use a multi-stage Dockerfile with `dev` and `runtime` targets. Configure Compose so that `docker compose up` builds `dev` locally and `docker compose -f compose.yaml up` (no override) pulls a released image.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A developer edits source code, runs `docker compose up -d`, and sees the old behavior. Explain why and list three ways to fix the workflow." *Hint:* consider when Compose builds images, `--build`, bind mounts, and file syncing.

#### Ports and Expose

**Who needs to reach the service?** There are two different audiences. **Other services in the project** reach each other over the project network by service name and container port; no publishing is needed. **Clients outside Docker** (your browser, another machine) need a port on the host forwarded into the container. `ports:` serves the second audience; `expose:` is documentation for the first.

```text
   Browser ---> host:8080 ---(ports: "8080:80")---> web:80
                                                     |
                                    project network  |  api:8000  (no "ports" needed)
                                                     v
                                                    api ---------> db:5432 (no "ports" needed)
```

**Short syntax.** `[HOST_IP:][HOST_PORT:]CONTAINER_PORT[/PROTOCOL]`, always quoted:

```yaml
services:
  web:
    image: nginx:1.27-alpine
    ports:
      - "8080:80"                  # all host interfaces, port 8080 -> container 80
      - "127.0.0.1:8443:443"       # only reachable from the host itself
      - "53:53/udp"                # UDP
      - "9000-9002:9000-9002"      # range
      - "80"                       # random host port -> container 80 (see "docker compose port")
```

**Long syntax.** More explicit and easier to merge or generate:

```yaml
    ports:
      - name: http                 # optional label
        target: 80                 # container port
        published: "8080"          # host port (string allows ranges like "8080-8081")
        host_ip: 127.0.0.1
        protocol: tcp
        app_protocol: http         # informational hint
        mode: host                 # "host" (direct) or "ingress" (Swarm routing mesh)
```

**`expose`.** Lists container ports that the service listens on, without publishing them on the host. It adds metadata (visible in `docker inspect`) but does **not** restrict anything: on a user-defined network, every port a container listens on is already reachable by other containers. Think of it as a comment the tooling can read.

```yaml
  api:
    build: ./api
    expose:
      - "8000"                     # documented for other services; not on the host
```

**Comparison**

| | `ports` | `expose` |
|---|---|---|
| Reachable from the host / other machines | Yes | No |
| Reachable from other services on the network | Yes (via the container port) | Yes (it always was) |
| Equivalent `docker run` flag | `-p` | `--expose` |
| Affects scaling | A fixed host port can be bound by only one replica | No |

**Rules of thumb**

- Publish only what humans or external systems need. Databases and internal APIs usually need no `ports` in production.
- In development, bind tools to localhost: `"127.0.0.1:5432:5432"`. Without a host IP, a published port listens on all interfaces, and on Linux Docker's NAT rules take effect before host firewalls such as `ufw` (see [iptables and Docker](#iptables-and-docker) in Chapter 7).
- Services always talk to each other on the **container** port (`db:5432`), never the published host port.

```bash
docker compose port web 80       # which host port maps to web:80?
# 0.0.0.0:8080
docker compose ps --format '{{.Service}} {{.Ports}}'
```

**Key takeaways**

- `ports` publishes container ports on the host; `expose` only documents ports for other services.
- Inter-service traffic uses service names and container ports, never published ports.
- Quote port mappings and bind development-only ports to `127.0.0.1`.
- A fixed host port prevents running more than one replica of a service.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run nginx with `"8080:80"`, then change it to `"127.0.0.1:8080:80"` and verify from another machine (or another network interface) that it is no longer reachable.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Remove all `ports` from an API service, add `expose: ["8000"]`, and prove with `docker compose exec web wget -qO- http://api:8000` that another service can still reach it. Then remove `expose` and repeat.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your team published PostgreSQL with `ports: ['5432:5432']` on a cloud VM protected by `ufw`, and the database was found by an internet scanner. How did this happen?" *Hint:* look at where Docker inserts its NAT and filter rules relative to the host firewall's chains.

#### Environment and env_file

**Why environment variables.** Following the twelve-factor approach, the same image should run in development, staging, and production; only the configuration differs. Environment variables are the simplest channel for that configuration: database URLs, log levels, feature flags. Compose offers two ways to set them in a container: inline with `environment:` and from files with `env_file:`.

**`environment`: map or list syntax**

```yaml
services:
  api:
    image: shop/api:1.4
    environment:                 # map syntax (preferred: one key per line, easy to merge)
      LOG_LEVEL: info
      WORKERS: "4"               # quote numbers and booleans to keep them strings
      FEATURE_X: "true"
      SENTRY_DSN:                # no value: passed through from the shell running compose (unset if absent)

  worker:
    image: shop/api:1.4
    environment:                 # list syntax (equivalent)
      - LOG_LEVEL=debug
      - SENTRY_DSN               # pass-through, same as above
```

**`env_file`: load variables from files**

```yaml
services:
  api:
    env_file:
      - ./config/common.env      # loaded first
      - path: ./config/local.env # later files override earlier ones
        required: false          # do not fail if the file is missing (Compose 2.24+)
```

```bash
# config/common.env
LOG_LEVEL=info
DATABASE_URL="postgres://app@db:5432/app"   # quotes are removed by Compose's parser
CACHE_URL=redis://cache:6379/${REDIS_DB:-0} # interpolation is supported in env_file values
# comments and blank lines are ignored
```

Unlike `docker run --env-file`, Compose's parser understands quotes and `${VAR}` expansion inside `env_file` values.

**Two different "env files": the crucial distinction**

| | `.env` in the project directory | `env_file:` in a service |
|---|---|---|
| Read by | Compose itself, when parsing `compose.yaml` | Compose, to set variables **inside the container** |
| Purpose | Values for `${VAR}` [interpolation](#variable-interpolation) in the YAML | Container runtime configuration |
| Reaches the container? | **No**, unless referenced, e.g. `LOG_LEVEL: ${LOG_LEVEL}` | **Yes**, every variable in the file |
| Selected with | Automatic, or `--env-file` on the CLI | The `env_file:` key |

```text
   .env  ---(interpolation)--->  compose.yaml  ---(environment / env_file)--->  container env
   shell ---(interpolation)--->      ^
                                     |  env_file: app.env  ------------------->  container env
```

**Precedence inside the container** (highest wins)

| Rank | Source |
|---|---|
| 1 | `docker compose run -e KEY=value` |
| 2 | `environment:` in the service |
| 3 | `env_file:` (later files override earlier ones) |
| 4 | `ENV` in the image's Dockerfile |

Values in ranks 2 and 3 may themselves be interpolated from the shell or `.env`.

**Verifying the result**

```bash
docker compose config --environment        # variables available for interpolation
docker compose config | sed -n '/api:/,/image:/p'   # resolved environment of "api"
docker compose exec api env | sort         # what the process actually sees
docker compose run --rm -e LOG_LEVEL=debug api env | grep LOG_LEVEL
# LOG_LEVEL=debug
```

**Secrets are not configuration.** Environment variables are visible in `docker inspect`, in `/proc/<pid>/environ`, in crash dumps, and are inherited by child processes. Use them for non-sensitive settings and prefer [Compose secrets](#secrets-and-configs-in-compose) for passwords and keys.

**Key takeaways**

- `environment:` sets variables inline; `env_file:` loads them from files; both end up in the container.
- The project's `.env` file feeds interpolation of the Compose file, not the container, unless a value references it.
- Precedence: `run -e` > `environment` > `env_file` > image `ENV`.
- A key without a value passes the variable through from the shell running Compose.
- Use `config --environment`, `config`, and `exec ... env` to see what is really set; keep secrets out of environment variables when possible.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Set `LOG_LEVEL` in the Dockerfile, in an `env_file`, and in `environment`, then print it in the container. Remove the sources one by one and record the value each time.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Put `DB_PASSWORD=secret` in `.env` but not in the service definition. Show that the container does not see it, then make it visible with interpolation and, separately, with `env_file: .env`, and explain the security implication of the second option.
> 3. **Interview question:** "What is the difference between the `.env` file and the `env_file` attribute in Compose, and why do people confuse them?" *Hint:* ask who reads each file and at which stage: parsing the YAML or creating the container.

#### Volumes in Compose

**Why declare storage in Compose.** Container filesystems are disposable; anything that must survive `docker compose up` recreating a container (database files, uploads) belongs in a **volume**, and anything you edit on the host and want to see live in the container (source code in development) belongs in a **bind mount**. Compose lets you declare both alongside the services that use them, and manages named volumes' lifecycle with the project. (Volume and bind-mount mechanics are covered in Chapter 6.)

**Short syntax.** `SOURCE:TARGET[:MODE]`. Compose decides the type from the source:

```yaml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:17
    volumes:
      - db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data         # name -> named volume (must be declared below)
      - ./initdb:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d:ro  # path (./, ../, /, ~) -> bind mount, read-only

  api:
    build: ./api
    volumes:
      - ./api/src:/app/src                       # bind mount for live code editing
      - /app/node_modules                        # target only -> anonymous volume (shields image content)

volumes:
  db-data:                                       # Compose creates "<project>_db-data"
```

Relative host paths are resolved from the **project directory** (normally the directory of the first Compose file), not the current shell directory, so the file works from wherever you run it.

**Long syntax.** Explicit fields and options the short form cannot express:

```yaml
    volumes:
      - type: volume
        source: db-data
        target: /var/lib/postgresql/data
        volume:
          nocopy: true            # do not pre-populate an empty volume from the image
          subpath: pg17           # mount only a subdirectory of the volume (Engine 26+)
      - type: bind
        source: ./config
        target: /etc/app
        read_only: true
        bind:
          create_host_path: false # fail if ./config is missing (short syntax silently creates it)
      - type: tmpfs
        target: /tmp
        tmpfs:
```
